issues.body:
## Summary

After an update on November 21, 2026 (Europe/Berlin), the user can no longer find the "On your computer" / "Auf deinem Computer" execution-location selector in ChatGPT Work on Windows. The user reports that selecting local execution had restored SSH access previously and still worked earlier the same morning, before the update. That workaround is now unavailable.

The user supplied an About ChatGPT screenshot confirming version **26.1117.41037**, labeled "Powered by Codex & OWL", with release date **November 20, 2026**. The user reports installing the update on November 21, 2026. The timing suggests a regression, but the update has not been independently established as the cause.

## Environment

- ChatGPT desktop / Work interface on Windows, German UI.
- User reports all relevant access/network settings are enabled.
- The supplied screenshot visibly shows the orange "Uneingeschränkter Zugriff" (Full access) control.
- The former location of the execution selector, at the lower right beneath the composer, is empty in the supplied screenshot. Full access is present; it is the execution-location selector that is missing in this report.
- Screenshots were inspected in the reporting conversation but are not attached to this issue.

## Observed behavior and diagnostics

PowerShell commands execute. Get-Location returned the configured project directory on an approved NAS share. This confirms shell execution and a configured working directory, not a full file-access or write test.

A read-only SSH test to an authorized private-LAN host was run repeatedly from the affected session (username/address redacted below):

```powershell
ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=6 -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes <user>@<private-LAN-host> hostname
```

The command tool returned exit code 1, with:

```text
Attempting to perform the InitializeDefaultDrives operation on the 'FileSystem' provider failed.
ssh: connect to host <private-LAN-host> port 22: Permission denied
```

The connection failed before authentication or remote command execution. The session's effective execution configuration reports restricted network access despite the visible Full access setting. The exact enforcing layer has not been identified; no claim is made that server credentials or host keys are faulty.

The user reports already fully restarting the app, with no recovery. No settings, SSH keys, host-key checks, or server configuration were changed during these diagnostics.

## Expected behavior

An authorized user should have a supported way to select local execution, or a clear replacement for the previous selector. The UI should accurately reflect the effective permissions, and explain why SSH is denied when Full access and network access are enabled.

## Impact

Existing infrastructure and development workflows requiring SSH to a private-LAN Docker host are blocked. The previously working local-execution workaround is no longer accessible.

## Related reports

- #60058 — related restricted-network/SSH behavior, with comments reporting that selecting local execution restored access.
- #61501 — missing permission controls and blocked SSH. This report differs: Full access remains visible, while the local/cloud execution selector is missing.
- #61120 — related Windows permission-selector/SSH report.

Please consolidate if appropriate. Is the missing execution-location selector intentional in the current rollout, and is there a supported recovery path or replacement control for affected users?

issues.title: Codex desktop resumed continuing chat with wrong workspace/cwd and AGENTS.md

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

issues.body:
## Summary
A continuing Codex desktop chat for `[WORK_PROJECT_REPO]` was resumed/routed with the wrong workspace context: `[PERSONAL_FOLDER]`.

The prompt was typed in an existing project chat, but the model context for the next turn loaded `cwd` and `AGENTS.md` from an unrelated personal folder. The assistant then attempted Git/repo operations in that unrelated folder before the mismatch was noticed.

## Environment
- App: Codex desktop
- App version: `26.519.5221.0`
- OS: Windows `10.0.26200.8457`
- Time observed: `2026-05-28 11:02 +08:00`

## Expected behavior
A continuing chat thread should preserve the original workspace binding and load the `cwd` / `AGENTS.md` associated with that thread's project.

If the app cannot safely restore the original workspace, it should warn the user or ask for confirmation before injecting a different workspace into the model context.

## Actual behavior
The continuing chat was presented to the model with:

- `cwd = [PERSONAL_FOLDER]`
- `AGENTS.md instructions for [PERSONAL_FOLDER]`

This did not match the ongoing conversation, which was about `[WORK_PROJECT_REPO]`.

## Impact
- Private local folder names can be exposed in model context and assistant replies.
- The assistant may run Git or filesystem commands in an unrelated workspace.
- The user can lose trust that a continuing project chat is still attached to the intended project.

## Privacy note
I am intentionally redacting local paths, repository names, and user-identifying folder names from this public report. I can provide sanitized logs or further details privately if needed.

## Mitigation attempted
I added a local global instruction telling Codex to verify that `cwd` matches the project implied by the conversation before running Git/filesystem/project commands. This is only a mitigation; the underlying issue appears to be in desktop thread/workspace routing or context restoration.

### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.171.0

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT subscription; tier not provided

### Which model were you using?

gpt-6.1-sol, high reasoning effort

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64 (native Windows)

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Windows Terminal 1.25.3131.0, PowerShell

### Codex doctor report

```json
Not attached. CLI version, OS, terminal version, and the relevant status-line configuration were checked locally.
```

### What issue are you seeing?

The context-used status line item intermittently disappears and reappears in the same conversation, although it is enabled and saved in config.toml.

Current relevant configuration:

```toml
[tui]
status_line = ["model-with-reasoning", "current-dir", "thread-name", "context-used", "weekly-limit"]
```

Observed footer states, with personal paths and the conversation title replaced by placeholders:

```text
Visible earlier:
GPT-6.1-Sol high · <cwd> · <thread name> · Context 52% used · weekly 29% left · 692K used

Missing later:
GPT-6.1-Sol high · <cwd> · <thread name> · weekly 29% left
```

The earlier state also had used-tokens enabled. I later removed used-tokens deliberately; its absence in the later state is expected. However, context-used remained enabled, and that item still disappeared.

The /statusline setup preview shows the selected context item, while the normal footer sometimes omits it. I have observed the behavior across multiple conversations. There is ample unused horizontal space in the terminal, and the weekly-limit item after context-used remains visible.

Local rollout records contain non-null token usage information even when the footer omits the context item. No error message explains the missing item.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Start Codex CLI 0.171.0 in Windows Terminal using PowerShell.
2. Enable context-used through /statusline and save. The configuration above is persisted.
3. Continue using the conversation over several turns and observe the footer.
4. The context usage item can appear, disappear, and later reappear. The selected item also appears in the setup preview when absent from the normal footer.

This is intermittent; I have not identified a reliable trigger. It is not limited to one conversation. The affected conversation originally started in the desktop app and was subsequently used in CLI; whether that matters is unknown.

### What is the expected behavior?

Once context usage data is available, keep the selected item visible and update it reliably. If the value becomes temporarily unavailable, show an explicit updating/unavailable state rather than silently removing it.

The setup preview and actual footer should make it clear when a displayed preview value is a placeholder rather than live usage data.

### Additional information

Observed on November 21, 2026 (Asia/Shanghai). Version 0.171.0 was also the latest npm release when checked during report preparation.

The report describes the visible behavior; the exact cause has not been established. Reopening the status-line configuration and saving the selection does not reliably resolve the issue.

Related but different reports found during search concern rate-limit fields (#14235, #36116), git-branch fields (#35979), or the whole status line disappearing while typing (#12881). In this case, context-used disappears while other configured fields remain visible.

issues.title: [Feedback] Codex persists with unproductive plans instead of clarifying intent, replanning, or stopping

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: model-behavior
labels.description: Issues related to behaviors exhibited by the model

issues.body:
## Summary

Firsthand feedback from a long-term, technically experienced GPT/Codex user who has moved much of their agentic development work to Claude Code because the difference in *useful work per token and per unit of human attention* feels dramatic.

This is **qualitative workflow feedback, not a benchmark claim**. The core complaint is not that Codex lacks coding power. It is that it can keep executing relentlessly without sufficiently reassessing whether it understands the objective or whether its current approach remains worthwhile.

## Observed behavior

- I initially tried establishing my exploratory development workflow with Codex, then used Claude Code in a similar Omarchy Linux / Herder agent-orchestration environment. The comparison is not simply that Claude inherited a mature environment from Codex.
- Codex is a capable **workhorse**: powerful, persistent, and willing to keep working. But it often behaves as if I should know and specify the entire solution before starting. In exploratory work, I *cannot* know the right specification until I uncover failures and constraints.
- When an approach fails or drifts from the real goal, Codex seems inclined to keep going, using time and tokens, rather than looking up, recognizing a dead end, and asking whether to change direction. Interrupting/reorienting the flow can feel unnecessarily difficult.
- In my experience, Claude Code more often figures out what I am actually trying to achieve *before* committing substantial work, anticipates likely failure points, and is willing to stop and explain a blocker or propose a better path. The result feels like vastly more useful work with much less intervention and token consumption.
- I also orchestrate agents across systems, sometimes invoking Claude from Codex and Codex from Claude. In that workflow, involving Codex often feels like it reduces overall throughput even while producing plenty of activity.

## Why this matters

An agent can be technically strong yet economically inferior if it spends its budget on an approach the user would have redirected. The important metric for this user is **completed, relevant work per token and per minute of user attention**, not benchmark scores or how long the agent can keep running.

This is a significant enough difference that a user with nearly four years of investment in ChatGPT/GPT now sees substantially less reason to use Codex.

## Requested product behavior

1. **Clarify intent before costly execution.** When the goal is underspecified, infer the likely objective, surface key assumptions, and ask only consequential questions.
2. **Anticipate and report likely failure modes.** Before deep execution, state what could invalidate the proposed direction.
3. **Use outcome-based checkpoints.** Detect repeated failures, low progress against the actual goal, or accumulating speculative work, and propose **continue / diagnose / replan / stop**.
4. **Make redirection inexpensive.** Support easy human course correction without treating the initial instructions as immutable.
5. **Optimize for useful work per quota.** Evaluate unnecessary iteration, resource use, and human supervision, not merely task activity or persistence.

## Additional feedback about feedback

I tried explaining this in a ChatGPT conversation and explicitly asked for it to be passed to developers. The assistant could discuss and rephrase my observations but said it had no direct channel to submit them. For an experienced user giving detailed, comparative product feedback, that makes the feedback experience feel unresponsive and the user's expertise feel unvalued. There should be a clearer, low-friction way to route such feedback to the relevant product team with visible acknowledgement that it was received.

Related ideas already raised in this repository include **#52564** (independent oversight and stop/replan checkpoints) and **#45383** (usage waste from context/recovery). This report emphasizes a different first-person failure mode: **understanding the user's evolving intent and proactively abandoning unproductive execution**.

*No project files, private logs, quantitative token measurements, or controlled benchmark data are included; these are qualitative comparative observations.*

issues.title: [Windows Desktop] Scheduled tasks wake, acknowledge or report status, then stop without completing assigned work

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app

issues.body:
## Primary user-reported failure: scheduled execution stops prematurely

The user's primary complaint is that scheduled tasks repeatedly **wake briefly, acknowledge or provide a status response, stop without doing the assigned work, and wait for the next scheduled run**.

The original issue focused too heavily on timer cadence. Please triage the execution/completion behavior as the primary concern. A timer firing successfully is not enough if the requested work is left unperformed. The user reports this as a recurring pattern across scheduled tasks; this statement describes the user's experience, not a measured failure rate or a proven universal runtime limit.

### Two independent acceptance tracks

**A — Execution:** a delivered wake must perform its assigned operation or establish a genuine blocked/failed outcome.  
**B — Cadence:** the completion-relative delays and unexplained gap remain open even if execution improves. Passing one track must not be treated as resolving the other.

The previously published timing evidence is reproduced here for visibility. Times are UTC; the recurrence was 30 minutes.

| Scheduled start | Immediately preceding completion | Delay |
|---|---|---:|
| Sep 11 22:35:49.702 | Sep 11 22:05:32.943 | 1,816.759 s |
| Sep 11 23:39:50.634 | Sep 11 23:09:21.892 — owner turn | 1,828.742 s |
| Sep 12 00:10:51.304 | Sep 11 23:40:23.121 | 1,828.183 s |
| Sep 12 00:41:21.885 | Sep 12 00:11:14.106 | 1,807.779 s |
| Sep 12 01:12:22.415 | Sep 12 00:42:13.314 | 1,809.101 s |

The first start-to-start interval is **64m 0.932s**, with no target-task start between 22:49:48.055 and 23:09:08.447. Completion/activity anchoring remains a hypothesis. The analytical fixed-rate deadline is not a recovered due record.

For track B, retain due occurrences across busy admission, record deferral/retry/coalescing, and fence by schedule revision. **Update `last_run_at` only after accepted start**, with a correlated turn ID; use a separate attempted-at field for attempted admission. Test rejected and ambiguous submissions so they cannot masquerade as a successful run or cause duplicate execution.

### Requested action from OpenAI

Please investigate the scheduled execution and completion path, provide a supported mitigation, and identify the release containing a verified fix when available.

Expected behavior:

- Perform the required check or authorized assignment before completing the scheduled invocation.
- Distinguish an actual no-change result from a check that was never performed.
- Keep notification suppression separate from execution success: a quiet result must not substitute for doing the work.
- For an execution assignment, continue beyond acknowledgment or preliminary status checks until it is complete or a real blocker is established.
- Surface unavailable access, approval requirements, skipped work and failures explicitly. Preserve approval boundaries, newer owner instructions and protection against duplicate actions.

### Required regression tests and before/after evaluation

These are **proposed tests, not claimed as executed**.

1. Schedule a harmless local fixture read, with notification only when its value changes. Change the fixture before a wake and verify that the invocation actually reads and observes it.
2. **Assert the required postcondition, not response text.** For monitoring, independently verify the observation and comparison against the fixture version. For a multi-step execution task, assert the required durable state transition/artifact or an independently substantiated blocked/failed outcome tied to the operation. “Done,” “no change,” or “blocked” text alone must not pass.
3. Keep the fixture unchanged: the read/comparison still occurs while notification remains quiet.
4. Make access unavailable: require an explicit failed/blocked outcome rather than a successful no-change claim. Distinguish actual approval denial, reviewer timeout, cancellation and absence of an answerer.
5. Test an authorized multi-step assignment to catch acknowledgment-only completion and termination after a preliminary status check. Preserve newer owner instructions, approval boundaries and duplicate-work protection.
6. Exercise long existing conversations before and after applicable local/remote compaction, and both supported automation input paths. Refresh mutable priorities and ensure the latest applicable objective survives; do not assume every compaction mode uses the same history limit.
7. For cadence separately, test idle delivery, owner input before due, sustained sub-interval activity, busy deferral, restart, coalescing, concurrent dispatchers, pause/edit races, rejected admission and lost submission acknowledgment.

**Repeated evaluation is required:** measure execution-failure rate before and after the change across repeated, comparable scheduled invocations. Define failure as missing the independently verified required postcondition within the test bound, without a substantiated permitted blocked outcome. Publish sample size, model/build, prompt/state controls and counts for success, justified block, skipped/unattempted work, error and timeout. Compare matched manual controls that require the same work; ordinary conversational owner turns are not an equivalent baseline. Record due-but-not-started failures separately for cadence.

Zero tool calls and DONT_NOTIFY are useful diagnostics, **not standalone failure labels**. A history projection can omit tool wrappers; validate call counts against original execution records. A small observed difference between scheduled and manual samples is not causal proof.

### Approval and context paths requiring targeted coverage

The public source provides specific test targets, but not a confirmed cause of every incomplete wake:

- [Exec policy](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/944d6fd1ba4baab69dbedd205282dc72ec20abb5/codex-rs/core/src/exec_policy.rs#L788) returns Forbidden for certain approval-requiring cases under `Never`, while other commands can still run within the sandbox. [MCP approval](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/944d6fd1ba4baab69dbedd205282dc72ec20abb5/codex-rs/core/src/mcp_tool_call.rs#L1535) can return an explicit denial under that policy. Verify that scheduled outcome reporting retains the actual reason. The examined September turns instead used `on-request` with an automatic reviewer.
- A dropped approval waiter can resolve to [Abort](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/944d6fd1ba4baab69dbedd205282dc72ec20abb5/codex-rs/core/src/session/mod.rs#L2875). [Turn handoff](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/944d6fd1ba4baab69dbedd205282dc72ec20abb5/codex-rs/core/src/session/turn_suspension.rs#L96) intentionally clears process-local waiters. However, [approval handling](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/944d6fd1ba4baab69dbedd205282dc72ec20abb5/codex-rs/core/src/tools/approvals.rs#L457) distinguishes Abort/TurnAborted from timeout and user denial, and [cancellation ordering](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/944d6fd1ba4baab69dbedd205282dc72ec20abb5/codex-rs/core/src/tasks/mod.rs#L530) already tries to prevent a spurious rejection. Test the full unattended lifecycle and preserve reason/provenance; do not assume a human must answer when an automatic reviewer is configured.
- Test a legitimately authorized self-pause under each applicable review policy, including unavailable reviewer and cancellation. A tool's prompting declaration alone does not establish that self-pause always fails unattended.
- [Local compaction](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/944d6fd1ba4baab69dbedd205282dc72ec20abb5/codex-rs/core/src/compact.rs#L61) has a 20,000-token user-message budget in that path. It is not a universal description of every remote compaction mode or proof of lost instructions in this incident. Treat compaction and stale-priority reinjection as companion regression cases, not established independent causes.

### Relation to the duplicate suggestion

The bot suggested #44123, which concerns a timing gap after a schedule update. The primary complaint here concerns **failure to carry out work after waking**. Please keep that distinction during triage; correcting recurrence timing alone would not address the user's reported behavior.

The previously published evidence and its limitations are preserved below. No new private-log excerpts or private-task details are added in this update.

---

<details>
<summary>Previously published timing evidence, source references and limitations</summary>

## Summary

A thread-attached 30-minute heartbeat showed a **64-minute start-to-start gap**. Across five examined wakes, each start occurred approximately 30 minutes after the immediately preceding task turn completed—including an intervening owner turn.

This is an observed incident with independently recomputed timestamps, **not a deterministic reproduction of a dropped occurrence**. Completion/activity anchoring is the leading explanation; intentional fixed-delay semantics, deadline reset, and other deferral mechanisms cannot be distinguished from the available records.

Please clarify the intended interval semantics and expose occurrence-level delivery outcomes. If “every 30 minutes” is fixed-rate, unrelated task activity should not continually postpone the deadline.

## Environment

- Windows 11, OS version `10.0.26200.0`.
- Installed/running package at submission-time inspection: `OpenAI.Codex_26.903.9818.0_x64`. This is **not independently established as the exact package revision at every incident timestamp**.
- Model in examined turns: `gpt-6-astra`.
- Local heartbeat attached to an existing long-running task.
- Saved recurrence: `RRULE:FREQ=MINUTELY;INTERVAL=30`.
- Examined execution policy: `on-request`, reviewer `auto_review`, workspace-write, restricted network.
- Local time zone: America/New_York. All timestamps below are UTC.
- Public source reviewed at `944d6fd1ba4baab69dbedd205282dc72ec20abb5`; this source revision is not asserted to match the installed binary.

## Expected behavior

An interval automation should have understandable, stable scheduling semantics. If due while its task is busy, it should retain pending work and report the deferral, then run within a documented bound after admission becomes possible. If multiple checks are coalesced, that disposition should be visible.

The user should be able to distinguish a planned deadline, an attempted submission, an accepted turn, a completed turn, and an actionable result. A last-run timestamp alone is insufficient.

## Actual timing

These are lifecycle timestamps from the original task rollout, not estimates from the UI.

| Scheduled start (UTC) | Immediately preceding turn completion (UTC) | Delay from completion |
|---|---|---:|
| Sep 11 22:35:49.702 | Sep 11 22:05:32.943 | 1,816.759 s |
| Sep 11 23:39:50.634 | Sep 11 23:09:21.892 — owner turn | 1,828.742 s |
| Sep 12 00:10:51.304 | Sep 11 23:40:23.121 | 1,828.183 s |
| Sep 12 00:41:21.885 | Sep 12 00:11:14.106 | 1,807.779 s |
| Sep 12 01:12:22.415 | Sep 12 00:42:13.314 | 1,809.101 s |

The interval from 22:35:49.702 to 23:39:50.634 is **64m 0.932s**.

For a fixed-rate interpretation, 23:05:49.702 would be the next analytical deadline after the first start. **That is not a recovered persisted due timestamp.**

The Governor task completed a turn at 22:49:48.055 and had no intervening task start until an owner turn at 23:09:08.447. Therefore continuous execution of that task does not explain the entire interval containing the analytical deadline.

Local logs contain activity in every five-minute bucket from 22:30 through 23:45. The 23:05–23:10 bucket contains 89 records from four processes. This weakens a simple whole-host outage explanation, but does not prove uninterrupted uptime or exclude a short dispatcher stall. No usage-cap error was identified as the cause of this gap.

## What the retained state can and cannot establish

Read-only inspection found:

- Actual heartbeat starts in the rollout and canonical task history.
- Zero rows for this automation in the inspected `automation_runs` table. This does **not** mean the heartbeat never ran; it means that table did not provide its occurrence history.
- Submission logs under general session logging targets, including incoming heartbeat payloads. No matched planned-due/admission/deferral/disposition chain was recovered.
- No occurrence ID or planned-due field identified in the inspected incoming payloads.
- The final saved `last_run_at` was 70 ms before the final recorded lifecycle start. That sample cannot prove whether a failed attempt would also advance it.
- The automation was later paused and remains paused. Current `next_run_at = null` and an empty queue snapshot are not evidence of historical delivery loss.

The investigation did not unpause the production automation or alter permissions to reproduce the incident.

## Workflow leading to the observation

1. Use a recurring 30-minute heartbeat attached to a persistent local task.
2. Continue ordinary owner interactions between scheduled checks.
3. Compare scheduled starts with both previous scheduled starts and the most recent turn completions.
4. Observe the timing above and the lack of an occurrence-level reason for the longer interval.

This sequence documents what happened. A controlled minimal reproduction is still needed; it has not been demonstrated that every owner message resets the timer.

Suggested maintainer test: use a fake clock around the actual dispatcher, send owner input shortly before due time, then repeat with sustained sub-interval activity. Compare behavior against a fully idle control. Include busy admission, restart, coalescing and pause/edit races.

## Public source boundary and narrow investigation direction

The public core already exposes start-if-idle and typed admission outcomes:

- [start_turn_if_idle](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/944d6fd1ba4baab69dbedd205282dc72ec20abb5/codex-rs/core/src/codex_thread.rs#L340)
- [Turn submission outcomes](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/944d6fd1ba4baab69dbedd205282dc72ec20abb5/codex-rs/protocol/src/turn_input.rs#L185)
- [Admission checks](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/944d6fd1ba4baab69dbedd205282dc72ec20abb5/codex-rs/core/src/session/turn_input.rs#L388)

These mechanisms do not prove that the Desktop dispatcher drops refused work. The recurrence dispatcher was not located in the inspected public checkout.

Please investigate whether next due is anchored to scheduled time, last completion, or last activity, and how `NotIdle`/`PendingTriggerTurn` are retained or retried. If fixed-rate delivery is intended, a narrow repair would preserve due-occurrence identity across admission attempts, fence by schedule revision, and avoid resetting the deadline on unrelated input. After an ambiguous submission timeout, reconcile the occurrence with its turn before replaying it to avoid duplicate actions.

Useful diagnostic fields: automation and occurrence identity, schedule revision, planned due, attempted/accepted/start/completion timestamps, turn identity, admission outcome, retry reason and coalesced count.

## Related observations: not asserted as the timer's cause

The same task also exhibited these separately evidenced behaviors:

- Two owner instructions ended with acknowledgment-only responses and zero tool calls. These were owner turns, so they do not establish a scheduler-only model failure.
- Subsequent scheduled checks read usage and room state without advancing dependent work. Some quiet monitoring was consistent with the saved instructions; no-tool/no-edit counts are not a failure-rate metric.
- All 96 indexed automation inputs were `automation_update` function outputs without a call ID. The [public toolOutput branch](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/944d6fd1ba4baab69dbedd205282dc72ec20abb5/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/turn_processor.rs#L594) constructs that shape. No strict-provider HTTP 400 was observed in this native-Astra incident.
- Scheduled filesystem profiles contained 18 entries versus 11 for manual turns, but both resolved to the **same 11 unique entries**, including project write access. A specific automatic-review rejection was recorded; lost human approval or a blanket permission downgrade was not proved.
- A later compaction rewrite occurred after the examined no-op checks. It does not prove that earlier instructions were erased.

These observations explain why the user experiences unreliable unattended progress, but should not be collapsed into one unverified root cause. No patch, end-to-end fix, or zero-regression guarantee is claimed.

## Related issues / duplicate check

- #44123: macOS 25-minute heartbeat with an unexplained next-run gap after a schedule update. This adds a Windows completion-relative sequence and an identified idle interval; please consolidate if the same underlying behavior is already tracked.
- #44723 and #44519: separate unpaired-tool-output/provider failures.
- #41995: scheduled NOTIFY result visibility after reload.
- #29610: permission snapshot/default fallback report; this incident did not reproduce effective access loss.
- #37556: background task-management calls hanging; no pending call explains the zero-call owner acknowledgments here.
- #43632: scheduled task answers an older request; related symptom, not a demonstrated common cause.

Prepared with GPT-6 Astra from read-only original-record inspection and public-source review. Only sanitized timestamps, settings and aggregate observations are included. Raw conversations, private project prompts and paths, credentials, account details, and task/automation identifiers are omitted.


</details>

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
### Summary
On macOS 27, the locked MacBook display repeatedly turns off for about 2 seconds and then turns back on while the ChatGPT/Codex desktop app is running. The cycle repeats approximately every 32 seconds. Each display-on event is immediately preceded by `SkyComputerUseService` creating a `UserIsActive` assertion named `Codex Computer Use interaction`. After fully quitting the desktop app, the user observed that the display appeared to sleep normally.

### Environment
- MacBook Air M2 (Mac14,2)
- macOS 27.0 (build 26A428)
- ChatGPT/Codex desktop app 26.917.71314 (build 10954)
- Computer Use helper 26.915.1001093
- AC power; `pmset` reports `displaysleep 5`

### Steps to reproduce
1. Leave the ChatGPT/Codex desktop app running.
2. Lock the Mac and let the display turn off.
3. Observe the locked display: it turns back on within about 2 seconds, remains on for about 30 seconds, turns off briefly, and repeats.

### Actual behavior
A representative sanitized power-log sequence from 2026-09-25 (+0800):

```text
11:41:37  Display is turned off
11:41:39  SkyComputerUseService Created UserIsActive "Codex Computer Use interaction"
11:41:39  SkyComputerUseService Created PreventUserIdleDisplaySleep "Codex Computer Use interaction"
11:41:39  Display is turned on
```

The same off/on cycle was recorded repeatedly from 11:34 through 11:41, with off events about 32 seconds apart and display-on events 2–3 seconds after each off event. This makes the locked display appear to stay on.

### Expected behavior
Background Computer Use activity should not declare user activity or wake a locked display. The display should remain off until an actual user action wakes it.

### Related issues
- #42902 and #45101 report similar `SkyComputerUseService` display wakes, but at approximately 10-minute intervals. This report has a much shorter ~32-second cycle on macOS 27.

The timing strongly implicates the service's activity assertion as the immediate wake trigger. The internal reason for the repeated service calls has not been determined.

issues.body:
# Locked Use screen cannot be dismissed, even after manual macOS unlock; forced reboot required

## Summary

After leaving an agent running unattended on a Mac laptop, I returned to a screen reading “ChatGPT is Using Your Mac: Press any key or click to unlock.” Neither keyboard nor pointer input released the screen. Unlocking the normal macOS lock screen with Touch ID/password returned me to the same ChatGPT screen. The only recovery I found was a forced reboot using the power button.

## Environment

- Desktop app: ChatGPT, version 26.1016.51333, build 21161 (installed version checked when preparing this report).
- macOS: 26.6.2, build 25G83.
- Hardware: Mac laptop; exact model not collected.
- Component: desktop Computer Use / Locked Use.
- Exact incident time, agent session, and whether the agent was still actively using the computer are not established.

## Observed sequence

1. Left an agent running and stepped away.
2. Returned to the “ChatGPT is Using Your Mac” screen.
3. Pressed keys and clicked, as instructed by the screen, without regaining access.
4. Clicking or swiping upward with multiple fingers sometimes revealed the Dock. It disappeared before I could interact with it, and clicking Dock items did not work.
5. Multi-finger left/right swipes appeared to switch desktops, but every desktop displayed the same ChatGPT screen.
6. A Calendar notification was visible but could not be interacted with.
7. Briefly pressing the power button showed the normal macOS lock screen asking for Touch ID or password. Unlocking returned to the ChatGPT screen rather than restoring desktop access.
8. Forced a reboot using the power button to recover access.

## Expected behavior

Local keyboard/pointer input should trigger the documented Locked Use handoff: relock macOS and pause automatic unlocking until the user manually unlocks. After successful manual authentication, the user should regain desktop access without the ChatGPT screen continuing to block interaction.

Documentation: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/computer-use#locked-use

## Actual behavior and impact

The ChatGPT screen continued to block access despite local input and successful manual authentication. Normal local takeover was unavailable, and recovery required a forced reboot, interrupting running work.

## Reproducibility and diagnosis

One reported occurrence; not deliberately reproduced. The initial entry into Locked Use was not observed. A stuck covering screen or failed handoff is a hypothesis, not a confirmed root cause. No logs, screenshots, or session transcripts are attached.

## Related reports

- #51125 also describes local input failing to dismiss the overlay, during a shell-only task. This report does not establish which tools the unattended agent was using, and specifically records that successful manual macOS authentication returned to the blocking screen.
- #26415 describes a locked Computer Use hang; no process samples or CPU measurements were collected in this incident, so a shared cause is not established.

labels.name: sandbox

labels.name: app

labels.name: app-server

issues.body:
## Environment

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| OS | Windows 11 Pro 22H2, build 22000, x64 |
| Desktop app | ChatGPT / `OpenAI.Codex_26.1021.2667.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0` (MSIX) |
| Desktop build available at time of report | `26.1021.3705.0` |
| CLI | `codex-cli 0.164.0-alpha.11.1` |
| MXC support | `MXC availability: false` → legacy `elevated` sandbox backend |
| Execution host | `local:C:\Users\<user>\.codex` (native Windows, not Cloud/durable) |
| Account | local administrator |

## What happens

1. In the composer permission selector, select **Full access** ("可不受限制地访问互联网和你电脑上的任何文件").
2. Start a new chat and ask the agent to create a folder on the Desktop.
3. The agent runs:

```powershell
$desktopPath = [Environment]::GetFolderPath('Desktop')
$targetPath = Join-Path $desktopPath 'test'
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $targetPath -Force
```

4. It fails:

```
New-Item: Access to the path 'C:\Users\<user>\Desktop\test' is denied.
```

The same session **can** write inside its working directory (`E:\...\日常工作`), so it is not a total write lockout — it behaves exactly like `workspace-write`.

The permission selector visibly shows **Full access** and the selection persists across restarts (`permission-selection-by-host-id:local = {"kind":"agent-mode","agentMode":"full-access"}`).

## Evidence

### 1. The client requests a profile name that does not exist

From `~/.codex/logs_2.sqlite` (`logs.feedback_log_body`), every turn:

```
op=TurnInput
requested_settings: ThreadSettingsOverrides {
  approval_policy: None,
  approvals_reviewer: None,
  sandbox_policy: None,
  permission_profile: Some("managed")
}
```

Observed on 2026-10-22 17:46, 2026-10-23 10:28, 2026-10-23 17:52 (three different sessions).

`managed` is **not** one of the three built-in profiles (`:read-only`, `:workspace`, `:danger-full-access`), and it is not defined locally:

```
$ codex doctor
  ✓ sandbox   restricted fs + restricted network · approval OnRequest
      filesystem sandbox       restricted
      managed filesystem source none
      sandbox backend          elevated
```

```
$ codex sandbox -P managed -- cmd /c echo hi
Error: default_permissions refers to undefined profile `managed`
```

Neither `~/.codex/requirements.toml` nor `C:\ProgramData\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml` exists.

### 2. The two profiles behave completely differently at runtime

```
$ codex sandbox -P :danger-full-access -C <cwd> -- cmd /c "whoami & mkdir C:\Users\<user>\Desktop\probe"
desktop-xxxx\administrator        # NOT dropped to a sandbox account
exit 0                            # probe created successfully

$ codex sandbox -P :workspace -C <cwd> -- cmd /c "whoami & mkdir C:\Users\<user>\Desktop\probe"
desktop-xxxx\codexsandboxoffline  # dropped to the sandbox user
exit 1                            # 拒绝访问 / Access denied
```

So the sandbox machinery and the full-access path both work. The failure is that the running command never gets the full-access profile.

### 3. The sandbox user is read-only on the Desktop

```
$ icacls C:\Users\<user>\Desktop
C:\Users\<user>\Desktop  DOMAIN\CodexSandboxUsers:(OI)(CI)(RX)     <-- explicit, read+execute only
                         NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(I)(OI)(CI)(F)
                         BUILTIN\Administrators:(I)(OI)(CI)(F)
                         DOMAIN\<user>:(I)(OI)(CI)(F)
```

`CodexSandboxUsers` is Codex's own managed group ("Codex sandbox internal group (managed)"), membership: `CodexSandboxOffline`, `CodexSandboxOnline`.

### 4. Sandbox log confirms workspace-write semantics

`~/.codex/.sandbox/sandbox.<date>.log`, for every turn from the desktop app:

```
START: ...pwsh.exe -NoProfile -Command $desktopPath = [Environment]::GetFolderPath('Desktop'); ...
read-acl-only mode: applying read ACLs
read ACL run completed
granting write ACE to C:\Users\<user>\Documents\Codex\<date>\new-chat-N for sandbox group and capability SID
setup refresh: processed 2 write roots (read roots delegated); errors=[]
```

It grants a write ACE only to the turn's CWD — precisely the `workspace-write` behaviour. No `dangerFullAccess` turn produces that `granting write ACE` line.

### 5. UI state and runtime state disagree

`.codex-global-state.json` → `electron-persisted-atom-state.heartbeat-thread-permissions-by-id`:

| Thread created | `activePermissionProfile` | `sandboxPolicy` |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-10-15 … 10-19 | `:danger-full-access` | `dangerFullAccess` ✅ |
| 2026-10-21 14:33 → now | `:danger-full-access` | **`workspaceWrite`** ❌ |

At the same time `permission-selection-by-host-id:local` and `agent-mode-by-host-id.local` both read `full-access`.

## Ruled out

- **Broken NTFS ACL** — creating a folder on the Desktop as the normal admin token succeeds (`WRITE_OK`), so the DACL is fine for non-sandboxed processes.
- **Broken sandbox / broken full-access implementation** — `-P :danger-full-access` runs unsandboxed as `administrator` and writes the Desktop successfully.
- **Enterprise/MDM policy** — `managed filesystem source: none`; `C:\ProgramData\OpenAI\Codex` does not exist; `Get-AppxPackage`-independent inspection shows no requirements.toml anywhere.
- **Project-level config overriding permissions** — `codex doctor` reports the project `.codex/config.toml` contributes only one ignored key (`notify`).
- **Stale client version** — behaviour is identical on `26.1013.3656.0` (CLI 0.163.0-alpha.10.2) and `26.1021.2667.0` (CLI 0.164.0-alpha.11.1).
- **config.toml leftovers** — removing `sandbox_mode` / `[sandbox_workspace_write]` / `default_permissions` (so that `codex doctor` reports a clean default stack) does not change the behaviour; the client still sends `managed`.
- **Granting `CodexSandboxUsers` Modify on the Desktop** — still `Access denied`, because the sandboxed process runs under a restricted token / integrity level, so group DACL grants do not apply.
- **`unelevated` sandbox backend** — also denied (`whoami` shows the real user, but writes are still blocked).
- **Defining a local `[permissions.managed]`** — not possible from user config:
  - `extends = ":danger-full-access"` → `permissions profile 'managed' cannot extend unsupported built-in profile ':danger-full-access'`
  - `"**" = "write"` → `filesystem glob path '**' only supports 'deny' access`
  - `"C:/**" = "write"` → `filesystem path 'C:' must be absolute`
  - `"~/**" = "write"` → `elevated Windows sandbox requires effective ':root' read access`
  - adding `":root" = "write"` → `runner failed during SpawnChild: resolve permission profile token mode`
  - `default_permissions = ":danger-full-access"` + `-P managed` → `default_permissions refers to undefined profile 'managed'`

## Expected behaviour

Selecting **Full access** in the composer should result in the turn's effective sandbox policy being `dangerFullAccess` (commands run unsandboxed), or at minimum the client should map `agent-mode: full-access` to the built-in `:danger-full-access` permission profile rather than to an undefined `managed` name.

If `managed` is intended to be provided by the service (cloud-managed policy), then the client should surface a visible error or a warning in the permission selector instead of silently degrading to `workspace-write` while still displaying "Full access".

## Impact

On Windows, a user who explicitly opted into full access still cannot write outside the workspace roots (Desktop, Downloads, other drives). `workspace-write` does allow writes inside the turn's CWD, which is why the issue is easy to misdiagnose as a filesystem permission problem.

issues.title: Windows Computer Use: capture access and gold/yellow display border remain open after screenshot-producing turn completes

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Incident package: `OpenAI.Codex 26.1021.3705.0`, Windows x64 MSIX. This version was obtained from the installed package path, not the About dialog.
Computer Use / unified-computer-use plugin: `26.1021.31345`.
Bundled CUA runtime directory identifier: `1fb7137c46617d50`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected for this report.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows x64, OS-reported version `Microsoft Windows 10.0.26200`.

### What issue are you seeing?

A gold/yellow border remained around the user's display after a Codex chat had finished its native desktop capture work. Investigation found the Windows Computer Use helper still running and its Windows capture-access record still open approximately five hours after the screenshot-producing turn completed.

The request is for capture resources to be released when their owning work ends, while preserving Computer Use for other chats that actually need it.

#### Verified incident timeline

Times below are UTC, with America/New_York (UTC-04:00) equivalents. Incident date was October 25, 2026 locally.

| UTC | Local time | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-10-25 19:58:05.097 | Oct 25, 15:58:05 | The originating chat called `driveClient.getScreenshot()` on a Google Drive desktop window during an authorized backup/restore verification. |
| 2026-10-25 19:58:07.456 | Oct 25, 15:58:07 | Windows CapabilityAccessManager's entry for this helper records capture-access start. |
| 2026-10-25 20:02:51.338 | Oct 25, 16:02:51 | Another `driveClient.getScreenshot()` call occurred in the same turn. |
| 2026-10-25 20:04:50.622 | Oct 25, 16:04:50 | The local transcript records `task_complete` for that screenshot-producing turn. |
| Before 2026-10-26 01:04:26 | Before Oct 25, 21:04:26 | The user reported the persistent gold display border. The helper remained running; its capture-access stop time was still zero. Latest inspected turns of active chats were using files, APIs, or browser automation, with no current native desktop-capture calls found in those turns. |
| 2026-10-26 01:04:26.466 | Oct 25, 21:04:26 | Only the positively identified stale `codex-computer-use.exe` helper was terminated. Windows then recorded a nonzero capture-access stop time. |

The completion timestamp comes from the original transcript's lifecycle event, not an assumption based on the chat appearing idle.

#### Process and Windows evidence

- The retained process was `codex-computer-use.exe`, PID 34140, directly parented by the main `ChatGPT.exe` process, PID 48532.
- Its command line was the bundled helper path followed by `--parent-pid 48532`.
- Loaded modules included `GraphicsCapture.dll`, `Windows.Graphics.dll`, `d3d11.dll`, and `dwmapi.dll`.
- A separate `codex-computer-use-swift.exe` helper was present and was left untouched.
- The relevant Windows record was under:
  `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\CapabilityAccessManager\ConsentStore\graphicsCaptureWithoutBorder\NonPackaged\<encoded-helper-path>`.
- Before cleanup: `LastUsedTimeStart = 134374318874561759`, `LastUsedTimeStop = 0`.
- After cleanup: `LastUsedTimeStop = 134374502664667304`, corresponding to `2026-10-26T01:04:26.4667304Z`.
- After cleanup, the old helper was absent; no replacement `codex-computer-use.exe` was observed in the follow-up checks. The main app and both checked Codex agent-server processes remained running, and ongoing chats continued.
- No app restart, broad process kill, plugin disablement, or Windows permission change was used.

The user-visible border was reported by the user. The verified post-cleanup result is helper termination plus Windows recording capture access as ended; no new desktop screenshot was taken merely to verify the border.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is one observed incident sequence, not a verified deterministic minimal reproduction:

1. Run multiple chats in the Windows desktop app with Computer Use enabled.
2. Have one chat capture a native application window using Computer Use.
3. Let the screenshot-producing chat turn complete, and continue ordinary work in other chats.
4. Observe whether the gold/yellow capture border and native helper persist after native desktop work has ended.
5. Check the helper's Windows capture-access record for an unset stop time.
6. In this incident, terminating only the identified stale native capture helper caused Windows to record the end of capture access while the app and other chat agents remained running.

Please do not use a blanket helper-killing rule as the product fix: another chat may legitimately be using the same helper.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Release native capture sessions, cached frames, and associated graphics resources promptly when the owning chat finishes or relinquishes desktop use.
- Remove the Windows capture indicator when no capture remains needed.
- Preserve any other chat's active native operation.
- Allow a later authorized Computer Use task to acquire a fresh session normally.
- Handle ordinary completion, interruption, errors, disconnects, and concurrent chats.

### Additional information

#### Existing cleanup and a possible lifecycle ordering gap

Local, read-only inspection found that cleanup mechanisms are already present:

- User configuration already had a `notify = [<bundled codex-computer-use.exe>, "turn-ended"]` entry.
- The installed unified-computer-use MCP configuration included its hidden `turn_ended` tool.
- The shipped Windows client registers an `addTurnEndedHandler` and sends an `end_turn` request.
- The shipped desktop JavaScript tracks active turns by native-pipe socket. Its `end_turn` path removes matching active-turn entries. Separately, `closeActiveTurn` first checks that tracking map and returns without closing the helper transport if the turn is no longer present.

**Hypothesis, not a confirmed root cause:** if the end-turn request removes ownership tracking before the outer `turn/completed` cleanup checks it, the later cleanup could skip closing the helper transport, allowing cached capture resources to outlive the turn. Please investigate the interaction between the end-turn callback, socket/turn ownership tracking, helper transport closure, and the native capture cache.

This was static inspection of the installed JavaScript plus process/registry observations. No instrumented race reproduction or native decompilation established the exact defect.

#### Scope and limitations

- The persistent border, retained graphics-capture helper, original turn-completion timestamp, open Windows access record, and successful targeted cleanup are the evidence being reported.
- The registry record alone does not prove continuous frame acquisition, video recording, uploading, or continuous model access to the display. No such claim is made here.
- Later native activity in other turns is not exhaustively ruled out. At diagnosis, no current native capture calls were found in the latest turns inspected.
- No full transcripts, screenshots, credentials, account email addresses, personal usernames, or unrelated project content are included.

Related, but a different primary symptom: #56941 reports a retained helper after Computer Use on the same desktop package version, with system-wide UI lag. This report concerns the lingering capture indicator and capture-access lifecycle; a common cause is not established.

Also related: #46675 describes the takeover overlay remaining until the entire agent turn ends on an older build. The present incident includes a verified completed screenshot-producing turn and Windows capture access remaining open afterward, rather than only an overlay persisting during the same active turn.

issues.title: Goal mode sends `function_call_output` input item without required `call_id`, breaking custom Responses API providers

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: custom-model
labels.description: Issues related to custom model providers (including local models)

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

issues.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

Codex CLI 0.169.0 / 0.170.0

### What subscription do you have?

Pro

### Which model were you using?

custom

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Kitty

### Codex doctor report

```json

```

### What issue are you seeing?

• Goal active Objective: This is a test
■ stream disconnected before completion: stream closed before response.completed

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Configure a custom provider with `wire_api = "responses"`:

```toml
model_provider = "dashscope"

[model_providers.dashscope]
name = "dashscope"
base_url = "https://dashscope.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1"
wire_api = "responses"
env_key = "DASHSCOPE_API_KEY"
```

2. Start codex with this provider, set a goal (any objective, e.g. `/goal 这是一个短goal测试`).
3. The goal continuation turn starts automatically. Every sampling request fails immediately; after 5 retries codex shows:

```text
stream disconnected before completion: stream closed before response.completed
```

Goal becomes "stalled". Without a goal, the same session/model/endpoint works fine.
## Root cause

When a goal is active, codex injects the goal objective into the request `input` as a custom item:

```json
{
  "type": "function_call_output",
  "id": "fco_01a1f6d0-b42b-7051-ace5-1a3ae4be459a",
  "name": "goal_objective",
  "namespace": "agent",
  "output": "这是一个短goal测试"
}
```

Per the Responses API schema, `function_call_output` requires a `call_id` referencing a preceding `function_call`. This item has none (and there is no matching `function_call` in the input). Providers that validate the schema reject the request.

The injection is **unconditional** with goal mode: it happens for short and long objectives alike, regardless of content. Short objectives are additionally inlined in the `user_goal` context message; long ones are redacted from the rollout, but the malformed item is always sent.

This is a regression: goals completed successfully on 2026-11-17 with the previous binary; the 0.169.0 binary was installed on 2026-11-18; all goal sessions fail from 2026-11-19 onward.

## Observed provider error

DashScope returns HTTP 200 with an SSE error event (also see secondary issue below):

```text
event:error
:HTTP_STATUS/400
data:{"code":"InvalidParameter","message":"Invalid 'call_id': call_id is required for function_call_output.","request_id":"0a6f00a1-cbe4-9d27-928a-cea5d65b1c77"}
```

## Minimal reproduction (no codex needed)

POST to `/v1/responses` on any strictly validating provider:

```json
{
  "model": "glm-5.3-prime",
  "stream": true,
  "input": [
    {"type": "function_call_output", "name": "goal_objective", "namespace": "agent", "output": "这是一个短goal测试"}
  ]
}
```

Result: `InvalidParameter: call_id is required for function_call_output`.

Control: the same text as a regular user message completes normally. Deleting only the `function_call_output` item from a captured 335KB real codex goal request and replaying it unchanged also completes normally — this isolates the single offending item.

## Secondary issue: SSE `event:error` not surfaced

Codex does not parse the provider's in-stream error event (`event: error` with `:HTTP_STATUS/400`), so a protocol-level rejection is reported as a connectivity problem:

```text
stream disconnected before completion: stream closed before response.completed
```

This misleads users toward network/moderation/upstream-outage hypotheses (our investigation spent several wrong turns on exactly those). Surfacing the in-stream error payload would make the real cause visible immediately.


### What is the expected behavior?

- Goal-mode requests should only contain schema-valid input items (e.g. inject the objective as a message, or a well-formed tool-call pair).
- In-stream `event: error` payloads should be surfaced to the user instead of being reported as a stream disconnect.


### Additional information

_No response_

issues.body:
Currently, editing text inside the Codex CLI TUI prompt composer relies on keyboard navigation rather than inline mouse editing. When writing and revising prompts all day as an SWE, lacking basic mouse text-editing in the prompt box creates constant friction compared to Claude Code's TUI.

### Requested behavior (inside the TUI prompt composer)
- **Click to position cursor:** Clicking anywhere in single-line or wrapped multi-line prompt text moves the editing cursor to that character offset.
- **Click-and-drag to select and edit:** Highlighting text in the prompt composer with the mouse and pressing `Backspace`/`Delete` or typing deletes/replaces the selected range (and `Ctrl+C`/`Ctrl+X` copies/cuts it).
- **Double-click to select word** (nice-to-have).

### Why it matters
- External editors (`Ctrl+G`) are far too heavyweight for quick inline edits (e.g., clicking back a few words to rewrite a phrase).
- Keyboard-only editing is a major daily UX gap for heavy CLI users coming from Claude Code—even when the underlying model is strong, basic input-box friction adds up quickly.

*(Related to #36439 for mouse-click cursor positioning; filing to explicitly include inline drag-to-highlight and delete/replace editing parity in the prompt composer.)*

issues.title: CLI 0.170.0: slash-command picker loses blue selection inside tmux despite working truecolor

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: TUI
labels.description: Issues related to the terminal user interface: text input, menus and dialogs, and terminal display

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

issues.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.170.0, official standalone Linux x86_64 musl binary.

Version scope: this was observed and captured on 0.170.0. Release 0.171.0 became available on November 20; this report has not been retested on 0.171.0.

### What subscription do you have?

Not included; this report concerns local TUI rendering before any model request.

### Which model were you using?

The issue is visible when opening the slash-command picker without submitting a model request.

### What platform is your computer?

Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS under WSL2, x86_64.
Linux 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2.

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

VS Code 1.147.0 integrated terminal, with tmux 3.6.
The attached tmux client reports xterm.js(6.1.0-beta.337), TERM=xterm-256color, and RGB among its terminal features.

The actual running native Codex process environment, inspected via /proc/<pid>/environ:

```text
TERM=tmux-256color
COLORTERM=truecolor
TERM_PROGRAM=tmux
TERM_PROGRAM_VERSION=3.6
NO_COLOR is unset
FORCE_COLOR is unset
```

Relevant settings:

```text
tmux default-terminal: tmux-256color
tmux allow-passthrough: off
Codex tui.alternate_screen: always
```

### Codex doctor report

Not collected for this report. The tool-running shell does not share the interactive terminal environment, so the terminal evidence below was collected directly from the live tmux pane and the actual Codex process instead.

### What issue are you seeing?

Inside tmux, typing `/` opens a slash-command picker whose command names appear white/monochrome, without the blue selection styling seen outside tmux in the same VS Code terminal. Other Codex highlighting remains colored.

A read-only `tmux capture-pane -p -e` capture of the live open picker shows the selected command rendered with reverse-video, without an explicit blue foreground/background:

```text
\x1b[1;7m› /ide       \x1b[0;7minclude current selection, open files, and other context from your IDE\x1b[1m
```

The escapes above are displayed in literal notation. SGR 7 is reverse-video; SGR 1 is bold. Other visible rows use default colors and dim descriptions. The same captured screen contains multiple truecolor `38;2;...` foreground sequences elsewhere, so this is not a complete loss of terminal color support.

The outside-tmux appearance is based on visual comparison; an equivalent outside-tmux escape-code capture has not yet been collected.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Open the VS Code integrated terminal connected to WSL2.
2. Run Codex CLI 0.170.0 inside tmux 3.6, with the environment above.
3. Type `/` and leave the command picker open without executing a command.
4. Observe the monochrome/reverse-video selection, while other Codex highlighting remains colored.
5. Compare with Codex outside tmux in the same terminal, where the expected blue selection styling appears.

### What is the expected behavior?

When truecolor works, the slash-command picker should retain its blue selection styling inside tmux, consistent with the same terminal outside tmux. A missing terminal-background response should not unnecessarily remove the selection color when a readable fallback is possible.

### Additional information

The version-matched source provides a plausible explanation, not a confirmed internal trace:

- [command_popup.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.170.0/codex-rs/tui/src/bottom_pane/command_popup.rs#L235-L248) uses the shared selection style.
- [style/contrast.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.170.0/codex-rs/tui/src/style/contrast.rs#L35-L78) falls back to default foreground/background plus bold and reverse-video when the terminal background is unavailable, or when the fill cannot be resolved for the color level.

The captured style matches that fallback. An unavailable terminal-background probe result is suspected, but the internal cached palette was not directly inspected, and this report does not establish the precise cause of a probe failure.

Related: #22761 tracks composer/pill background loss in tmux; #36918 was closed as its duplicate. This report focuses specifically on the slash-command picker's selected-row styling in 0.170.0. The symptoms may be related, but a shared root cause has not been confirmed.

issues.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

IDE Extension

cc @etraut-openai, opening this as a fresh feature request per your guidance in https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/17185#issuecomment-4583634793.

### What feature would you like to see?

In the Codex VS Code extension, chat/thread history should be scoped, grouped, or filtered by the current workspace/project.

Right now, chats from different projects appear together in one shared history list. When working across multiple repositories, VS Code windows, remote workspaces, WSL/SSH sessions, or unrelated codebases, it becomes easy to resume the wrong thread or confuse which chat belongs to which project.

This creates a real workflow problem because Codex threads carry project-specific context. Accidentally continuing a thread from another project can lead to irrelevant suggestions, wrong assumptions, and extra mental overhead.

A useful MVP could be:

- Associate each thread with its originating VS Code workspace folder or working directory.
- Show current-workspace threads first in the extension history.
- Hide, collapse, or visually separate threads from other workspaces.
- Provide an “all threads” view or toggle for users who intentionally want global history.
- Preserve existing thread rename/archive behavior.

This does not need to introduce a full project-management system. The most important behavior is that when I am in Project A, I should not have to scan through chats from Projects B, C, and D to find the relevant Codex thread.

### Additional information

This is related to the closed issue #17185, but I am opening a new feature request per maintainer guidance here:

https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/17185#issuecomment-4583634793

There is also related discussion in #12564, where the VS Code extension recently gained thread renaming. Renaming helps, but it is only a mitigation for the broader issue: chats from unrelated projects are still mixed together.

A commenter noted that Codex CLI already appears to have working-directory-based isolation by default, with `codex resume --all` available for showing all threads:

https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/17185#issuecomment-4582037042

If that is accurate, the VS Code extension could potentially reuse the same working-directory concept and expose it in the extension history UI.

issues.title: App-server starts and completes turns while the history database is unavailable

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

issues.body:
### Summary

If `thread_history_1.sqlite` cannot be opened, app-server initialization succeeds and new turns can report `completed`, but paginated history cannot be read or resumed. This affects both existing threads and newly completed threads. The canonical rollout is still written in the reproduction; the problem is the unavailable history projection and lack of an actionable startup indication.

After restoring a valid earlier history database in the fixture, an existing thread's history is readable, but the new thread initially returns an empty history page even though its rollout contains the prompt and answer. Resuming that thread and running another turn later materializes both turns and retains the prior model context. This does **not** demonstrate permanent loss of the rollout.

### Reproduction

Use a checkout at `6eea32808167c4b87508e9611ba116f061ee315c`, install the Python SDK test dependencies, put `sdk/python/src` and `sdk/python/tests` on `PYTHONPATH`, and set `CODEX_EXEC_PATH` to the CLI executable. The script modifies only a newly created temporary database and its WAL; it uses a local mock Responses server.

```python
import json
import sqlite3
import time
import tomllib
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from app_server_harness import AppServerHarness
from openai_codex import Codex

def history(client, thread_id):
    try:
        result = client._client._request_raw(
            "thread/turns/list", {"threadId": thread_id, "limit": 10}
        )
        return len(result["data"])
    except Exception as exc:
        return type(exc).__name__ + ": " + str(exc).split(" at ")[0]

with TemporaryDirectory(ignore_cleanup_errors=True) as directory:
    with AppServerHarness(Path(directory)) as h:
        config = tomllib.loads((h.codex_home / "config.toml").read_text(encoding="utf8"))
        assert config["model_provider"] == "mock_provider"
        assert config["model_providers"]["mock_provider"]["base_url"].startswith(h.responses.url)
        for text, response_id in [
            ("first answer", "r1"), ("second answer", "r2"), ("continued", "r3")
        ]:
            h.responses.enqueue_assistant_message(text, response_id=response_id)

        with Codex(config=h.app_server_config()) as client:
            thread = client.thread_start()
            old_id = thread.id
            assert thread.run("first prompt").final_response == "first answer"
            print("healthy history:", history(client, old_id))

        db = h.codex_home / "thread_history_1.sqlite"
        backup = Path(directory) / "good.sqlite"
        source = sqlite3.connect(db)
        destination = sqlite3.connect(backup)
        source.backup(destination)
        destination.close()
        source.close()
        wal = Path(str(db) + "-wal")
        if wal.exists():
            wal.write_bytes(b"")
        db.write_bytes(b"invalid fixture database" * 32)

        with Codex(config=h.app_server_config()) as client:
            print("old history with damaged DB:", history(client, old_id))
            thread = client.thread_start()
            new_id = thread.id
            result = thread.run("new prompt")
            print("new turn:", result.status.value, result.final_response)
            print("new history with damaged DB:", history(client, new_id))
            time.sleep(0.5)

        rollout = next(h.codex_home.rglob("*" + new_id + "*.jsonl"))
        text = rollout.read_text(encoding="utf8")
        print("new rollout has prompt and answer:",
              "new prompt" in text and "second answer" in text)

        db.write_bytes(backup.read_bytes())
        if wal.exists():
            wal.write_bytes(b"")
        with Codex(config=h.app_server_config()) as client:
            print("restored old/new counts:", history(client, old_id), history(client, new_id))
            client.thread_resume(new_id).run("followup")
            body = json.dumps(h.responses.wait_for_requests(3)[2].body_json()["input"])
            print("after resume count:", history(client, new_id),
                  "previous context preserved:",
                  "new prompt" in body and "second answer" in body)
```

On Windows with CLI **0.170.0** and **0.172.0-alpha.2**, both runs produced:

```text
healthy history: 1
old history with damaged DB: InternalRpcError: ... failed to open thread history database ...
new turn: completed second answer
new history with damaged DB: InternalRpcError: ... failed to open thread history database ...
new rollout has prompt and answer: True
restored old/new counts: 1 0
after resume count: 2 previous context preserved: True
```

I independently reproduced the initialization, completed turn, failing history calls, and empty page after backup restoration using raw app-server stdio JSON-RPC with graceful stdin shutdown. The app-server logged the projection failure; in that test no history-specific warning notification was observed. A directory occupying the database path produced the same initialized/completed-but-unreadable behavior.

### Suggested fix

Check history-store health at startup or before accepting persisted work, and surface an actionable degraded-state notification. Preserve the damaged database and rollout files; provide a safe recovery/reprojection path, and avoid returning an apparently complete empty history page while a known rollout has not been projected. The current [history DB is opened lazily](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/6eea32808167c4b87508e9611ba116f061ee315c/codex-rs/thread-store/src/local/mod.rs#L333-L346), while [projection errors are logged and the write continues](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/6eea32808167c4b87508e9611ba116f061ee315c/codex-rs/thread-store/src/local/live_writer.rs#L563-L588).

Related #61516 describes a different single-rollout ordinal failure; this reproduction fails to open the history database itself and affects multiple threads.

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64

>A JavaScript error occurred in the main process

The app should reopen normally or wait for the previous instance to finish shutting down before opening a new window.

issues.body:
## Clarification requested

Please clarify the source/build provenance of the Windows app-bundled Codex CLI below and the supported noninteractive isolation controls after the `worktrees` and `realtime_conversation` feature keys became removed compatibility flags.

The tagged source appears consistent with the observed output. This is a provenance/documentation question, not a claim that an active flag was silently ignored or that a sandbox escape occurred.

## Retained environment and executable descriptors

- Component: CLI bundled with the Codex desktop app, Windows.
- Reported CLI version: `0.164.0-alpha.11.1`.
- Exact Windows/app build numbers were not retained in this evidence set.
- App-bundled executable: **354,661,168 bytes**, SHA-256:
  `1103e9e09c71fa2cd0afd6d8f3b9a2d63174fe8efd7cb5bd09f1cb14ef58a098`.
- The same-version release metadata read on 2026-11-20 lists `codex-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.exe` with the same byte length but SHA-256:
  `4fd2f057bad603bf53dc202457ffd0c3591de62e867a8b01e73816e3fbce5a73`.

No asset in the retained release metadata matched both the app-bundled size and digest. We have not assumed that signing or packaging explains the difference, and have not treated a matching version string as proof of exact binary/source identity.

## Bounded observations

Two separately approved local diagnostics completed normally on 2026-11-20:

1. The worker's 82 existing `--disable <feature>` pairs, followed by `features list`.
2. The same 82 pairs, then `--config features.realtime_conversation=false --config features.worktrees=false`, followed by `features list`.

These are descriptions of the recorded commands, not a verified minimal reproduction with only two disable pairs.

Both recognized all 82 required names and reported:

| Feature | Reported state |
| --- | --- |
| `realtime_conversation` | `true` |
| `worktrees` | `true` |
| `shell_tool` | `false` |

Each diagnostic launched the CLI once and observed normal zero exit/close. The second also verified executable/source hashes before and after. Raw output was intentionally not retained; allowlisted feature states and stream metadata were retained.

Neither command requested model/image review, account-model discovery, login, or a persistent configuration edit. Hidden startup/configuration/authentication/network behavior was not instrumented, and we do not claim its absence.

## Matching-version source findings

The official tag [`rust-v0.164.0-alpha.11.1`](https://github.com/openai/codex/releases/tag/rust-v0.164.0-alpha.11.1) resolves to commit [`6905ecede7816e91373e9eabda3f6b0368fc747b`](https://github.com/openai/codex/commit/6905ecede7816e91373e9eabda3f6b0368fc747b).

At that commit:

- [`features/src/lib.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/6905ecede7816e91373e9eabda3f6b0368fc747b/codex-rs/features/src/lib.rs#L685) explicitly skips both keys in `apply_map`. Their registry entries are `Stage::Removed` with `default_enabled: true`.
- [`cli/src/main.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/6905ecede7816e91373e9eabda3f6b0368fc747b/codex-rs/cli/src/main.rs) converts disable flags to false configuration overrides, forwards them into configuration loading, and prints `config.features.enabled` in the feature-list path.
- The source comments describe changed capability gating, not removal of the underlying voice/worktree capabilities.

This explains the tagged source's output, but the different app-bundled digest leaves its exact implementation mapping unverified.

## Questions

1. Which source commit and build/signing provenance correspond to the app-bundled SHA-256 above? Is the difference from the same-size published Windows asset expected, and is there a supported way to verify that mapping?
2. For that exact build, what supported controls or independently verifiable checks prevent voice sessions and managed-worktree creation during a noninteractive `exec` invocation? Our intended worker already requires a read-only sandbox, `--ephemeral`, `--ignore-user-config`, disabled shell/tool features, and never requests `--worktree` or a voice action. These intended controls are not presented as a complete capability-exposure proof.
3. Can the documentation state the version-specific meaning of these two feature-list values and the supported replacement checks? We need capability semantics before changing a required-off compatibility check.

The worker/pilot remains off and the existing guards remain unchanged. We are not asking to bypass safeguards, change managed policy, or make a model call to obtain this clarification.

No private configuration, credentials, account/thread identifiers, local filesystem paths, prompts, images, raw logs, or attachments are included.
