issues.body:
### Summary

Add `openclaw sessions list --archived` to list only archived sessions from the local session store.

### Problem to solve

When reviewing a headless Gateway over SSH or inspecting a stopped Gateway’s copied state, operators need to find archived session keys for retention review or recovery. The stock CLI lists active and archived rows together, with a default limit of 100. Newer active sessions can fill that window and hide older archived rows.

### Proposed solution

- Support `--archived` on both `openclaw sessions list` and the shorthand `openclaw sessions`.
- Use the stored archive state and apply the filter before sorting and applying `--limit`. For JSON output, `count`, `totalCount`, and `hasMore` describe the filtered result.
- Allow it to compose with the existing agent/store selectors and JSON output. Keep the current listing behavior when the flag is omitted.

### Alternatives considered

- The Control UI’s Archived view and `openclaw gateway call sessions.list --json --params '{"archived":true,"limit":25}'` cover the live Gateway workflow. Offline inspection needs a local store query.
- Filtering CLI JSON with `jq` would be possible once archive metadata is exposed by #124540. To find older matches, that approach still needs `--limit all` and serializes unrelated rows before filtering.

### Impact

This affects headless operators and scripts that audit retained sessions or identify a session to restore. It matters when active and archived sessions coexist and newer activity fills the requested result window. A bounded read-only listing would work even when the Gateway is stopped.

### Evidence/examples

Verified on Linux with a locally built upstream commit `81a962707f7`, a loopback Gateway, and an isolated SQLite session store.

1. Create a session with `sessions.create`, archive it with `openclaw sessions archive <key> --json`, and create a newer active session.
2. `openclaw sessions list --limit 1 --json` returns only the active row, with `totalCount: 2` and `hasMore: true`. `--limit all` returns both rows. After stopping the Gateway, the bounded CLI result is the same.
3. `openclaw sessions list --archived --limit 1 --json` exits 1 with an unrecognized option. The live Gateway query in Alternatives returns the archived row with `archived: true`.

With the proposed flag, the bounded CLI listing should return the archived row with `totalCount: 1` and `hasMore: false` on the same store after the Gateway stops.

[Sessions CLI reference](https://docs.openclaw.ai/cli/sessions)

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance.

### Additional information

[PR #124540](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/124540) tracks JSON archive metadata. [PR #184316](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/184316) tracks the restore operation. The requested filter is a read-only CLI option over existing session metadata.

issues.title: 2026.11.5: migrated Claw/Template install records still enforce consent provenance, but there's no supported way to manage or retire them
issues.body:
## Summary
In 2026.11.5, `openclaw templates` documents that "Add is a one-way action: it creates an ordinary agent… It does not create an installed Template to manage… There is no Template ownership record."

But installs migrated from Claws (pre-11.x, `claw_installs` → `template_installs`, schema v36 template-names migration) still keep a row per agent, including `agent_config_digest`. The runtime keeps enforcing that row: any ordinary edit to the agent (model, tools.allow/deny, memory.search) blocks every turn with:

```
TemplateToolProfileConsentStateError: Cannot verify the installed tool authority for Template-managed agent "main". Repair the OpenClaw state database before running it.
… Template agent configuration does not match its consent provenance.
```

11.5 also removed `claws status/update/remove`, and the docs say there are "no Template status, update, remove, or export commands". Doctor neither repairs nor retires these rows. The only code path that deletes a `template_installs` row is agent deletion (`agent-deletion.worker`). So the only supported fix is to delete the agent.

## Impact (one host, 12 migrated agents)
- An ordinary model change (`agents.entries.main.model.primary`) blocked the main agent on Telegram and in the Control UI until the record was re-baselined by hand.
- 11.5's own doctor migration (it moves `agents.entries.<id>.heartbeat` into heartbeat automations) changed main, home and ops, which blocked them straight after the update.
- An 11.4 tool-name normalisation (`server__tool` → `server_tool` in tools.allow) blocked main and reader.
- Agents deleted from config leave orphan `template_installs` rows behind.

## Expected
One of these:
- doctor migrates legacy installs to ordinary agents (it retires the `template_installs` / `agent_provenance` rows), as the 11.x "one-way Add" model implies; or
- a supported command re-baselines or releases a legacy install; or
- consent enforcement is skipped for agents that have no live Template ownership.

## Constraint for any fix: keep the referenced cron jobs
The state database also has `template_cron_refs` rows (next to `template_workspace_files`, `template_package_refs` and `template_mcp_server_refs`) that link these legacy installs to automations. Any fix that retires or releases the legacy install records must not detach, disable or delete the cron jobs they reference. After the fix, those jobs should remain as ordinary automations owned by the agent, as the 11.5 docs describe ("manage ... its automations with cron commands").

## Environment
OpenClaw 2026.11.5 (e13cf15), Linux, Node 26.13.1. The agents were originally created and adopted with `claws add` / `claws migrate` (Oct 2026).

issues.body:
### Problem

Returning to the end of the Logs stream can leave Auto-follow off when the first scroll caused by a wheel event arrives after the reader-intent idle deadline but before the first input frame.

### Expected behavior

A genuine wheel return to the end resumes following. A horizontal or no-motion gesture must still expire, and a later programmatic scroll must not resume following.

### Evidence

On base `749e2aed7`, the new controlled ordering regression fails with the original production code and passes after the patch. The idle interval remains 200 ms; the fix starts that interval after the first input frame, or on observed scrolling.

The view and page-consumer suites pass 29 tests. The real built Logs UI also passes the existing native Chromium wheel/append/re-enable scenario on both base and candidate, with following enabled and a zero-pixel end gap. This establishes preservation of normal behavior, not a native reproduction of the delayed-first-frame defect.

Proposed fix: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202349

### Limits and related context

Native WebKit attribution to the original CI flake is not established.

Existing issue https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/150693 describes resize-without-input, a distinct mechanism. This issue does not claim that problem is fixed.

### Problem

A viewport whose initial placement has completed may admit an earlier row before the first reader gesture. That row can enter normal flow before its height is measured, moving retained rows by the estimate error.

### Expected behavior

Reuse the existing measure-before-flow path after placement, including before the first gesture, while preserving pending-placement and end-preparation exceptions.

### Existing related context

https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/198500 covers predecessor estimation and reading-position jumps and is closed. This is a narrower cold-viewport follow-up, not a request to reopen that issue.

### Evidence

The new Chromium regression fails on unchanged production with 48 px of unexpected first-frame movement, then passes with the patch. The complete geometry suite passes 33/33 tests. The existing initial-range suite passes 16/16 tests.

Proposed fix: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202348

### Limits

The supplied report measured disclosure movement of 47.61 → 0.39 px and a separate remaining 112 px canvas resize. Those numbers are not independently established here.

Both existing disclosure and raw-details end-to-end cases passed on baseline and candidate, with 0 px in their captured traces. Those flows and matched screenshots establish preserved behavior, not proof that the original disclosure/canvas symptoms were reproduced or fully fixed.

issues.body:
### Summary

Give each person on a multi-user Gateway a personal vault of secrets that commands can use in the sessions that person creates, so an agent can run a CLI or call an API with that person's own token. Proposed as a narrow host capability in core, with the vault as a plugin.

### Problem to solve

On a multi-user Gateway, developers need their own credentials in agent commands: a token for a service's CLI or API, a private package registry, a personal cloud login. An MCP server with per-user auth (#122034) is the better route where one exists. Many services have none, and CLIs, registries and test environments need the credential in the process environment or in their requests.

OpenClaw has no place for such a credential:

- **Team secret store:** Gateway-wide. "Identity-scoped secrets are not supported; only the team store participates" ([secret-store-and-egress.md](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/docs/gateway/secrets/secret-store-and-egress.md)).
- **Personal model accounts:** model credentials only.
- **Personal GitHub connections (#133799):** GitHub only.

So a personal token is either stored where every operator and agent on the Gateway can use it, or not stored at all.

Issue #148764 asked for identity-scoped entries in the shared store. Its author closed it with four questions from its review still open: whose identity applies in shared sessions and background work, revocation, precedence, and what administrators can see. The design below answers all four.

### Proposed solution

> **Note:** An earlier version of this issue proposed a different model. In a shared session, each participant could turn on their own vault for their own turns, and it switched off as soon as someone else sent a message. The older comments refer to that version. It is now listed under Alternatives, and its spikes under Evidence.

**A session uses one person's secrets: its creator's.** Every Gateway-host `exec` command in the session gets that person's current vault entries, read when the command launches. It makes no difference who or what caused the turn: the creator, a teammate, a steer, a cron job or a hook.

There is no switch, per session or per person. Sharing, visibility, members, owner changes and resets change nothing.

Entries are protected by default: a command sees only a sentinel, and the existing egress proxy substitutes the real value in HTTPS requests to the entry's allowed hosts. The proxy is off by default (`secrets.egressProxy.enabled`). Until a Gateway admin enables it, protected entries are not delivered and commands get a warning.

Personal model accounts set the precedent. They are session-sticky ("other people steering into that session use its selected account"), which the docs call "account-selection convenience inside one trust domain, not isolation from administrators or code running as the Gateway OS user" ([multi-user.md](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/docs/concepts/multi-user.md)).

**The design in brief**

- **Entries.** `secret` (protected, the default) reaches a command as a sentinel with a per-command egress-proxy grant, on the path that team-store `secret` entries use today. `env` (plaintext) is an explicit choice per entry and reaches the command as a real environment variable.
- **Whose vault.** The session's write-once creator (`createdActor`), if that is a person with a verified Gateway profile. Sessions created on a person's behalf count, such as the run sessions of their cron jobs. The assignable owner never decides.
- **Sessions that get nothing.** The agent's main session and threads under it, sessions with a channel-shaped key, and sessions bound to an external channel conversation. Also sessions created by the shared Gateway owner profile, by a channel sender, or by an agent with no person behind it. The channel rules exist because channel DMs go to the main session by default: without them, a person who started the main session from the Control UI would hand their secrets to anyone who messages the agent on a linked channel.
- **Sub-agents.** A spawned session uses what the session it was spawned from uses, up the `spawnedBy` chain, whoever's turn spawned it. Children of a session that gets nothing get nothing.
- **Authority.** The repository rule is "Check authority one time, when work starts. … A started request may finish" (root `AGENTS.md`). Here the request is one command launch: it reads the creator's current entries once, also after an approval wait, and a started command finishes, background processes included (question 3). There is no in-memory state, no hook on sharing changes and no new admission phase.
- **Precedence.** A person's entry replaces a team entry of the same name, including its proxy binding, and both replace the Gateway's own environment. What wins over team entries today wins over both: env passed in the `exec` call itself, plugin `resolve_exec_env`, and the variables OpenClaw manages (GitHub identity, egress proxy settings).
- **Disclosure.** The vault page says who can use the entries. Everyone who can see a session, administrators included, sees whose secrets it uses and the entry names, and the agent can list the names. None of these show values. Status says why the main session, a channel session and their sub-agents get none. A bound session gives no reason yet (question 4).
- **First PR.** Non-durable Gateway-host `exec` only. Sandbox, durable and node exec get nothing, and a warning. Native harness shells (Codex, Claude CLI, ACP) get nothing, as with team-store `secret` entries, and OpenClaw can't add a warning to their tool results. The follow-ups are under Additional information.

**Host and plugin**

This follows step 3 of the [capability ladder](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/plugin-sdk/AGENTS.md#choose-the-capability-surface): a missing contract becomes a narrow generic core capability, and the feature stays at the edge. The ongoing cost is a permanent provider contract and one optional `secrets` tool parameter. The parameter appears, and launches read a vault, only when a provider is registered.

- **Host (core):** decides which session uses whose secrets, delivers entries at launch, keeps values out of approvals, hooks and tool results, and supplies the status, the banner and the disclosure text, so every vault plugin gets the same disclosure.
- **Plugin:** stores the entries and edits them through owner-only RPCs and a settings page that shows the host's disclosure, for example **Settings → Profile → Vault**. It never sees sessions, turns or senders. It is proposed as a bundled plugin; publishing it on ClawHub is the alternative (question 2).
- **Admin control:** enabling the vault plugin and the egress proxy, and one plugin setting that turns off plaintext `env` entries, so only protected entries are stored and delivered. This mirrors the team store, where plaintext is an operator choice.

The plugin PR is stacked on the host PR, and the two land together, so the host contract never ships without a real consumer.

**What this does not protect against**

- **Teammates act as the creator.** Anything that can make an agent run a command in an eligible session uses its creator's secrets at external services: teammates who can send, other sessions' agents through `sessions_send`, automations, and hooks and node requests routed to the session. Only the transcript records who prompted.
- **The exclusions cover message routing, not agent tools.** An agent in the main session, prompted by a channel sender, can use `sessions_send` to make an eligible session run commands with its creator's secrets.
- **Plaintext entries can be printed.** Anything a command prints is visible in the session, unmasked in the transcript and sent to the model, and files that CLIs write persist on the host.
- **A protected entry is only as private as its allowed hosts.** A host that echoes or stores request credentials can return the value, and in a shared session a teammate can make it do so on purpose.
- **The Gateway host can read the vault.** The reference plugin stores values unencrypted, and anyone who can run commands on the Gateway host can read them.
- **Deleting is the only stop, and it applies to new launches.** Running commands, background processes included, keep their environment and their proxy grant.

<details>
<summary>Further limits (to be documented)</summary>

- **Draft visibility doesn't stop every route.** Upstream cron (`session:<key>` targets) and node `agent.request` don't check session sharing, so a teammate's job can run in someone else's Draft with that person's secrets. Those gaps are separate from this proposal.
- **Gateways with outside channel senders** can deny the agents those senders reach `sessions_send` and scheduling into other sessions (the automations tool's `session:<key>` target), or narrow `tools.sessions.visibility`, which defaults to `all`.
- **Background processes.** The `process` tool sees processes started by ancestor sessions (`docs/gateway/background-process.md`). A thread-bound sub-agent of Alice's session, which gets nothing itself, can write to a background shell that her session started.
- **A person who leaves** keeps supplying their sessions for as long as their profile resolves and their entries exist. There is deliberately no admin RPC for someone else's vault. The fix is revoking their tokens at each service; disabling the vault plugin stops all delivery at once.
- **Protected entries** cover only HTTPS requests that go through the egress proxy to an allowed host. SSH, `sshpass`, `sudo -S` and local token-format checks need `env`. Request signing works with neither kind (see Names and sizes). A command or CLI that bypasses the proxy, for example because of `NO_PROXY`, sends the sentinel in place of the value.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Which sessions use whose secrets: the exact rules</summary>

- **Creator.** Resolved with upstream's creator rule (`sessionCreatorProfileId`). A profile merged with the creator counts, and the surviving profile's vault is read. The shared Gateway owner profile is the one that token and password connections use. A session created by a channel message gets nothing, even from a linked person.
- **Excluded by key.** Every main- or channel-shaped key (a channel DM, group or channel, with or without a thread), whether or not a channel is configured to produce it. The check uses upstream's session-key predicates with the configured `session.mainKey` and `session.scope`. So cron jobs and hooks that target the main session get nothing.
- **Excluded by binding.** Thread-bound sub-agents, plugin bindings, and bindings migrated from the retired `/focus` command. Bindings to the Control UI's own internal conversation (`webchat`) don't count. The check runs at each launch, for sessions that pass the key check and have a qualifying creator: it asks the session-binding service whether a routable conversation is bound to the session (`listSessionBindingsBySessionAsync`). That costs one SQLite read plus one per account-scoped binding adapter, and an occasional write when the store prunes expired bindings. If the query fails, the command gets nothing. A binding created after a launch affects the next launch.
- **Sub-agents.** The chain follows only `spawnedBy`, which upstream uses for spawn lineage. This differs on purpose from upstream's creator attribution for children, which records the requester, so that a session's secrets never depend on who happened to prompt. Every session in the chain applies its own key and binding checks. A sub-agent also gets nothing if a parent can't be read, on a cycle, or on a chain of more than 16 spawn hops.
- **`parentSessionKey` is not followed.** It also links ordinary sessions created from the Control UI, including, under the default DM and session scopes, every new dashboard session under the main session ("only spawnedBy carries lineage", `src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-depth-policy.ts`).
- **Channel messages** routed by session keys or conversation bindings never reach an eligible session.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Delivery at launch, precedence and names</summary>

**Delivery**

- Entries are read inside the spawn function that both direct and post-approval launches call, before the proxy grant is registered and the process is spawned. A launch costs one session read per session in the spawn chain (usually one), one binding query per session in the chain when it ends at a qualifying creator, and one provider read. Team-store exec takes one snapshot per run, so a deleted session secret stops being delivered sooner than a deleted team entry.
- The stored creator only selects whose vault is read, as a session's stored auth selection picks a model account. The authority is the person keeping entries there.
- `secret` entries use the team-store path (`sealSecretSentinel`, `registerSecretEgressProxyProcess`). One without an allowed host is not delivered, and the command gets a warning.
- If no vault provider is registered, or the plugin is disabled, nothing is delivered. If the provider or the creator lookup fails, the command runs without session secrets and gets a fixed warning, even when that person has no entries. The provider's error text never reaches the tool result.
- Values never travel in `requestedEnv` (which is passed to exec approval requests), approval records, auto-review input or hook events, and OpenClaw never adds them to prompts or tool results. The exception is a command that prints a plaintext entry: its output is a tool result.

**Precedence**

Variables OpenClaw manages (the GitHub identity binding, the egress proxy's own settings, credential scrubs, markers such as `OPENCLAW_SHELL`) > plugin `resolve_exec_env` > per-call `env` > session secrets > team store > the Gateway's own environment.

- Everything except session secrets is today's order (`bash-tools.exec-request-preparation.ts`).
- OpenClaw-managed variables stay on top because an entry that overrode them could bypass the egress proxy or the identity binding. Most of those names are refused for session secrets, and an entry whose name OpenClaw sets for the command is skipped with a warning.
- Per-call and plugin env can replace a session secret for one command. They can't read it.

**Names and sizes**

- Names match the team store's pattern (`^[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]{0,127}$`). If the provider returns two entries with the same name, neither is delivered, and the command gets a warning.
- `env` entries follow the host-env denylist, the Gateway-credential checks and OpenClaw-owned names (`GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `PATH`, `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_*`). That rejects names such as `NPM_TOKEN`, `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN`, `KUBECONFIG` and `DATABASE_URL`.
- `secret` entries are checked less strictly, because commands only see sentinels, but more strictly than in the team store, which seals `secret` entries under any valid name. They can't use `PATH`, `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_*` or names that change how commands run (`NODE_OPTIONS`, `LD_PRELOAD`). Override names such as `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` or `HTTPS_PROXY` are refused unless they look like credentials (`*_TOKEN`, `*_API_KEY`, `*_PASSWORD`, `*_SECRET`, `*_PRIVATE_KEY`). So `NPM_TOKEN` or `GH_TOKEN` works as a protected entry, unless OpenClaw manages that name for the agent (for example `GH_TOKEN` under a managed GitHub identity). Then the entry is skipped with a warning.
- CLIs that sign requests with the secret, such as the AWS CLI, work with neither kind in the first PR: signing can't happen through the proxy, and the AWS credential names are on the host-env denylist that `env` entries follow.
- Limits: 64 KiB per value, as in the team store, and at most 16 entries per person. The cap keeps one vault from filling the Gateway's shared log-redaction registry (512 entries, oldest evicted, up to three per value), which also protects provider and team values. Logs are written raw; redaction applies where they leave the Gateway (`logs.tail`, support bundles, exports).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Host/plugin interface (sketch), the reference vault plugin and the agent's view</summary>

A sketch, not a committed API:

```ts
// Host (core): which session uses whose secrets, delivery and the authority contract.
interface SessionSecrets {
  /** Whose secrets and which names; never values. Anyone who can see the session. */
  status(request: VerifiedRequest, session: SessionRef):
    | { creatorProfileId: string; entryNames: string[] }
    | { excluded: "main-session" | "channel-session" | "inherited"; from?: string /* ancestor session key */ }
    | undefined;
}

// Plugin: owns storage, its RPCs and its settings UI.
interface SessionSecretProvider {
  /** Metadata only: the banner and the agent's list. */
  listNames(profileId: string): Promise<Array<{ name: string; kind: "secret" | "env"; allowedHosts?: string[] }>>;
  /** Values: read only at launch. */
  readEntries(profileId: string): Promise<Array<{ name: string; kind: "secret" | "env"; value: string; allowedHosts?: string[] }>>;
}
```

**Reference vault plugin**

- **Storage:** its own plugin storage. An alternative is a narrow host API over `secret_store_entries` with `scope_kind = 'identity'`, a scope that already exists and that `src/state/user-model-accounts.ts` uses. Either way, the host reads entries only through the provider.
- **Owner-only RPCs:** list (metadata only), set (masked) and delete (hard delete). The owner always comes from the caller's verified profile, never from a parameter. Plugin Gateway methods already receive that profile (`client.authenticatedUserProfile`) and default to `profileAccess: "required"`.

**What the agent sees**

- The `secrets` tool gets an optional `scope: "session"` for `list`, which appears only when a vault provider is registered. The default, `"team"`, is unchanged. `request` and `delete` reject `scope: "session"`. Agents can't write to the vault.
- `list` returns the creator's entry names, kinds and allowed hosts, never values, not even for `env` entries. The team scope's `list` prints `env` values today.
- The `secrets` tool exists only in primary sessions (`docs/tools/secrets.md`). For sub-agents and ACP workers, only status shows whose secrets apply.
- In a session that gets nothing because it is the main session, a channel session or a sub-agent of one, status says why, and so does `list` where the tool exists. Commands get no per-launch warning.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Draft disclosure wording</summary>

- **Vault page:** *"Commands in every session you create can use these entries and act as you at the services they reach. That includes sessions created for you, such as your automations, and sub-agents started from your sessions, whoever's turn started them. It excludes the agent's main chat and sessions that chat channels reach. Sessions are shared by default: everyone who can send in them, and agents, automations and hooks routed to them, can run such commands. Protected secrets need the Gateway's egress proxy, which an admin must enable; until then they aren't delivered. They are sent only to their allowed hosts, but a host that echoes or stores what it receives can return them. Plaintext secrets can be printed: anything a command prints is visible in the session and sent to the model, and files it writes stay on the host. Anyone who can run commands on this Gateway host may be able to read your stored entries. Deleting an entry stops its use from the next command; commands already running keep it."*
- **Banner for participants:** *"Commands in this session use Alice's secrets and act as her."*
- **Tool result for an unsupported launch** (only when the creator has entries): *"Session secrets were not provided to this command: sandbox exec is not supported."*

</details>

### Alternatives considered

- **Each participant's own vault, switched off when someone else prompts** (the earlier version of this issue). Each participant can turn on their own vault for their own turns, and another person's message switches it off. This keeps per-person attribution. Its costs:
  - It needs a breaker on every human input path. In the spikes of this design, most of the code is that breaker and its ingress marking, and several ingress paths would still need marking (OpenAI-compatible HTTP, node voice transcripts, node `agent.request`, embedded TUI).
  - A steer has to become an exception to steering "under that turn's unchanged identity and prepared permissions" (`docs/concepts/queue.md`).
  - It still leaks through background processes. In a review E2E, Bob's turn wrote to Alice's background shell with the `process` tool and read back the hash of her secret after her grant was revoked.
  - Switching between people's secrets leaves half-switched state, such as a CLI that cached a login as Alice before the next command runs without her token.
- **A creator switch per session, ended when more people can send.** The creator turns secrets on per session, and they end on reset, on Gateway restart, or when visibility, members or roles let anyone new send. This needs a record of who could send, a comparison of every profile at each launch, in-memory state and "ended" notices. It is still only as strong as session sharing, which upstream calls a usability feature, not a security boundary. Cron, for example, doesn't check sharing for `session:<key>` targets.
- **A per-person global switch.** Old sessions keep whatever was on, and the switch suggests control it doesn't give. Deleting entries is simpler and does what it says.
- **Bind to the session owner.** Anyone who can see a session can reassign its owner, so Bob could pull Carol's secrets into a session.
- **Plaintext by default.** Simpler, and it covers every CLI, but every printed value lands in the transcript and the model. The team store already chose protected by default, with plaintext as an explicit operator choice.
- **A plugin on the exec environment hook** (`resolve_exec_env`). The closest existing extension point, but its context has agent, session and channel fields and no verified requester profile, and it covers OpenClaw `exec` only. Its values are approval metadata by design: they are merged into `requestedEnv` and so reach exec approval requests. So this proposal adds a separate contract.
- **A vault in core.** Adds a storage owner, RPCs and UI to core for an optional feature. The host contract would be the same, so a core vault could still be built on it later.
- **Selecting which entries a session gets** (suggested in this issue's comments). Useful, but it brings back per-session state and UI. A follow-up once the base contract is accepted.

### Impact

- **Affected:** multi-user Gateways where agents do development work.
- **Severity:** blocks workflow.
- **Frequency:** always, for every command that needs a personal credential.
- **Consequence:** such commands can run only if the credential is stored where every operator and agent on the Gateway can use it.

### Evidence/examples

**Prior art**

- [Amp: Handling Secrets](https://ampcode.com/docs/orbs/handling-secrets): personal secrets, delivered as environment variables to the remote environment (orb) where the agent's commands run. They apply only to the user's own orbs and override project and workspace values.
- [GitHub Codespaces account-specific secrets](https://docs.github.com/en/codespaces/managing-your-codespaces/managing-your-account-specific-secrets-for-github-codespaces): personal secrets, delivered as environment variables. The user chooses which repositories may use each one.

In both, an environment belongs to one user. An OpenClaw session can be shared, so this proposal binds session secrets to the creator and tells everyone in the session whose secrets it uses.

**Local spike**

[`spike/session-secrets-creator-bound`](https://github.com/fetzig/openclaw/tree/spike/session-secrets-creator-bound) in my fork, at [`4b028a4`](https://github.com/fetzig/openclaw/commit/4b028a41d5a), based on `main` at `204216d02a7`. It is evidence, not a PR: it uses a synthetic value provider and has no vault storage, RPCs or UI.

- **Size:** +585/−24 production lines against `main`. The feature lives in `src/agents/session-secrets.ts` (532 lines).
- **Reuse:** the egress proxy is used unchanged (`sealSecretSentinel`, `registerSecretEgressProxyProcess`, one grant per command). The creator comes from upstream's `sessionCreatorProfileId`.
- **End to end:** four E2E tests run an in-process Gateway with Alice and Bob signed in as separate people, real `chat.send`, real `exec` child processes and the real egress-proxy worker. The model is scripted, and the value provider and the Slack binding adapter are test stand-ins.
  - Bob's turn in Alice's Shared session sees only a sentinel for her `secret` entry. The allowed host receives her real value, and a host that isn't allowed receives nothing.
  - Changing visibility (Shared to Draft) and `/new` change nothing. After Alice deletes an entry, Bob's next command no longer has it.
  - The main session gets none of Alice's entries although its row records her as creator. A session bound to a Slack thread gets none.
  - A sub-agent spawned by Bob's turn in Alice's session gets Alice's entries.
  - No value appears in `chat.history`, Gateway events, model requests, logs, stdout/stderr or any file under the Gateway's home.
- **Unit tests:** 63 tests in two files, plus two approval-wait cases in `bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts`, cover the remaining rules, such as precedence, spawn chains and name checks. A mutation check for each rule fails the expected tests.
- **Runs:** the 63 unit tests, 36 host-gateway tests and 4 E2E tests pass. The wider regression set (752 tests across 53 files, 6 skipped) passed at the previous commit, `52ef71f`.
- **Not built or not proven yet:** the vault plugin, a status RPC (status is a function the tests call), the `secrets` tool scope and the banner; a warning for node exec; plain HTTP and CLIs that bypass the proxy (the E2E clears `NO_PROXY` for `curl`); cron jobs after an ownership transfer.

<details>
<summary>More spike results and the earlier spikes</summary>

**End to end, beyond the list above**

- Alice's `env` entry reaches the process, and is still delivered after she deletes her `secret` entry. The deletion gives no notice.
- Status shows Alice and Bob the creator and the entry names.
- Cron: Alice's `session:<key>`, isolated and current-session jobs all get her entries, because their run sessions record her as creator. Bob's isolated job gets nothing. Bob's `session:<key>` job in Alice's Draft gets Alice's entries (see Further limits).
- Sub-agents are spawned through the real `sessions_spawn`. Upstream records Bob as the creator of the one his turn spawns, yet its command gets Alice's entries. A sub-agent spawned from the main session gets nothing, and its status names the main session as the reason.
- A `sessions_send` from the main session into Alice's dashboard session runs a command there that gets her entries.
- Bindings: a session bound to its own `webchat` conversation through the real binding store still gets entries. The Slack thread is bound through a registered stand-in Slack binding adapter, and unbinding it restores delivery.
- The leak checks have positive controls for the transcript, model requests and state files. One case runs on a custom `session.store`.

**Unit tests** cover approval waits (an entry replaced during the wait is not delivered), precedence, sandbox and durable warnings, creator kinds, spawn chains (cycles, deleted and bound parents, `parentSessionKey` not followed, the 16-hop cap), main and channel key shapes, bindings, `session.scope: "global"`, fresh reads at every launch, status visibility and rejected names.

**Other checks**

- Type checks, lint and import-cycle checks are clean.
- One change outside the feature: warnings added at a launch after an approval wait now reach the approval follow-up. Before, they were dropped.
- Commits for the exclusions: [b8ac8a2](https://github.com/fetzig/openclaw/commit/b8ac8a2040c) (main and channel-shaped keys, refused before the session entry or the provider is read), [92ef780](https://github.com/fetzig/openclaw/commit/92ef78000c1) (the binding check) and [23ec3cd](https://github.com/fetzig/openclaw/commit/23ec3cda9bf) (internal `webchat` bindings ignored).

**Earlier spikes (first version of this issue)**

Two spikes in my fork implement the first, per-person design: [`spike/requester-bound-exec-grant`](https://github.com/fetzig/openclaw/tree/spike/requester-bound-exec-grant) against `main` (`204216d02a70`), and [`spike/requester-bound-exec-grant-2`](https://github.com/fetzig/openclaw/tree/spike/requester-bound-exec-grant-2) on top of it ([06cf381](https://github.com/fetzig/openclaw/commit/06cf3811c95), [373b539](https://github.com/fetzig/openclaw/commit/373b5392398)). They are not for merge: they use a synthetic value provider and a test-only setter, deliver plaintext only, and have no vault storage, RPCs or UI. In the second, 365 unit tests across 21 files and 5 E2E tests pass.

The current spike keeps their session resolution, delivery inside the shared spawn path after approvals and hooks, name validation, leak assertions and real-Gateway E2E harness. It does not keep the breaker, ingress marking, the per-input custody flag, the run-sequence check or the in-memory grant registry.

</details>

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance

### Additional information

This proposal changes public contracts and credential permissions, so it asks for design acceptance before any PR.

- **Needs acceptance:** the new host contract. That is session secrets (status and delivery), the provider interface, egress-proxy grants for personal `secret` entries and one optional parameter on the `secrets` tool. The vault plugin's RPCs and UI are its own and use existing plugin Gateway methods.
- **Not needed:** a database schema change, a core config option, a new tool or a new prompt line.
- **Review:** the host PR touches credential handling and exec, so it falls under the security-sensitive review policy.

**Questions for maintainers**

1. **Binding model.** Is it acceptable that every command in a session uses the vault of the person who created the session, with no switch, and with the disclosure on the vault page and in the session? Personal model accounts are session-sticky in a similar way, with two differences: their account is fixed when the session is created, while session secrets read the creator's current entries at each launch; and `sessions_spawn` children don't inherit the account, while sub-agents do inherit session secrets. The two other models, each participant's own vault switched off when someone else prompts, and a per-session switch, are under Alternatives with their costs.
2. **Ownership.** Is a narrow host capability acceptable in core, with the vault shipped as a plugin behind a provider interface? And should the reference plugin be bundled, which `VISION.md` sets a high bar for, or published on ClawHub? Bundling gives the host contract a consumer in the repository.
3. **Authority.** Is one read per command launch the right reading of "a started request may finish"? Running commands, background processes included, then keep their environment and proxy grant after an entry is deleted. The other option is that deleting an entry also stops background processes that received it, as background exec is already cancelled when the launching operator loses access.
4. **Bound sessions.** A session that a channel conversation is bound to, for example a thread-bound sub-agent, gets nothing, and nobody is told why. Should it get nothing, and if so, how should that be shown? The key-based exclusions already report a reason in status, and in `list` where the tool exists.

<details>
<summary>After the first PR: sandbox exec, durable exec and other transports</summary>

Sandbox exec and durable exec are separate decisions, one PR each:

- **Sandbox exec** needs an exemption from the sandbox env filter, which drops secret-looking names such as `*_TOKEN`.
- **Durable exec** would keep its launch environment in plaintext in systemd unit properties on Linux (and the macOS equivalent). That environment would survive Gateway restarts and could not be withdrawn.

The other transports follow, one PR each. Each reuses an existing credential or env mechanism. Where a remote side lacks the new feature, the result is no session secrets, never a fallback route. `secret` entries reach a transport only where the egress proxy covers its traffic.

| Transport | Delivery | A deleted entry stops | Old builds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cloud worker (`worker-turn`) | Snapshot in a new launch-descriptor field, next to the GitHub binding | Within one heartbeat | New worker protocol feature, like `WORKER_GITHUB_REFRESH_PROTOCOL_FEATURE`; binding to an old worker fails |
| Paired node (`system.run`) | Private field in the invoke, applied at spawn after the node's own sanitization; never in `requestedEnv` or approvals | Next launch (decided on the Gateway) | Node capability, like `SYSTEM_RUN_EXECUTION_CONTEXT_CAPABILITY`; without it: nothing, warning in the tool result |
| Codex native shell | Disabled in sessions whose creator has entries; commands go through `gateway_exec` and get the shared delivery, the existing managed-GitHub-identity pattern | Next launch | n/a |
| Codex `remote-exec` | Snapshot delivered to the node workspace lease; applied to exec-server command spawns only, never the node app-server | Next spawn after the node learns of the change | Node capability; without it: nothing, warning |
| ACP (acpx) | Explicit agent-process grant at child spawn | Next turn: on any change the child is closed and respawned | n/a |

Open point: verify that acpx restores the session's context after a respawn.

</details>

issues.body:
### Summary

Add an opt-in inventory to `openclaw backup verify` so operators can see what an existing archive contains before choosing it for recovery.

### Problem to solve

When choosing a backup for rollback or migration, I want to verify that I picked an archive containing the data I need. An archive made with `--only-config` and an archive made with `--no-include-workspace` can both pass verification and report one asset. In a local run, one asset was the config file and the other was the state directory. The verification result gives the count but leaves the distinction in the embedded manifest.

### Proposed solution

Add an opt-in view such as `openclaw backup verify <archive> --inventory` and expose the same inventory as structured data with `--json`. After successful verification, show the archive's recorded asset kinds (for example, config, state, workspace) and the SQLite snapshot roles and agent IDs where recorded. Make a legacy archive with no recorded SQLite inventory distinguishable from an archive whose recorded inventory is empty. Keep the output limited to recovery metadata.

Use the manifest and facts already read during verification. The operator should be able to review them in one invocation without a separate archive scan or a staged restore.

### Alternatives considered

- Read the root `manifest.json` with `tar` and `jq`, then run `backup verify`. This works today, but scripts have to find the timestamped root and interpret the on-disk manifest themselves. The [backup reference](https://docs.openclaw.ai/cli/backup) already walks operators through this workaround.
- Save the JSON from `backup create`. That helps when the operator controls creation and keeps the output. It does not help when reviewing an archive copied from another machine or recovered from storage.

### Impact

This affects operators checking archived backups before a rollback, restore drill, or migration. The extra inspection is required whenever they need to confirm recovery coverage from an archive alone. A single verified inventory would also let preflight scripts check for a required asset before allocating space for a restore.

### Evidence/examples

Ran the actual CLI on Linux at [`3d0900e4ac0`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3d0900e4ac041522836c83fe7672200806361fba) with a temporary state directory, config, and an external workspace containing a test file. Created three local archives with `openclaw backup create --output <archive> --json` and the options below. Ran `openclaw backup verify <archive> --json` on each and checked the embedded manifest with `tar -xOzf <archive> <archiveRoot>/manifest.json`.

| Creation option | Verification result | Asset kinds in the archived manifest |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default | `ok: true`, `assetCount: 2` | `state`, `workspace` |
| `--no-include-workspace` | `ok: true`, `assetCount: 1` | `state` |
| `--only-config` | `ok: true`, `assetCount: 1` | `config` |

All three reported `sqliteInventoryVerified: true` with an empty recorded snapshot inventory in this fixture. The CLI JSON exposed neither the asset kinds nor the snapshot inventory. This run exercised local archive creation and verification.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance

issues.body:
### Bug type
Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker
No

### Summary
When an npm update fails during activation and rolls back, `restoreUpdateDatabaseBackup` puts back database snapshots that are in `journal_mode=DELETE`, even though the live databases were in WAL. This happens on a filesystem whose resolved journal policy is `wal` (local APFS). Nothing restores WAL afterwards.

On the next update, activation Doctor fails with `store unavailable (sqlite-busy)` while acquiring `core:agent-database-maintenance/global`. That run rolls back too, restores DELETE again, and every later retry fails the same way. Converting the databases back to WAL by hand, while nothing held them, let the next update's Doctor complete.

### Steps to reproduce
Observed sequence on one host (npm global install, macOS):
1. Run `openclaw update --tag 2026.11.6` from 2026.11.3 with all databases in WAL. Activation Doctor failed for an unrelated reason (a stale gateway lock), and rollback ran `restoreUpdateDatabaseBackup`.
2. After the rollback, the state database and all 11 agent databases are in `journal_mode=delete` (SQLite header byte 18 = `01`).
3. Retry the update. Activation Doctor fails with `failed to acquire agent database maintenance lease core:agent-database-maintenance/global: store unavailable (sqlite-busy)`, and the run rolls back again, restoring DELETE once more.
4. Steps 2–3 repeated identically on three more retries.
5. With no OpenClaw process holding the files (checked with `lsof`), run `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` on each of the 12 databases (`quick_check` = `ok` on each). The next `openclaw update` gets through activation Doctor ("Doctor complete.").

Suggested minimal repro, not yet run in a clean environment:
- Use a scratch `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` on a local APFS or ext4 volume with WAL databases.
- Force any activation failure after `database snapshot`, so the rollback restores the DBs.
- Check `PRAGMA journal_mode` on the restored files.
- Retry while any reader connection to `state/openclaw.sqlite` is open.

### Expected behavior
After a rollback, each restored SQLite database is in the journal mode that `resolvePathJournalPolicy()` resolves for its path. That is WAL on local APFS/ext4, the same as before the update.

### Actual behavior
Restored databases stay in rollback-journal (DELETE) mode. The next update's Doctor cannot get its maintenance lease while the updater holds reader connections, so updates keep failing in a loop.

### OpenClaw version
2026.11.6. `openclaw --version` reports `06afb10`. The annotated tag `v2026.11.6` (tag object `e780fed3`) points to commit `06afb10d3272cc9deaf38ca6a3b7b839d5935638`; the GitHub compare shows the two as identical. I also compared the installed npm `dist/` files involved against a separate npm install of `openclaw@2026.11.6`: `update-database-restore-*.mjs`, `update-database-restore-source-*.mjs`, `sqlite-snapshot-*.mjs`, `openclaw-agent-db-maintenance-lease-*.mjs` and `openclaw-state-lease-*.mjs` have identical SHA-256. Source line numbers below are from tag `v2026.11.6`. The matching statements are present in the shipped dist.

### Operating system
- **Affected host:** macOS 27.0.1 (26A434), arm64 (Apple M2). State directory on the internal APFS Data volume; `resolvePathJournalPolicy` → `wal`, `statfs` type 26.
- **Unaffected comparison:** Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, aarch64, ext4, same OpenClaw build. Its first 11.6 update succeeded, it never rolled back, and its databases are WAL.

### Install method
npm global (Homebrew Node v26.12.1, bundled `node:sqlite` 3.54.1).

### Model
N/A

### Provider / routing chain
N/A

### Logs
Sanitized; home and state paths replaced, PIDs and hostnames removed.

```
# attempt 2 (first rollback, unrelated Doctor failure)
Failing check doctor (doctor-failed): Doctor could not enter maintenance. cannot verify Gateway ownership from this process; heartbeat age does not prove that the holder stopped. holder <dead pid> at unknown host, last renewed ~51 days ago.
Databases snapshotted at <npm-prefix>/lib/node_modules/.openclaw.package-backup-<id>.databases.
Restored pre-migration databases from <npm-prefix>/lib/node_modules/.openclaw.package-backup-<id>.databases.

# attempts 3, 4, 5 (identical)
Failing check doctor (doctor-failed): failed to acquire agent database maintenance lease core:agent-database-maintenance/global: store unavailable (sqlite-busy)
Failing check openclaw doctor (ERR_SQLITE_ERROR): Doctor: Update schema admission
Restored pre-migration databases from <npm-prefix>/lib/node_modules/.openclaw.package-backup-<id>.databases.
Phases: requested (~110s) → staging → validating (~430–600s) → activating (~440–490s)

# attempt 6, after manual PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL on all 12 DBs
└  Doctor complete.
Phases: requested (101.87s) → staging (11ms) → validating (571.17s) → activating (925.21s) → restarting (5.47s) → verifying
```

No `could not enable WAL`, `database is locked` or `journal_mode` messages appear in the gateway or updater logs, so the mode change is never reported.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

**Observed: SQLite header byte 18/19** (`01 01` = rollback journal, `02 02` = WAL):

| File | state DB | chief agent DB |
|---|---|---|
| Live DB before the first rollback (displaced as `*.migrated-<runId>`) | `02` | `02` |
| All 5 `.openclaw.package-backup-*.databases` snapshots (attempts 2–6) | `01` | `01` |
| Live DBs after rollback (byte-verified backup taken before manual conversion) | `01` | `01` |
| Agent DB displaced at attempts 3–5 (mtime = first restore, never rewritten) | n/a | `01` |
| Live DBs after manual WAL conversion, and after the successful update | `02` | `02` |
| Comparison host that never rolled back | `wal` | `wal` |

**Observed:** while Doctor was failing, `lsof` sampling every 3 s showed only the updater's own processes (driver plus workers) holding files under the state and agent directories. No gateway, app, node host or HA process held them.

**Observed: code path at `v2026.11.6`:**
- **Capture deliberately writes DELETE.** `configureSqliteSnapshotPragmas` (`src/infra/sqlite-wal.ts:139`) runs `PRAGMA journal_mode = DELETE`. It is called from `createStoppedSqliteSnapshot` (`src/infra/sqlite-snapshot.ts:149`, call at `:165`) and `createVerifiedSqliteSnapshot` (`:554`, call at `:683`). `UpdateDatabaseBackupSchema` (`src/infra/update-database-backup.ts:63`) does not record the source journal mode.
- **The shared state DB restore image is forced to DELETE.** `prepareUpdateDatabaseRestoreSourceInProcess`, `src/infra/update-database-restore-source.ts:46`.
- **Restore publishes those bytes and never reapplies the journal policy.**
  - `restoreUpdateDatabaseBackup` (`src/infra/update-database-restore.ts:123`) displaces live files and their `-wal/-shm/-journal` sidecars (`:264–276`, `:307–325`).
  - It publishes SHA-verified copies (`prepareVerifiedSqliteFile` `:284–303`; `afterPublish` hash check `:302`; publish loop `:326–331`).
  - `resolvePathJournalPolicy` (`src/infra/sqlite-wal-filesystem.ts:322`) is not called anywhere in this path.
- **Normal opens only switch to WAL when they can.** `configureSqliteWalMaintenance` (`src/infra/sqlite-wal.ts:278`; policy branch `:303–311`) calls `enableWalJournalMode` (`:206`), which needs exclusive access.
- **Lease acquisition.**
  - `withAgentDatabaseMaintenanceLease` uses `waitMs: 5000`, `leaseMs: 60000`.
  - The lease write runs with `busyTimeoutMs: 0`.
  - `acquireOpenClawStateLease` retries lock errors every 25 ms until `waitMs`, then throws `kind: "store-unavailable", reason: "sqlite-busy"`.

**Inferred, not directly observed:**
- In DELETE mode, the lease commit needs an EXCLUSIVE lock, which any reader's SHARED lock blocks. The updater's open reader connections therefore keep the 5 s, zero-busy-timeout lease write failing. WAL would let the commit proceed alongside readers.
- I did not capture the specific connection holding the SHARED lock at the moment of failure. `lsof` shows open files, not lock state.
- The state DBs displaced at attempts 3–5 are WAL, with mtimes at each failure time. That suggests something switched the state DB to WAL after Doctor's connections closed, before the rollback displaced it. Agent DBs were never switched.

### Impact and severity
- **Affected:** npm installs on WAL-capable local filesystems where an update fails after `database snapshot` and rolls back.
- **Severity:** blocks every later update with no clear cause. The error names the lease, not the journal mode, and each retry costs about 20–25 min of validation and activation, with gateway downtime on single-gateway hosts. Rollback restores the data correctly; there is no data loss.
- **Frequency:** every retry after the first rollback on this host (4 of 4).

### Additional information

**Proposed fix (not implemented):**
1. **Preflight, before any live file is moved.**
   - Inside the `withDatabaseExclusion` callback, before the displacement loop at `src/infra/update-database-restore.ts:264`, resolve `resolvePathJournalPolicy(entry.path)` for every SQLite entry in `sources`.
   - If any resolves to `unsupported` (SSHFS), refuse exactly as `refuseUnsupportedFilesystem` does (`src/infra/sqlite-wal.ts:269`), while no live DB has been displaced. Otherwise the refusal would only surface after publication and leave a half-reconciled family.
   - Keep the resolved policies for step 2.
2. **Reconcile after publication.**
   - After the publish loop (`:326–331`) and before `restoreClientCredentials?.()` (`:332`), still under the gateway lock (`acquireGatewayLock`, role `sqlite-maintenance`, `:56`), the `prepareOpenClawStateDatabaseRemoval` exclusions and the drained agent resources.
   - Apply each preflighted policy: `wal` → `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL`, requiring `wal` (reuse `enableWalJournalMode` through a small export); `rollback` → keep DELETE (`requireRollbackJournalMode` semantics).
   - Call `assertOwned()` before and after each database, and close each handle before the next.
   - This has to come after `afterPublish` (`:302`), which verifies the DELETE snapshot bytes.
3. **Exclusions and failures.**
   - Skip `engine === "postgres"` entries; they are restored through `preparePostgresRestore` (`:192–219`).
   - If any `output.publish()` throws, skip reconciliation and leave the existing `retainPreparedCopy` recovery path unchanged.
   - If WAL cannot be enabled on a published DB, keep the restored data and report the rollback step with the path and the actual mode.
4. **Optional:**
   - Record the source journal mode in `UpdateDatabaseBackupSchema` and restore that.
   - Include `journal_mode` in the `sqlite-busy` lease error.
   - Have Doctor or update admission warn when the policy is `wal` but a DB is in `delete` mode.

**Regression tests,** in this order. Each pins the order of operations, not just the end state:
1. **End-to-end reproduction (write first):** WAL state + agent DBs → backup → forced activation failure → `restoreUpdateDatabaseBackup` → open a reader on `openclaw.sqlite` → `withAgentDatabaseMaintenanceLease`. It should fail with `store unavailable (sqlite-busy)` before the fix and acquire the lease after.
2. **Mode restored:** after restore, every SQLite DB reports `PRAGMA journal_mode` = `wal`, and `afterPublish` saw the snapshot SHA-256 before any header change. Assert the call order: `publish` → hash check → journal reconcile → `restoreClientCredentials`.
3. **Preflight refusal:** with the policy mocked to `unsupported`, the restore refuses before any `publishFileExclusive` displacement. No `.migrated-<runId>` files exist and live DBs are untouched.
4. **Rollback policy:** with the policy mocked to `rollback`, the restored DBs stay `delete`.
5. **PostgreSQL:** entries are skipped; no `DatabaseSync` is opened on their paths.
6. **Partial publication:** the 2nd `output.publish()` throws → no reconciliation PRAGMA runs, `retainPreparedCopy` stays true, and the original error comes out unchanged.
7. **Ownership loss:** `assertOwned` throws before reconciliation → no PRAGMA runs.

Natural homes: `src/cli/update-cli/update-command-database-rollback.test.ts` (with `.test-support.ts`), or a new `src/infra/update-database-restore.journal-mode.test.ts`.

**Related:**
- #200594 / #200659: earlier 11.5 Mac blocker; 11.6 validation on this host passed with that fix.
- #202700: update rollback when Doctor cannot enter maintenance (different trigger, same rollback path).
- #193859, #120597: journal-policy resolution for macOS and VM filesystems that the restore path should honour.
- #200830: other agent-database maintenance failure, not the same cause.

**Workaround, for affected users:**
1. Stop every OpenClaw process using the state dir.
2. Back up the database files.
3. Run `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;` on `state/openclaw.sqlite` and each `agents/*/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite`.
4. Check that `PRAGMA quick_check` returns `ok`, then retry the update.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On 2026.11.3, `openclaw update status` keeps reporting `Plugin "codex" data/settings upgrade is unfinished` after both `openclaw update repair` and `openclaw doctor --fix`, and the published `@openclaw/codex@2026.11.3` still contains the lifecycle check that #186506 (f61cb97d825, merged 2026-11-02) replaced on `main`.

### Steps to reproduce

Observed on one production install; this is not a synthetic reproducer.

1. Install: npm global, LaunchAgent-managed Gateway, and a long-lived default session `agent:main:main` (current session id started 2026-09-23) that has run on the Codex harness.
2. Update 2026.10.9 → 2026.11.3 through the Gateway update action. The run succeeded.
3. `openclaw update status` lists the Codex warning quoted below. Whether it was already pending on 2026.10.9 was not recorded.
4. Run `openclaw update repair`. The run succeeded. Its summary includes `Preserved Codex assignments with unknown lifecycle evidence in session-key:main:<id>`, where `<id>` is the base64url SHA-256 of `agent:main:main`. The Codex warning remains.
5. Run `openclaw doctor --fix`. `openclaw update status` still lists the Codex warning. Doctor's terminal output from this pass was not kept.

### Expected behavior

Doctor finishes the Codex migration. The 2026-11-02 maintainer comment on #190608 describes this for a build containing f61cb97d825: Doctor prints `Deferred state migration completed for plugin "codex"` and `migrationWarnings` clears when the assignment and its requester both lack a lifecycle revision. The same comment says the fix "ships with the next release that includes main".

### Actual behavior

`openclaw update status --json` after both repair passes:

```json
"migrationWarnings": [
  "Plugin \"codex\" data/settings upgrade is unfinished: The installed plugin has not confirmed that its saved data and settings are ready for this version. If Doctor cannot finish the upgrade, report this warning to the plugin maintainer. Your existing data and settings have been kept. Run \"openclaw doctor --fix\" to retry the upgrade."
]
```

The Codex harness itself works: a Codex-runtime agent turn completed normally after each pass.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.3 (847611d); `@openclaw/codex` 2026.11.3 (npm, trusted-official)

### Operating system

macOS 27.2.1 (arm64)

### Install method

npm global; LaunchAgent-managed Gateway; Node v24.22.2

### Model

Not model-dependent. The defect is in the Doctor state-migration path.

### Provider / routing chain

Not applicable to the defect. Agents run on the Codex app-server harness (bundled app-server 0.164.0).

### Logs

From the recorded `openclaw update repair` run:

```text
Warning: Preserved Codex assignments with unknown lifecycle evidence in session-key:main:<id>.
Warning: Plugin "codex" data/settings upgrade is unfinished: The installed plugin has not confirmed that its saved data and settings are ready for this version. [...]
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Source comparison, read through the GitHub API on 2026-11-12 UTC:

- `extensions/codex/src/migration/native-assignment-repair.ts` at `v2026.11.3` (lines 105–109) and at `v2026.11.5-beta.2` (lines 114–118) still warns whenever either revision is missing, including when both are:
  ```ts
  if (!assignment.owner.lifecycleRevision || !current.entry.lifecycleRevision) {
    unknownLifecycle = true;
  ```
  The installed package's `dist/.setup/native-assignment-repair-*.mjs` matches.
- On `main` the equal-revisions check comes first (line 132): `if (assignment.owner.lifecycleRevision === current.entry.lifecycleRevision) {`.
- `GET /repos/openclaw/openclaw/compare/f61cb97d825...<tag>` returns `diverged` for `v2026.10.10`, `v2026.11.1`, `v2026.11.2`, `v2026.11.3` and `v2026.11.5-beta.2`. It returns `ahead` only for `main`.

In the installed core, `migratePluginDoctorStatePlans` removes a plugin from `completedPluginIds` when any of its migrations returns a warning. This recoverable warning therefore keeps the deferred Codex migration pending on every pass.

### Impact and severity

- Affected: this install. Other 2026.11.x stable installs with a revision-less same-session assignment would presumably behave the same; that is not observed here.
- Severity: annoying. Codex works and its settings are kept. The warning is permanent, and the recovery command it recommends cannot clear it.
- Frequency: 2 of 2 repair passes.
- Consequence: each pass restarts the Gateway without changing the result. Here `update repair` ran for about 4 minutes and `doctor --fix` kept the Gateway down for about 7 minutes.

### Additional information

- I could not determine from supported read-only surfaces whether the preserved assignment is the both-revisions-absent case that f61cb97d825 covers or the one-sided case that still warns by design. `openclaw sessions list --json` does not expose `lifecycleRevision`, and the warning does not name the missing side. The state databases were not opened or edited.
- Requests:
  1. Include f61cb97d825 in the next stable release.
  2. Name the missing side in the warning, or document a read-only way to tell the two cases apart.
  3. If the one-sided case applies, document the supported way to settle it.
- Related: #186506, #190608, #169423.

Filed from the affected Gateway by the operator's OpenClaw agent at the operator's request.

issues.body:
### Summary

Add `gateway.resources.profile: auto | standard | lean`, with automatic selection and diagnostics that show which profile is active, why, and which workers are alive.

### Problem to solve

Worker topology is tuned only for throughput on large machines, and operators can't see or control it. Without a single profile switch, each lean change would need its own setting.

### Proposed solution

- **Setting:** `auto` reads the effective cgroup v2 `memory.max` (otherwise total RAM) and `availableParallelism()`. It picks `lean` below a threshold, provisionally ~2 GiB or ≤2 CPUs, to be calibrated. An explicit value overrides it.
- **One owner:** the resolved profile is exposed through one runtime owner that worker pools and plugins can read. This item doesn't change any pool behaviour yet.
- **Diagnostics:** `openclaw status` and gateway diagnostics report:
  - the profile and the reason it was chosen;
  - the memory limit and CPUs it was based on;
  - a live worker census: kind, count, floor, cap, idle policy and heap used.

### Alternatives considered

Separate per-pool settings. They're harder to reason about and would multiply the test matrix.

### Impact

This is the foundation for the lean profile. The diagnostics alone help operators who report high memory today.

### Evidence/examples

A topology census of main found 86 logical worker roles. Users investigating memory currently can't see which workers exist or why (#159858).

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes.

### Additional information

Part of #202373. Standard must behave exactly as today.
