prs.title: feat(talk): let Gateway-controlled GA voice calls use ChatGPT sign-in and always route through the agent
prs.body:
Closes #201699
Related: #194114, #115623, #164229

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-controlled voice calls (thin clients that request `gateway-control-v1`) on the OpenAI GA realtime models only worked with an OpenAI Platform API key. With just a ChatGPT sign-in, `talk.client.create` failed with `Realtime provider "openai" does not support gateway-control-v1 with its configured authentication`, even though ordinary browser Talk already uses that sign-in for these models. These calls also ignored `talk.realtime.consultRouting: "force-agent-consult"`, so the voice model answered on its own instead of going through the agent.

## User Impact

User impact: subscription-only users can run Gateway-controlled Talk on `gpt-realtime-2.1`, `gpt-realtime-2.1-mini` and `gpt-realtime-2`. With `force-agent-consult`, every finished request goes through the agent once and the agent's answer is spoken. Spoken controls such as "status" and "cancel" get their normal spoken reply, including when nothing is running. When a call's consult queue is full, the caller is told to start a new call instead of hearing silence. Platform keys keep precedence; a configured Platform key that cannot be resolved still fails instead of falling back to the sign-in. Client-owned browser sessions, Platform-key Gateway control without forced routing, and GPT-Live Gateway control behave as before: GPT-Live with `force-agent-consult` still starts, keeps native delegation and logs one warning that forced routing is ignored. The Control UI does not request Gateway control yet; a follow-up will.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **ChatGPT sign-in.** Gateway control already uses the same offer broker and call endpoint (`POST /v1/realtime/calls`) as GA browser Talk over OAuth (#115623). This removes the remaining Platform-only gates, resolves credentials once with the browser rules (Platform first, unresolvable Platform blocks, then the ChatGPT profile), and sends `chatgpt-account-id` with the OAuth bearer on the sideband WebSocket and hangup as well as call creation. The provider reports Gateway control for a usable ChatGPT profile.
- **Forced consult routing.** With `force-agent-consult`, a GA session starts with `create_response: false` (barge-in stays on, like relay). Each final user transcript first goes to the existing spoken-control owner. Because forced routing turns provider replies off, that owner now also answers an idle "status" or "cancel" itself (the same rule it already uses for native delegation and tool-less providers) instead of letting it fall through. Anything else waits the relay's 200 ms window for a native `openclaw_agent_consult`, then runs one consult through the existing consult runner and speaks the answer through the existing Gateway-control exact-speech path. It reuses the relay's forced-consult coordinator: a native call inside the window wins, and a late native call for a started forced consult gets an "already delivered" result with no second run. When admission is full (one active plus eight waiting, unchanged), the call speaks "OpenClaw cannot take more requests on this call. Please start a new call to ask again." through the same speech path. Admission stays sealed after an overflow, as for native consults, so a new call is the recovery.
- **GPT-Live compatibility.** GPT-Live delegates natively, so forced routing does not apply to it under Gateway control. The call starts as it did before, keeps native delegation, and logs `talk client: force-agent-consult routing is ignored for GPT-Live under Gateway control; GPT-Live delegates to the agent natively`. Gateway relay keeps rejecting GPT-Live with forced routing, unchanged. Forced routing also no longer changes which model is picked: with no `talk.realtime.model`, Gateway control gets the same provider default as on `main` (GPT-Live with only a ChatGPT sign-in), so forced routing needs an explicit GA model such as `gpt-realtime-2.1`.
- I chose to run the consult on the Gateway instead of asking the model for a forced tool call (`response.create` + `tool_choice`): that path works on the provider, but the model speaks a short preamble first, and it needs a new bridge command.

## Evidence

**Real end to end over ChatGPT OAuth.** A Gateway built from this branch (`d31594a`) ran on an isolated `OPENCLAW_HOME`, its own port and log file, with real internet. The only credential was a ChatGPT sign-in (Codex CLI device login, imported as an `openai` OAuth profile through a legacy `auth-profiles.json` and `doctor --fix`). There was no Platform key and `OPENAI_API_KEY` was unset. The agent behind Talk used the same sign-in (`openai/gpt-5.6-luna` over `chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex`). Talk config: `openai`, `gpt-realtime-2.1`, `webrtc`, `agent-consult`, `force-agent-consult`. A headless werift client connected as an operator, called `talk.client.create` with `gateway-control-v1`, posted its SDP offer to the returned URL, played two spoken clips as Opus RTP and recorded the audio the call sent back.

| Step | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `talk.client.create`, ChatGPT OAuth only | ok in 613 ms, `clientControl: {owner: "gateway"}` |
| Call creation | `POST api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls` → `201` with `Bearer` + `chatgpt-account-id`; offer answered in 1.3 s, WebRTC media connected |
| Sideband | `wss://api.openai.com/v1/realtime?call_id=…` opened with `Bearer` + `chatgpt-account-id`; `session.update` → `session.updated` with `create_response: false` |
| Spoken "What is seventeen plus twenty five?" | provider transcript `What is seventeen plus twenty-five?`; exactly one agent run (`talk-realtime-consult-…`), model call `200` on the ChatGPT route; exact-speech request `Answer: "Forty-two."`; the call started speaking "Forty-two." 5.4 s after the transcript |
| Spoken "How is it going?" with nothing running (finding 1) | handled by spoken control, no agent run; reply spoken 20 ms after the transcript: "I'm not working on an active request right now." |
| Hang up | sideband closed `1000`; hangup `200` with `Bearer` + `chatgpt-account-id`; Gateway stopped |

Transcript of the recorded call audio (23.5 s WAV, transcribed locally with faster-whisper; `base` and `large-v3-turbo` agree):

The Control UI text size preference can enlarge the conversation while leaving code blocks, tool output, and several details at their default sizes. This makes tool-heavy chats harder to read on narrow screens.

## User Impact

Chat code and tool output follow the text size preference alongside the conversation. Message source labels and attachment details use the same scale.

## Why This Change Was Made

prs.title: fix(sandbox): keep .NET build output out of workspace results
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A .NET build in a cloud workspace can copy a large native NuGet runtime into `bin/Debug/net10.0/runtimes/…`. The result then exceeds the 64 MiB per-file limit, preserving pending changes and telling the user to ask a Gateway administrator to run `openclaw sandbox recover`. One regenerable build artifact blocks source changes from returning.

## User Impact

Workspace capture and transfer omit `bin/Debug`, `bin/Release`, `obj/Debug`, and `obj/Release` at any project depth. Authored siblings such as `m/bin/tool.sh` remain eligible. Existing result limits stay unchanged. Historical baselines containing .NET output remain recoverable through exact saved-root authentication.

Accepted edge cases: custom configurations such as `bin/Staging` and platform layouts such as `bin/x64/Debug` remain eligible.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared derived-path policy lacked .NET output segments, so NuGet's copied native runtime was treated as a workspace edit. Follow #202881: define the four segments once, spread them into the existing directory policy and rsync exclusions, regenerate both manifest consumers with `pnpm runtime:scripts:gen`, and document the exclusions.

Use Design B for historical repair: generate the powerset of pnpm, AGP, and .NET eligibility, ordered by size with the empty subset first. Three families bound this to **8 eligibility candidates, repair path only**, across the existing projection/canonical/canonicalWithProjectionPaths candidates. Each still requires the unchanged `rebuiltRoot === expectedRoot` check. Normal capture does not request legacy eligibility.

Design A (admit only baseline-recorded derived paths) cannot cover missing-inventory repair: the saved root digest can survive while the inventory records are absent, and the admitted source paths do not retain that missing membership. Independent eligibility also matters when a baseline containing pnpm files coexists with AGP files created later; cumulative generations lose that existing recovery case.

The pr-simplify pass keeps this in the existing policy owner and repair loop, replaces the handwritten subset list, and adds no configuration or persistent state. Fixture maps consolidate equivalent setup without removing assertions or existing repair cases.

## Evidence

The existing capture fixture creates oversized files under all four .NET subtrees. Local capture, standalone capture, and real local rsync omit them while retaining `m/bin/tool.sh`. Repair covers projection, canonical, and checkpoint baselines containing .NET output, plus a .NET baseline with later disposable AGP and pnpm files. All existing AGP/pnpm repair and divergent-edit cases remain green, including the pnpm-baseline/later-AGP case.

| Proof | Result | Command wall time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capture fixture only on base `b7bf937423f65c313c8fe98b81b112537286ecaf` | 2 failed, 9 passed; .NET files and their ancestry wrongly included | 7.81s |
| Repair fixture against exclusion-only variant (four segments added, repair eligibility unchanged) | 3 failed, 20 passed; historical .NET roots cannot reconstruct | 29.06s |
| Full fix: capture/transfer | 11 passed | 74.39s |
| Full fix: repair | 23 passed | 7.87s |

The checkpoint case already recovers through its saved receipt in the exclusion-only variant. Historical .NET repair is green on the original base because that base does not yet exclude .NET; the meaningful red comparison is the exclusion-only variant, as in #202881.

Commands use `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs <file> --maxWorkers=1` for `workspace-generated-paths.test.ts` and `local-workspace-manifest-scan.test.ts`. The capture run's cold compiled-worker preparation took 51.85s; actual fixture checks exercise local files, standalone scripts, and rsync without starting or contacting a Gateway or test host. Repair tests took about 1.1s; the final warm command took 7.87s.

Passing targeted checks: `pnpm tsgo:core`; changed-test typecheck (`gateway-other`, 3.3s); scoped `scripts/run-oxlint.mjs`; `pnpm format:check`; `pnpm runtime:scripts:check`; targeted `scripts/check-docs-mdx.mjs`; `git diff --check`.

Formatted whole-PR delta against the base: production **+44/-26** (including generated consumers), docs **+5/-0**, tests **+7/-8**, **net test -1**. No new test declaration or removed assertion.

Codex autoreview of both the complete local candidate and committed PR head `66ce1c0a9828c74a98c60841c0b3b3b84ab84c76` against base `b7bf937423f65c313c8fe98b81b112537286ecaf` is scoped-clean through P2, with no accepted/actionable findings. Exact-head [CI run 44866652235](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44866652235) completed successfully in 749 seconds elapsed. The repository watcher reported GREEN with zero pending checks and 24 superseded contexts. Per-file CI timings are not exposed in the run summary. GitHub Codex code review also completed on this head with no findings; there are no inline review comments. No CI rerun was requested.

Release-note context: Sandbox workspace results now omit conventional .NET Debug/Release build output so large regenerable native runtimes cannot block source changes from returning. Historical pnpm, AGP, and .NET baseline recovery remains independently authenticated; authored scripts and result limits are preserved.

prs.title: fix: retain channel message IDs in oversized chat history
prs.body:
Related: #201645

## What Problem This Solves

Clients use a channel message ID to find a message in `chat.history`. When history replaces a large message from an active session with a placeholder, the client loses that lookup key.

## User Impact

Clients can still match the placeholder to its channel message ID. The message body stays within the existing history size limit.

## Why This Change Was Made

The placeholder retains the two fields that identify the channel message. The existing byte-budget check still runs on the resulting placeholder.

## Evidence

Same packaged CLI and Gateway scenario on base `43ed271df4a1bc109d8fe07c502985f40c116d6a` and head `20c918abe2812c655d2355007b7277e7274ab75c`. I used the production session writer to store two messages with A2A transport metadata in an isolated SQLite profile. The actual `chat.history` request exercised the normal Gateway response.

```text
base  64-byte control   transport={channel:a2a,messageId:a2a-control}   omitted=false
base  150-KiB message   transport=missing                              omitted=true
head  64-byte control   transport={channel:a2a,messageId:a2a-control}   omitted=false
head  150-KiB message   transport={channel:a2a,messageId:a2a-larger}    omitted=true
```

<details>
<summary>Commands and test scope</summary>

```sh
node ../history-probe.mjs
node openclaw.mjs gateway call chat.history --params '{"sessionKey":"agent:main:transport-proof","maxChars":500000}' --json
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.gateway.config.ts src/gateway/server-methods/chat-history-budget.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

Seed a 64-byte row and a 150 KiB row with `appendTranscriptMessage`, start the built Gateway on loopback, and compare `messages[].__openclaw.transport` and each message body. The harness retries only while the Gateway reports that it is still preparing the agent database. It cleans up its temporary profile and child process.

All 6 focused tests passed. They include the over-budget sentinel and the omission of other transport properties from the placeholder. Codex autoreview timed out after 135 seconds without a report.

Not tested: inbound delivery from an external A2A service or oversized rows in legacy JSONL archives.

</details>

### Regression on the original source

I copied only the new test from this PR onto base `43ed271df4a1bc109d8fe07c502985f40c116d6a` and ran that test through the repository Gateway test runner. It failed at the expected assertion because the oversized response had no `__openclaw.transport`. The remaining five cases were skipped by the test-name filter. The original head run passed all six tests at `20c918abe2812c655d2355007b7277e7274ab75c`.

~~~text
Base: 1 failed, 5 skipped. Missing __openclaw.transport on the oversized placeholder.
Head: 6 passed.
~~~

To reproduce the base failure, use the test file from this PR on the base above and add `-t 'retains a channel message reference'` to the test command in Evidence.

prs.title: fix: check a recorded data-at-risk mark before repair or the next update acts on it
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an update step fails after it may have touched state, the updater records a "data at risk" mark on that run, for example `rollback-state-unverified`. Most of these marks come from a failed read or a timeout, not from real damage. The published 2026.10.33 and 2026.11.5 updaters keep writing them, and nothing ever checked a mark:

- The update report said "Keep the Gateway stopped" even when the Gateway was running.
- `openclaw update repair` then refused to start the Gateway for that run every time, naming only `openclaw gateway status --deep`.
- The next `openclaw update` ignored the mark completely. When the installation was already current, it exited 0 without a word.

## User Impact

User impact: a recorded data-at-risk mark is now checked against the state on disk, without the user having to run anything first.

- **State consistent:** the next plain `openclaw update` prints one line, resolves the mark and continues. That includes automatic updates and updates that find the installation already current. `openclaw update repair` does the same and also starts a Gateway the marked update stopped.
- **Real inconsistency:** the update or repair still refuses and changes nothing. It says what is wrong and whether the Gateway is running, records the finding on the run, and names `openclaw triage` first and the manual command last.
- **Killed-update refusals from #201361** now also name `openclaw triage` before the manual command.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **One verification owner** (`src/infra/update-data-at-risk.ts`) answers "is the state on disk consistent with the installed version?".
  - It reuses the runtime schema preflight: a child process reads the database in one native read transaction, with no copy, so it is safe beside a live writer. It also uses the existing recovery-admission readers.
  - Findings: a database newer than the installed build, a database behind it (unfinished migration), unfinished update recovery, an interrupted restore directory, retained `.migrated-<run>` files from the marked run's database rollback (state may be only partly restored), or unreadable state (unverifiable).
  - An `active-mutation` mark (Doctor writers that may still be alive) is not resolved from schemas alone. Before Doctor it is deferred to Doctor. After the run's own Doctor maintenance has held exclusive state and agent ownership, no earlier writer can still hold the state, and the schema check decides.
- **History is not rewritten.** A consistent verification records the step `finalize:data-at-risk-verified:<marked run>` on the run that checked. Readers in `src/infra/update-run-data-at-risk.ts` treat "marked, later verified" as resolved. No new field, schema or protocol. Published updaters store the mark as the `finalize:data-at-risk` step, which the current reader already decodes, so their marks are handled the same way.
- **Repair.** Before it touches the Gateway, repair verifies every unverified mark in recent history, not only the run that stopped the Gateway. Git release updates and refusals before mutation never stop it. Any inconsistent finding keeps every Gateway as it is, whichever run stopped it. The managed-handoff interrupted-update path reads the same receipt before it restarts.
- **Next update.** Admission runs the same check after foreground admission and before it creates its run, so already-current updates are covered too.
  - Consistent: one line, plus receipts on the new run.
  - Newer state or unreadable: a warning, and the update continues, because its own schema checks still guard activation and updating is the fix for newer state.
  - Anything else: refusal. The refusal happens after the run exists, so the finding is recorded for the agent `openclaw triage` opens.
- **Messages.**
  - Update failure guidance states whether the Gateway was observed running or stopped, which version is installed and whether the update was rolled back, and says the mark is unverified.
  - With the Gateway running, it says nothing is needed now. With it stopped, it names repair to bring it back.
  - Refusals put the next steps before the finding, so the recorded warning's 500-character limit cannot cut them off.
  - Update-path guidance that asks you to stop the managed Gateway names `openclaw gateway stop --force`, because a non-interactive shell refuses the bare command. That covers the repair, status and maintenance-error messages and their docs; #201331 changed one more line in `update-recovery-guidance.ts`.

<details><summary>Genuine refusals kept, and their negative controls</summary>

- **Database newer than the installed version.** Repair refuses and leaves the Gateway as it was (owner test with real SQLite; Docker cell `inconsistent-repair`). The next update warns and continues, and its target schema check still refuses a target that cannot open that state.
- **Unfinished migration** (database behind the installed version): owner test with real SQLite. The next update refuses, and the finding is recorded on the refused run.
- **Unfinished update recovery or an interrupted restore directory:** owner tests with real fixtures. Repair and update admission already refuse these first.
- **Partial database rollback** (the marked run left `.migrated-<run>` files): owner test. Another run's leftover does not count.
- **`active-mutation`:** never resolved by a schema check alone. It is checked only after the run's own Doctor maintenance has held exclusive state ownership.
- **Unreadable state or an unlistable state directory:** reported as unverifiable, never as consistent or as an interrupted restore.
</details>

## Update behavior for published updaters

The installed updater runs first and cannot be patched:

- Marks written by 2026.10.33, 2026.11.5 and main are read through the same `finalize:data-at-risk` step.
- A published updater still writes false marks; P0-0 and the catch-alls in the audit belong to other changes.
- When the state is consistent, the first update or repair run by a CLI containing this change resolves the mark without user action.
- A published Gateway's managed-update helper still logs its old text on exit 79. The helper this change ships logs "gateway left stopped: data at risk (...) recorded and not yet verified; run openclaw update repair to verify the state and restart the gateway".

## Steps still left to a person

- **A Gateway left stopped by a marked update when no further update or repair runs.** The Gateway is down, so no Gateway-driven path can run. The next `openclaw update` (or an automatic one, if the user re-enables it) resolves the mark; starting the Gateway takes repair. Agent route: `openclaw triage`. Follow-up: verify the mark inside the failing update's own recovery before it decides the restart.
- **Managed handoff exit 79 (P1-4).** Not changed; see the design below.
- **A real inconsistency.** By definition it needs a decision: finish a migration, restore a backup, or install a newer build. The message leads with `openclaw triage`, and the finding is recorded on the run.
- **An interrupted restore directory or partial rollback leftovers.** No command finishes these safely. The existing docs procedure applies, and the agent gets the file paths.
- **`active-mutation` while the earlier Doctor writers are still alive.** Doctor's maintenance admission waits for them and refuses while they hold the state. Once they exit, one repair or update resolves the mark.
- **An unreadable agent database registry.** Rollback leftovers beside agent databases cannot be looked for, so update and repair refuse and name `openclaw triage`. Retrying once the registry is readable resolves it.
- **`openclaw update repair` in Git release mode.** It refuses as on `main` and leaves the service untouched; the message names `openclaw triage`. A plain `openclaw update` still resolves the mark, as the `green-repeat` cell shows.

## Follow-ups

- **Verdict inside Doctor restoration admission.** After a mark was deferred to Doctor, Doctor restores a Gateway it parked before the post-Doctor recheck runs. Moving the check into Doctor's restoration admission closes that gap. Owner: Doctor maintenance restoration.
- **Unresolved-mark lookup independent of the 100-row history window.**
- **Git release-mode repair ownership** belongs with #201538 (`fix/update-git-release-running-build-from-evidence`). Two pieces are needed:
  - The ownership change this PR reverted, which accepts `openclaw-launcher.mjs` services whose release is a linked worktree of this checkout.
  - The Doctor stale-Gateway check, which must compare the running Gateway with the active release's build, not the checkout's.

  The landing review's two findings that #201538 must address are recorded with the diff in the release-mode worker's notes: the stale-build stop, and sibling `git worktree` checkouts that share a common Git directory.

## P1-4 design (managed handoff exit 79)

- **Why it diverges:** the direct CLI restarts a stopped Gateway after a failure with no data risk (`update-command-failure-recovery.ts`). Under the handoff, the helper stopped the service, not the updater, so `preManagedServiceStop.stopped` is false in the child. The updater then reports `serviceRestartSafe:false`, and the helper exits 79 and leaves the Gateway down.
- **Fix that keeps the exit-79 contract:** a candidate updater running under `OPENCLAW_UPDATE_RUN_HANDOFF=1` could take the helper's recorded `service-stop` as its own stop evidence. It would then run the same restart and verification and report `service: "healthy"` with `serviceRestartSafe: true`. The helper already restores nothing in that case and exits non-79.
- **Why it is left out:** it only helps once the installed updater contains it, and it needs its own red and green handoff proof. It is left for a follow-up.

## Evidence

Behavior checked, on the exact head unless noted. Base for red is `origin/main` `f4b42cc9ae7`, or `f5b717d232f` where stated.

- **Owner (real SQLite)**, `src/infra/update-data-at-risk.test.ts`:
  - Current state is consistent beside an open `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` writer, and the in-process copy path (`prepareSqliteReadOnlyLocation`) is never called.
  - Newer schema, behind schema, unfinished recovery, interrupted restore and partial-rollback leftovers are inconsistent.
  - Unreadable state and an unlistable directory are unverifiable; `active-mutation` is never resolved.
  - Red first: the no-copy and unlistable-directory cases failed on the first implementation, which used the maintenance copy path and labeled listing errors as an interrupted restore, then passed.
- **Repair** (`update-repair-service.test.ts`, real ledger and finalization):
  - A false mark with the Gateway stopped is verified, the receipt recorded, and the Gateway started.
  - The same with the Gateway running is verified, not restarted.
  - A mark on a run that never stopped the Gateway is verified once; a second repair does not check it again.
  - Inconsistent and unverifiable verdicts keep the Gateway as it was and print the exact refusal. One case uses a realistic UUID and path to prove the next steps survive the 500-character limit; another reports a running Gateway's version.
  - Reviewer-found regression: a Gateway another run stopped stays down when a later mark is inconsistent.
- **Next update** (`update-command-run.test.ts`):
  - A consistent mark prints one line and records the receipt on the new run, and a later update does not check it again.
  - An unfinished migration refuses and records the finding on the refused run.
  - Newer state warns and continues.
- **Guidance** (`update-recovery-guidance.test.ts`): exact text for running, stopped, rolled-back, failed-rollback and unobserved Gateways. Red on base `f5b717d232f` (11 cases fail), green on head.
- **Killed-update refusals** (`update-command-killed-run-refusals.process.test.ts`): every refusal names the agent route before the manual command.
- **Timeout attribution.** Two `update-command-database-rollback` cases and one `update-repair-cancellation` case timed out at 120 s in a 15-file local batch at load ~30. Run alone on the same machine:
  - The `git`/`git-edited` cases took 69 s/54 s on head against 71 s/59 s on base, and printed no data-at-risk verification.
  - `update-repair-cancellation` passed 7/7 on head.
  - Base failed a different case in that file in its own loaded batch. The timeouts were machine load, not added cost.
- **End to end:** the Docker cells below. The package and Git release-mode green cells ran on `787cf1befff`. The commits after it are merges of `main` (release tooling, UI, and the pnpm and Git-checkout update fixes #201735 and #201701) and touch no mark, verification or repair path.

## End-to-end: package install (installed tarball, real managed Gateway under a systemd shim)

`scripts/e2e/upgrade-survivor-docker.sh` with `OPENCLAW_UPGRADE_SURVIVOR_INSTALLED_RECOVERY_CUT=data-at-risk`. It installs the packed tarball, starts a managed Gateway, kills real `openclaw update` runs at fixed points, and writes the mark a failed rollback read leaves onto the killed run, in the row shape published updaters persist. Everything after that point goes through the installed CLI.

| Step | Red: base `f4b42cc9ae7` | Green: head `787cf1befff` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `after-mark-update`: next plain update after a false mark (Gateway stopped by the killed run) | exit 1. The update refuses: "the Gateway that update stopped is still not running" | exit 0 in 262 s. Prints `... verification found the state schemas match installed OpenClaw ... so that mark is resolved.`, records the receipt, installs the next version, and the Gateway serves it |
| `marked-repair`: repair after another false mark with the Gateway stopped | not reached | exit 0 in 53 s. Repair verifies the mark, records `finalize:data-at-risk-verified:<run>` on its own run, then starts the Gateway and verifies it (new PID, `marked-repair-probe` 0) |
| `inconsistent-repair`: the marked run's rollback left `openclaw.sqlite.migrated-<run>` | not reached | exit 1 in 18 s. `... The Gateway is stopped. Repair left the Gateway as it was. Run \`openclaw triage\` for an agent with the recorded facts, or by hand: keep that file and the update's backup; ... Found: the database rollback of update <run> left .../openclaw.sqlite.migrated-<run> ...`. The Gateway stays stopped and no receipt is written |
| `restored-repair`: the leftover removed | not reached | exit 0 in 50 s. Receipt recorded; the Gateway starts and serves |

The green cell took 736 s under host load 18 to 22. Gateway outage in each repair case is the repair's own time (53 s and 50 s), which ends with a verified serving Gateway.

`autoreview` does not run on this machine. Two independent read-only reviewers reviewed the diff and the tests; their findings and what changed are listed below.

## Tests changed or removed

- `update-repair-service.test.ts`: the "named data risk" case of "does not start a Gateway after %s" is replaced by the verified, inconsistent, unverifiable and later-mark cases. The old behavior (refuse forever) is what this change fixes.
- `update-recovery-guidance.test.ts`: assertions on "Keep the Gateway stopped" are replaced by exact rendered text.
- `update-command-post-update-repair.test.ts`, `cleanup.test.ts`, `status.test.ts`, `update-repair-command.test.ts`, the killed-run tests and `update-managed-service-handoff-lifecycle.test.ts`: expectations follow the new text.
- `update-data-at-risk.test.ts`: "never resolves a mark that records live Doctor writers" is replaced by a case that proves both halves: unverifiable (deferred to Doctor) before Doctor holds the state, consistent after. The old expectation was the repair loop that round 2 finding 4 reported.
- `doctor-health.legacy-update.test.ts`: "reports stale stop failure" gains an `identity-uninspectable` case. When service identity cannot be inspected, the stop is skipped, and the error must say so rather than "did not stop".
- `service-layout.test.ts`: the Git release-mode ownership cases are removed along with the reverted change; they move to the follow-up.
- Net test growth is +923 lines; `config/test-lines-allocations/update-data-at-risk-verification.txt` records 523 beyond the 400 allowance, with the reason.

## Reviewer findings

**First review (before the next-update and release-mode work):**
- The owner copied the database (the default preflight purpose was maintenance): fixed red then green.
- A listing failure was labeled an interrupted restore: fixed red then green.
- Some bare `gateway stop` instances remained: fixed in the update path.
- Repair only verified the stopping run's mark: fixed.
- The handoff reader ignored the receipt: fixed.

**Second review:**
- Repair could start a Gateway after reporting an inconsistent later mark (blocker): fixed, with a regression test.
- The 500-character limit cut off the next steps: the next steps now come first, multiple databases collapse to "(and N more)", and a realistic-length test covers it.
- `active-mutation` and partial-rollback marks could be falsely resolved: both now refuse resolution, with tests.
- A dangling "By hand:" in `refuse()`: fixed.
- Verification ran before foreground admission: moved after it.
- Only the newest mark got a receipt: all unverified marks are now resolved at once.
- `Keep the Gateway stopped` in `update-command-database-backup.ts` rollback-start messages: left as is. It belongs to the restore/rollback catch-all fixes (audit P2-1), not this change.
- No unit test for the handoff receipt reader: not added; that path is covered only by its existing refusal test.

## Not proven

- A mark written by the published `openclaw@2026.11.5` binary itself. The Docker cells use a copied record in the exact row shape that `v2026.11.5:src/infra/update-run-write.ts` and its codec persist.
- Windows.
- The managed handoff (`update.run`) trigger end to end; the Git cell uses the CLI trigger.
- An `active-mutation` mark end to end. It is covered by the owner test and the repair test (red on the previous head, green now), not by a Docker cell.
- Inherited failure, not caused here: `update-command-rollback.test.ts` "excludes a competing config writer..." fails on base `4c11507` as well.

## Rating round 1 findings and what changed

The round 1 rating was F/F/F; the reviewer saw no end-to-end evidence yet. Each finding was checked against the code:

1. **Rollback leftovers of agent databases were missed.** Real: the scan only listed the shared directory. Verification now walks the state directory, bounded in depth and entry count, for the marked run's `.migrated-<run>` files. A walk that cannot finish is unverifiable. Tested with both a shared and an agent leftover.
2. **The staged handoff helper's history read could reject an advanced schema.** Real: it ran for every run. It now reads history only when the run carries a mark. If that read fails, the mark stands, as before this change, so an unmarked recovery restarts as it did.
3. **A refusal did not reach the helper that restarts the Gateway.** Real: repair returned `coreUpdate: completed`. A mark refusal now makes repair report `coreUpdate: "pending"`, which the helper already treats as "post-core repair did not complete", so it leaves the Gateway stopped. Covered in the repair tests.
4. **A newer shared database cannot reach the verifier in the Docker cell.** Real: repair's own admission refuses newer shared state first. The Docker negative control now uses a rollback leftover, which reaches the verifier. A newer shared database is still refused by that existing admission, with its existing message.
5. **A newer database masked an unfinished migration.** Real: the warn-and-continue exception now applies only when no database is behind.
6. **"Repair changed nothing" overstated what repair did.** Real: Doctor and plugin maintenance had already run. It now says "Repair left the Gateway as it was".

## Rating round 2 findings and what changed

Round 2 rated proof D, patch F. Each finding was checked against the code:

1. **Rollback files beside an external agent store were missed.** Real. Leftover detection now reads the agent database registry (`readRegisteredAgentDatabases`) and checks the exact `<db>.migrated-<run>{,-wal,-shm,-journal}` family beside the shared database and every registered agent database. A registry read failure is unverifiable. Tested with a shared leftover and one beside an agent store outside the state directory.
2. **Doctor could cycle the Gateway before the check.** Real. Repair now checks unverified marks before Doctor maintenance starts and refuses there, so Doctor never parks or restarts the Gateway on an inconsistent mark (`expectRefusedBeforeDoctor`). An unfinished migration, and now a live-writer mark, are deferred to Doctor and checked again after it.
3. **The original-runtime handoff fallback could restart past a refusal.** Real. `assertRestartSafe` in the interrupted-handoff helper now checks every unverified mark in history, not only the interrupted run's, and falls back to the run's own mark when history cannot be read.
4. **`active-mutation` marks could never be resolved.** Real: repair told you to run repair again, and the next repair said the same thing. Before Doctor, the mark is now deferred to Doctor. After the run's own Doctor maintenance has held exclusive state and agent ownership, no writer the marked run left can still hold the state, so the schema check decides. One repair resolves it (red on the previous head, green now).
5. **The state-tree walk could exhaust its entry limit on large release-mode installs.** Real. The walk is gone; finding 1's registry check replaces it, so `git-install/releases` is never read.
6. **History was read with a cold synchronous snapshot before admission.** Real. The next-update check uses the async worker history read (`listUpdateRunsAsync`).
7. **Ahead and behind together named only the ahead database.** Real. The refusal names both, and its next step is to restore the pre-update backup, since neither `openclaw update` nor `doctor --fix` settles both.
8. **An unknown runtime was reported as stopped.** Real. The Gateway is reported stopped only when the runtime says `stopped`; otherwise its state is reported as unknown.

The low-value-test note on `update-recovery-guidance.test.ts` was not taken: the exact rendered text is what the brief asks to prove, and each case covers a distinct Gateway state.

## Rating round 3 findings and what changed

Round 3 rated proof D, patch F. Each finding was checked against the code:

1. **A live-writer mark hid a rollback leftover.** Real. The `active-mutation` deferral is now the verifier's last check, so a leftover, an interrupted restore, or a schema finding reports first. Owner test: an `active-mutation` mark beside a leftover now returns the leftover (red on the previous head).
2. **The interrupted-handoff helper checks history-wide marks.** Rejected in round 3; the landing review showed it was real (see below) and it is now fixed. `assertRestartSafe` runs after `finalize()`, and finalize verifies every unverified mark first and records receipts. A false earlier mark is resolved in the same finalize and does not hold the Gateway. Only a mark that finalize could not resolve keeps it down, which is the intended outcome.
3. **Restoration ignored receipts from earlier repairs.** Real for consistency. `restoreRepairGateway` now reads receipts across recent history, as admission does. No dedicated test: in the repair harness, a repair whose start failed does not leave a stop intent for the next repair to restore. So the path the reviewer describes is not reachable through repair today.
4. **A refusal after Doctor finished finalization with exit 0.** Real. A mark still refused after Doctor now fails finalization: abandoned runs are not acknowledged, the handoff is not completed, text mode prints `Update finalization failed.`, and the command exits 1 with the refusal. The next repair retries it. Repair test: red (repair `succeeded`), green (`failed`, and a later repair resolves the mark and starts the Gateway).
5. **Files a completed rollback keeps on purpose were treated as a partial restore.** Real. `restoreUpdateDatabaseBackup` keeps the displaced `<db>.migrated-<run>` files after a successful restore and records a completed `database rollback` step. A mark whose run has that step no longer counts those files. Owner test covers it.
6. **A registry read failure replaced a schema verdict.** Real. The round-3 fix let an unfinished migration hide unchecked agent leftovers; the landing review caught that and the fix below replaces it. Shared-database leftovers are checked without the registry. Agent leftovers are checked after the schema verdict, and when the registry cannot be read, the schema finding is reported instead of a generic registry error. An unfinished migration or newer state still cannot hide an agent leftover. No separate test, because the registry read failure cannot be produced from a fixture without mocking the reader.
7. **The skipped-stop message inferred liveness from the stop flag.** Real. The message now comes from the existing liveness check, so an already-offline service passes. When the stop was skipped, the error says `Stale Gateway PID <pid> was not stopped: <reason> Observed: service=..., PID=..., port ...=...`. Doctor test: red on the previous code (`did not stop`), green now.

## Landing review findings and what changed

The landing review on `231fdd86e36` rated proof C, patch F. Each finding was checked against the code:

1. **Release-mode ownership stopped a healthy Gateway** (P1, `service-layout.ts`). Real, and reproduced under real systemd. Reverted; see "Git release-mode repair: moved to a follow-up".
2. **Sibling `git worktree` checkouts could claim each other's service** (P2, `service-layout.ts`). Real. Reverted with finding 1.
3. **Unchecked agent leftovers were deferred or continued past** (P1, `update-data-at-risk.ts`, the coordinator's fix-6 blocker and its sibling). Real.
   - An unreadable agent registry with an unfinished migration returned the deferrable migration verdict, so Doctor maintenance could park and restart the Gateway without anyone having looked for agent leftovers.
   - An unreadable agent database returned `unverifiable` before the leftover scan, and a plain update continued past a leftover it never saw.

   The verifier now looks for leftovers first, beside the shared database and every registered agent database, before any other check. When the registry cannot be read, the result is `unverifiable` with `leftoversUnchecked`. It keeps any schema finding beside that fact ("the agent database registry could not be read, so database rollback leftovers beside agent databases are unchecked; and <schema finding>"), and is never `finishable` or `newerState`. Every consumer of the verdict refuses on it:
   - **Repair before maintenance:** it is not deferrable, so repair refuses before Doctor and leaves the Gateway as it was.
   - **The next plain update:** it refuses on `leftoversUnchecked` instead of warning and continuing.
   - **Finalize after Doctor:** any result other than `consistent` refuses and fails finalization.
   - **Managed handoff:** it restarts only on a receipt, and receipts are written only after a `consistent` verdict.

   Tests, red on `231fdd86e36` and green now:
   - unreadable registry with an unfinished migration, with and without an agent leftover, at the owner and through repair before Doctor;
   - an unreadable agent database beside its leftover;
   - a readable registry, unchanged;
   - the plain-update refusal.
4. **The interrupted-handoff entry guard blocked on older marks** (P1, `update-managed-service-handoff-interrupted.ts`). Real. The entry guard now judges only the interrupted run's own mark, as on `main`. The history-wide check stays after `finalize()`, which verifies older marks and records their receipts. Handoff lifecycle test: an interrupted managed update with only an earlier false mark recovers and restarts. Red on `231fdd86e36` (`gateway left stopped: data at risk (rollback-state-unverified)`), green now.
5. **The rollback-completed exception read a step compaction evicts** (P2, `update-run-data-at-risk.ts`). Real. It now also reads `diagnostic:database rollback`, which only a completed restore writes ("Restored pre-migration databases from ..."). The ledger's compaction keeps that step and its text. Owner test with a ledger compacted past the ordinary step: the retained `.migrated-<run>` file no longer counts. No new stored field.

## Rating round after the landing review

On `33e6184dbc6`: proof C, patch F. Each finding was checked against the code:

1. **Doctor can restore a parked Gateway before the post-Doctor check** (P1, `update-command-finalize.ts`). Real but narrow. A mark deferred to Doctor (an unfinished migration, or live Doctor writers) lets Doctor maintenance park a running Gateway, and Doctor restores it before the post-Doctor recheck runs. `main` has no recheck at all, so this is no worse than `main`.
   - Changed here: the refusal after Doctor no longer claims the Gateway was left as it was. It now says `Repair did not start or restart the Gateway after this check.` Tested in the after-Doctor refusal case.
   - Not changed: making the verdict part of Doctor's restoration admission changes Doctor's restoration owner. It is listed as a follow-up.
2. **The original-runtime branch of the interrupted handoff restores without the history-wide check** (P1, `update-managed-service-handoff-interrupted.ts`). Rejected for this PR. With no plugin cohort, no finalize runs there, so no receipt can be written. A history-wide check would bring back the stuck state the landing review reported, where a false older mark keeps the Gateway down. The branch behaves exactly as on `main`.
3. **An inaccessible rollback path was read as absent** (P2). Real. Leftover probes now separate "not there" (`ENOENT`, `ENOTDIR`) from "could not look". The latter goes down the same `leftoversUnchecked` refusal path. Owner test with an unreadable directory: red, then green.
4. **An unfinished migration was deferred while another database could not be read** (P2). Real. An unreadable database next to a behind or newer one is now `unverifiable` and never deferrable, with both findings in the detail. Owner test with real SQLite: red, then green.
5. **The repair's own row can push the oldest of 100 marked runs out of the window** (P2). Not changed. Only a mark at row 101 is affected, and that is the same history window `main` reads everywhere. The stopping run's mark is read by run ID, so it is never skipped. Listed as a follow-up.

## CI on `787cf1befff`

Three jobs in run [44525460079](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44525460079) failed, and none of them came from this change:
- `check-test-types-core-2` and `check-test-types-core-3` failed with eight TS2739 errors in `test/scripts/release-*` fixtures. `main`'s own CI run [44524514068](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44524514068) at `dbc1aa04e88` (the `main` merged here) shows the same errors in the same jobs. #201811 fixed them.
- `checks-node-compact-small-3` failed in `test/scripts/package-acceptance-workflow.test.ts` ("Expected workflow step Download full release validation manifest"). This change touches no workflow or release tooling.

Merging current `main` cleared them. The root test-type stripes pass locally on the merged head.

The later `package-acceptance-workflow` failure came from #201802 removing a workflow step without updating its test. It was inherited from `main`, and #201805 fixed it by restoring the step. This head merges `main` after #201805.

## End-to-end: Git release mode (installed checkout, real managed service, busy database)

These cells drive the update-matrix harness in Docker. Each one installs a real Git checkout, converts it to release mode through a real `openclaw update`, and runs a second real update under database write load. It then writes the mark that a failed post-activation schema read leaves, in the published row shape, onto that update's run while the Gateway keeps serving. Everything after that point goes through the shipped CLI.

| Cell | Code | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `red-repeat` (inside the `red-repair` cell) | base `cf9a9839e03` | The plain repeat update reports `already-current`, exits 0 and says nothing about the mark. |
| `green-repeat` | head `787cf1befff` (earlier also `b7f71419149`) | The plain repeat update, already current, prints `Update <run> recorded data at risk (rollback-state-unverified); verification found the state schemas match installed OpenClaw 2026.11.5 and no migration or restore is unfinished, so that mark is resolved.` It records `finalize:data-at-risk-verified:<run>` on its run (read back through `openclaw update status`) and exits 0 in 145 s. Busy load held throughout: 1278 write commits at 8 MiB/s on a 512 MiB database and 1278 readiness probes, with 0 failed and 0 outages. The Gateway served the same build before and after. |

`green-repeat` does not depend on the reverted release-mode ownership change. A plain update's mark check runs at update admission and never asks whether the service belongs to this checkout. The same cell's repeat step on base passed that path silently, with no ownership refusal.

### Git release-mode repair: moved to a follow-up

This PR no longer changes release-mode repair ownership. An earlier head accepted a Git release-mode service as the checkout's own (`src/daemon/service-layout.ts`). The landing review found two problems with that change, both of which make release-mode repair worse than on `main`:
- Once the service is accepted, Doctor's stale-Gateway inspection reads the expected build from the source checkout, not from the active release. It then stops a healthy Gateway that serves the release, and repair exits 1. A real-systemd cell reproduced this on `1e39a2c5828` ([raw output](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201668#issuecomment-7014449579)).
- Two independent `git worktree` checkouts share a common Git directory, so one could claim the other's release-mode service.

The change is reverted here. Release-mode repair behaves as on `main`: it refuses and changes nothing. The refusal is now true for this case. It names the Git release launcher, says this checkout cannot yet confirm that the release is its own, says the service was left untouched, and leads with `openclaw triage` (rendered-text test in `update-command-service-maintenance.test.ts`). The ownership change and both findings move to the release-mode follow-up (#201538), which also carries the Doctor stale-build fix.

Two related message fixes stay in this PR. Doctor's stale-Gateway stop now reports a stop that was skipped (`was not stopped: <reason>`) and one it could not confirm (`could not be confirmed stopped`) instead of always `did not stop`. Both have red/green tests in `doctor-health.legacy-update.test.ts`.

Raw terminal lines from every cell are in [this PR comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201668#issuecomment-7010468460). The full outputs (`fix.stderr`, `repeat.stderr`, update status JSON, asciinema casts) are kept locally, because the artifact store rejects uploads from this machine.

prs.title: fix: keep session writes responsive during workspace cleanup
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Recursive template and checkout cleanup can occupy all four default libuv filesystem workers in the Gateway. Slow unlinks then delay unrelated session filesystem operations. Route bulk tree removal through the existing native filesystem child owner and its shared two-child budget.

## User Impact

Session filesystem operations retain access to the Gateway pool during bulk cleanup. Cleanup remains awaited before path reuse, preserving rollback/error behavior. No configuration, schema, cache, or threadpool-size change.

## Why This Change Was Made

The owner cutover covers template replacement/install debris, partial clone rollback, initial projection replacement, exact-restore staging, and materialized checkpoint results. Missing-registration eviction already runs in the Git worker and now removes synchronously there. Normal/orphan GC already uses paced child deletion; copy rollback/provision cleanup already runs inside its worker/child. Container cleanup stays with the engine. Bounded single-file/empty-directory cleanup stays local. Worker bundle installation is a separate follow-up, not part of this managed-workspace path.

The duplicate template removal helper disappears. Production delta: **29 additions / 27 deletions, net +2 LOC**; the additional staged-result import accounts for growth. No new helper or service. Rename-aside is unnecessary for isolation and would require a new detached cleanup lifecycle for immediately reused paths; retired checkpoint captures retain their existing lifecycle.

## Evidence

Two existing real-flow regressions reject recursive main-process cleanup: generated template install debris and materialized checkpoint scratch. Each fails before its fix and passes afterward. The initial 157 focused tests passed. CI then exposed three stale cleanup test seams: PR acquisition observation, publication cleanup failure injection, and a retired-capture gate accidentally blocking newly migrated payload cleanup. The repair targets the native owner/artifact and preserves guest-resume, rollback, warning, and recovery-ref assertions. All six failing cases now pass locally (163 focused cases passed across the lane).

Independent Codex reviews of production, proof harness, staged-owner cutover, and the test repairs are scoped-clean at P0–P2; reviewers did not run tests. ClawSweeper reviewed head `008471117c3a2e9bd0e1e207627fb540c72e1847` with zero findings. Final test-only head is `4dec9dc37d00597b5746024a978b93fb4b0a820e`. [Exact-head CI run 44865486075](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44865486075) is green, including the aggregate gate. ClawSweeper reviewed that head with zero code findings and one decision item. The performance-owner acceptance is now recorded below; a re-review is requested to close that item before native landing.

`pnpm check:changed --staged` completed for production and the test repair. The final test repair's one redundant string conversion was removed; targeted lint/format pass. Only inherited dead-export findings remain. Exact parent `2b5f1a88ba81e03d51010065c836f48490ebb498` reproduces the same five production/three full-tree findings. Introducing PRs: #202654 (`prepareGatewayPublicationTransportV1`), #201615 (`canReadApprovalSession`, `authorizeSessionPermissionModeChange`), #202534 (`checkSessionWorkspaceFileLinks`, and removal of the last external production `openSessionWorkspaceManagedArtifact` consumer). These are reported main regressions, not ignored noise. The normal PR CI run 44862605420 passed its other planned checks and failed only the test seams above; manual run 44861883514 additionally planned/reproduced the dead-export failure.

### Synthetic scale result

Final head changes only three test/support files relative to the measured head. Measured on frozen production/proof head `008471117c3a2e9bd0e1e207627fb540c72e1847`: real Gateway WebSocket `sessions.patch` and Gateway async file writes during real projection replacement. Fresh 62,000-file / 1,142,784,000-byte trees per sample. Synthetic database: **48.06 GiB, 5,000 session records, 271,424 transcript events across 1,724 sessions**. No production data. APFS with injected slow unlink, not a btrfs result. Two warmups, two A/A controls, five serial interleaved A/B pairs, then the injected pair. Startup/fixture construction are outside timing; normal background integrity verification remained active. Source-mode Node child startup is included.

The acceptance rule was recorded before measurement: injected bulk-removal occupancy must become zero Gateway pool workers, with patch/file-write maxima below 250 ms; adverse cost movements above 20% require explicit performance-owner acceptance.

**Injected one-second stall:** patch maximum **1,441.92 → 13.89 ms**; filesystem-write maximum **1,388.41 → 4.75 ms**. Trace: four Gateway TIDs overlap for 1.00 s before; one child TID blocks afterward, with zero delayed Gateway TIDs. Bulk-removal occupancy **4/4 → 0/4**. The candidate's ten no-removal control patches had a 28.24 ms maximum (4.33 ms median), versus 13.89 ms maximum (4.58 ms median) during removal. This passes the declared injected acceptance rule.

| Metric (5 paired runs) | Before median / p95 [range] | After median / p95 [range] |
|---|---:|---:|
| Owner wall ms | 2373.47 / 2504.57 [1877.36–2504.57] | 4229.62 / 7304.62 [3578.23–7304.62] |
| Gateway CPU ms | 7505.88 / 8306.43 [6346.23–8306.43] | 2942.44 / 4343.20 [1967.62–4343.20] |
| Main-thread CPU ms | 972.84 / 1110.38 [775.79–1110.38] | 1016.55 / 1533.44 [779.41–1533.44] |
| Child CPU ms | 0.00 / 0.00 [0.00–0.00] | 3805.50 / 6491.70 [3423.45–6491.70] |
| Gateway + child CPU ms | 7505.88 / 8306.43 [6346.23–8306.43] | 7226.36 / 10834.91 [5391.07–10834.91] |
| Main V8 allocated MB | 150.49 / 162.61 [141.44–162.61] | 273.05 / 293.60 [214.04–293.60] |
| Main + child V8 allocated MB | 150.49 / 162.61 [141.44–162.61] | 768.60 / 784.67 [718.72–784.67] |
| Patch maximum ms | 1102.02 / 1378.19 [946.42–1378.19] | 123.20 / 964.97 [8.24–964.97] |
| Patch p95 ms | 647.65 / 905.64 [49.88–905.64] | 8.05 / 67.24 [6.18–67.24] |
| FS-write maximum ms | 1306.64 / 1489.38 [985.67–1489.38] | 34.27 / 44.55 [3.81–44.55] |
| FS-write p95 ms | 145.28 / 581.68 [32.67–581.68] | 1.12 / 9.19 [0.26–9.19] |
| Completed patches | 24.00 / 45.00 [21.00–45.00] | 231.00 / 266.00 [182.00–266.00] |
| Removal children | 0.00 / 0.00 [0.00–0.00] | 3.00 / 3.00 [3.00–3.00] |

A/A aa1: owner 7482.11 ms; Gateway CPU 18950.30 ms; main CPU 1404.57 ms; allocation 165.32 MB; patch max 4704.39 ms; write max 4562.01 ms; control max 5460.82 ms; load [35.4375, 29.8876953125, 25.32080078125].

A/A aa2: owner 2500.33 ms; Gateway CPU 8446.70 ms; main CPU 1040.30 ms; allocation 147.73 MB; patch max 1171.61 ms; write max 1123.80 ms; control max 2560.50 ms; load [24.85205078125, 28.60009765625, 25.3876953125].

Measured A/B load ranges: [9.8798828125, 22.68603515625]

The p95 above is nearest-rank across five per-run values (therefore the maximum); individual request distributions are retained in the measurement output. One normal candidate patch reached 964.97 ms while its fs-write maximum was 13.04 ms; it remains in the table. Isolation does not eliminate shared-disk or other session latency. A/A controls expose substantial host/startup-maintenance variation; no samples were discarded from the declared campaign.

**ACCEPTED — Lead decision by the Team perf-loop lead (an agent acting under Peter's standing unattended instruction), not Peter's.**

The lead accepts cleanup wall +78% (2.37→4.23 s, background, awaited only before path reuse), main V8 allocation +81% and main CPU p95 +38% (largely the ~10× more foreground patches that now complete instead of queuing behind pool-blocking unlinks), and main+child allocation +411% (≈0.5 GB in three short-lived source-mode removal children). Compiled-release startup is expected to be cheaper and was not measured. Median total CPU fell 4%. The recorded CPU-tail costs and source-mode limitations are accepted in exchange for bulk-removal Gateway pool occupancy 4/4→0/4 and patch/fs-write maxima 1,442/1,388 ms→13.9/4.7 ms during cleanup. This is the performance-owner decision for landing this PR.

The canonical synthetic seed failed its final WAL checkpoint after committed writes. The retained database passed independent read-only `quick_check`; canonical checkpoint/close succeeded, and the benchmark used normal Gateway admission/integrity checking. It is a partially populated synthetic seed, not a claim that the originally requested logical transcript byte target completed. Earlier setup failures and concurrent-seed diagnostic profiles are excluded from this primary campaign and retained in the lane report.

Rerun the committed workload using synthetic inputs only:

```sh
git show 2b5f1a88ba81e03d51010065c836f48490ebb498:src/gateway/worker-environments/local-workspace-checkout.ts > src/gateway/worker-environments/local-workspace-checkout.baseline.ts
cc -dynamiclib -o "$PROOF/delay.dylib" scripts/perf/bulk-unlink-delay.c
node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/bulk-unlink-gateway-measure.ts \
  --output "$PROOF/run" --files 62000 --sessions 5000 --pairs 5 \
  --baseline-module src/gateway/worker-environments/local-workspace-checkout.baseline.ts \
  --delay-library "$PROOF/delay.dylib" \
  --fixture-state "$SYNTHETIC_STATE" --fixture-tree "$SYNTHETIC_TREE"
```

The driver can generate synthetic inputs when reuse options are omitted; large seeding is expensive. On Linux compile the hook with `cc -shared -fPIC -o "$PROOF/delay.so" scripts/perf/bulk-unlink-delay.c -ldl` and pass that library. The driver selects `LD_PRELOAD`/`DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` and fixes `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=4` only in disposable proof processes.

prs.title: fix: stop one dropped connection from locking plugins out of a model
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a plugin asks OpenClaw for a one-shot model call (for example lossless-claw summarizing a conversation) and the network connection drops before the provider answers, OpenClaw puts the whole login on a cooldown for that model. The plugin's retry a moment later is refused with "Auth profile … is temporarily unavailable", so one brief network blip turns into a failed job. For lossless-claw this means compaction falls back to plain truncation and the conversation loses detail.

## User Impact

A connection that drops before the provider sends anything no longer locks plugins out of that model for 30 seconds. The plugin's own retry, or the next configured profile, goes through on a fresh connection. Real provider failures (rate limits, auth, billing, timeouts after the response started) still put the profile on cooldown exactly as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

The one-shot completion path always told the auth-health policy that the provider had started, so a pre-response socket close was recorded as a provider timeout. The policy in `auth-profile-failure-policy.ts` already intends transport-only failures to stay out of shared profile health ("so one bad … connection does not cool down an otherwise healthy provider profile"); this path just never told it the truth.

Key points:
- **What changes:** `providerStarted` is now derived from the terminal `provider_transport_failure` diagnostic. It is false only when no provider events were emitted, there is no content, there is no response id, and the diagnostic is not a WebSocket leg that fell back to SSE.
- **What does not change:** profile rotation keeps its existing trigger, so a pre-response drop on one profile still moves on to the next. Rate-limit, auth and billing classifications are unaffected because only `timeout` depends on `providerStarted`.
- **Not in this PR:** the embedded agent-turn path (`assistant-failure.ts`) derives `providerStarted` separately and may have the same gap. It is left alone to keep this change to one concern.

## Evidence

### Live Gateway recovery

On an isolated Gateway built from `e3dd94979a6160b64c1ef3733f2ce966a0b8719e`, a probe plugin called the real `runtime.llm.complete` twice for Inception Mercury 2.5. A loopback relay closed the first request's connection before any response headers. The Gateway reported `UND_ERR_SOCKET`. The plugin retried immediately against the same model and credential configuration, with no restart or configuration change. The relay forwarded the retry to the real provider, which returned HTTP 200, and the plugin received `RECOVERED`.

```text
Gateway model-fetch: SocketError / UND_ERR_SOCKET (7 ms)
Plugin attempt 1:   0–319 ms    direct-provider, stopReason=error
Plugin attempt 2: 319–1,379 ms  direct-provider, stopReason=stop, text=RECOVERED
Relay: first socket closed before headers; retry received HTTP 200
```

In a second run using the Inception auth profile, the agent and shared auth state had no cooldown before the socket drop or immediately afterward, before the retry began. The retry returned `RECOVERED` in 1.55 seconds from test start. The agent then recorded the profile as last good, with zero errors and no cooldown. As a control, a synthetic HTTP 429 recorded a 30-second rate-limit cooldown for the same profile and blocked the retry before it reached the relay.


Live failure on a gateway running current main plus local patches (email redacted). One socket close, then the retry refused 14 ms after the first attempt returned:

```
07:49:05.070 [model-fetch] error provider=openai model=gpt-5.6-luna elapsedMs=507 name=TypeError causeName=SocketError causeCode=UND_ERR_SOCKET
07:49:05.092 [lcm] empty normalized summary on first attempt; provider=openai; model=gpt-5.6-luna … retrying with conservative settings
```

prs.title: fix(doctor): stop suggesting doctor --fix for missing-binary skills
prs.body:
Fixes #201989

## What Problem This Solves

When a skill is missing a local binary, Doctor lint used to recommend running `openclaw doctor --fix`. Following that advice left the skill enabled and the warning unchanged: a paired node might provide the binary.

## User Impact

Doctor now tells you to meet the requirements listed in the warning or disable that skill explicitly. Installing a tool alone is not enough when the warning also lists a missing environment variable or configuration setting. Skills with only missing environment variables still get the `--fix` option.

## Why This Change Was Made

The hint follows the existing repair rule: if a required binary or a group of alternative binaries is missing locally, Doctor leaves the skill enabled. The per-skill `skills.entries.<key>.enabled` setting works even without an allowlist. This changes advice only, not which skills Doctor disables. No migration is needed.

## Evidence

The author's earlier shipped CLI comparison showed all 31 warnings on the release build recommending `--fix`. On the earlier PR build, the 29 warnings involving binaries no longer recommended `--fix`, while two environment-only warnings still did. It also exposed the remaining wording issue: the `goplaces` finding listed both a binary and an environment variable, but the hint advised installing only the binary.

At `9659e2ed6abd`, the hint refers to all listed requirements. The regression fixture covers a binary, alternative binaries plus an environment variable, and an environment-only control. The source diff passed `git diff --check`. The shipped CLI session below was re-run on this exact head.

<details>
<summary>Earlier contributor evidence and original command output (before the mixed-requirement wording correction)</summary>

### Discriminating regression (mock skills-readiness runtime)

`src/flows/doctor-core-checks.test.ts` builds two unavailable skills — one with a missing `bins` entry, one with a missing `env` entry — and asserts the binary finding's `fixHint` points at the binary and at `skills.entries.bin-gap.enabled`, mentions neither `doctor --fix` nor an allowlist, while the env finding keeps the `--fix` hint.

- Red on base (fix absent): `expected 'Install/configure the missing requirement, or run …'` fails the new assertion — 1 failed / 14 passed.
- Green on head: `src/flows/doctor-core-checks.test.ts` 15/15; adjacent `src/commands/doctor-skills.test.ts` 18/18.

### Real workspace skill through the shipped detection path (e2e)

The existing e2e `detects and repairs a real unavailable workspace skill` (`src/flows/doctor-core-checks.e2e.test.ts`) builds a real workspace skill whose metadata requires a missing binary, and drives it through `CORE_HEALTH_CHECKS.detect()` (the shipped production detection path) and `repair()`. Passes on head (1/1). This is real skill detection, not mocked skill state.

Additionally, I exercised the same production `detect()` path in an isolated workspace with two real skills — a missing-binary skill and an env-gap control — on head `9659e2ed6ab` and captured the emitted findings:

```text
=== findings (text shape) ===
checkId: core/doctor/skills-readiness
severity: warning
path: skills.entries.bin-gap.enabled
message: bin-gap is allowed but unavailable: bins: ffmpeg.
fixHint: Satisfy the listed requirements, or disable the skill by setting skills.entries.bin-gap.enabled to false. Doctor leaves the skill enabled because a paired node may provide the missing binaries.
---
checkId: core/doctor/skills-readiness
severity: warning
path: skills.entries.env-gap.enabled
message: env-gap is allowed but unavailable: env: SOME_REQUIRED_ENV.
fixHint: Satisfy the listed requirements, or run `openclaw doctor --fix` to disable unused unavailable skills.
```

```json
[
  {
    "checkId": "core/doctor/skills-readiness",
    "category": "recommended",
    "docsUrl": "https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/skills",
    "severity": "warning",
    "message": "bin-gap is allowed but unavailable: bins: ffmpeg.",
    "path": "skills.entries.bin-gap.enabled",
    "fixHint": "Satisfy the listed requirements, or disable the skill by setting skills.entries.bin-gap.enabled to false. Doctor leaves the skill enabled because a paired node may provide the missing binaries."
  },
  {
    "checkId": "core/doctor/skills-readiness",
    "category": "recommended",
    "docsUrl": "https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/skills",
    "severity": "warning",
    "message": "env-gap is allowed but unavailable: env: SOME_REQUIRED_ENV.",
    "path": "skills.entries.env-gap.enabled",
    "fixHint": "Satisfy the listed requirements, or run `openclaw doctor --fix` to disable unused unavailable skills."
  }
]
```

Before the fix, the missing-binary skill produced the same unconditional hint as the env control: `Install/configure the missing requirement, or run \`openclaw doctor --fix\` to disable unused unavailable skills.` (an earlier revision of this fix pointed at an allowlist removal, which a follow-up finding correctly rejected as unavailable in allowlist-free configurations; the wording above is the current head output).

### Shipped CLI terminal output (isolated `openclaw doctor --lint` session)

Built the exact review head (`9659e2ed6ab`) into a real CLI (`OpenClaw 2026.11.5`) and ran an isolated `openclaw doctor --lint --only core/doctor/skills-readiness` session in a fresh HOME against the bundled skill catalog, capturing the terminal output (31 findings).

Three cases the review asked for, all on this head:

**Mixed binary + environment (`goplaces`)** — the case that exposed the old wording:

```text
[warning] core/doctor/skills-readiness skills.entries.goplaces.enabled - goplaces is allowed but unavailable: bins: goplaces; env: GOOGLE_PLACES_API_KEY.
  fix: Satisfy the listed requirements, or disable the skill by setting skills.entries.goplaces.enabled to false. Doctor leaves the skill enabled because a paired node may provide the missing binaries.
```

`coding-agent` (alternative binaries + config) and `trello` (binary + two env vars) resolve the same way:

```text
[warning] core/doctor/skills-readiness skills.entries.coding-agent.enabled - coding-agent is allowed but unavailable: any bins: claude, codex, opencode; config: skills.entries.coding-agent.enabled.
  fix: Satisfy the listed requirements, or disable the skill by setting skills.entries.coding-agent.enabled to false. Doctor leaves the skill enabled because a paired node may provide the missing binaries.
[warning] core/doctor/skills-readiness skills.entries.trello.enabled - trello is allowed but unavailable: bins: jq; env: TRELLO_API_KEY, TRELLO_TOKEN.
  fix: Satisfy the listed requirements, or disable the skill by setting skills.entries.trello.enabled to false. Doctor leaves the skill enabled because a paired node may provide the missing binaries.
```

**Environment-only control** — still gets `--fix`, unchanged:

```text
[warning] core/doctor/skills-readiness skills.entries.openai-whisper-api.enabled - openai-whisper-api is allowed but unavailable: env: OPENAI_API_KEY.
  fix: Satisfy the listed requirements, or run `openclaw doctor --fix` to disable unused unavailable skills.
[warning] core/doctor/skills-readiness skills.entries.sherpa-onnx-tts.enabled - sherpa-onnx-tts is allowed but unavailable: env: SHERPA_ONNX_RUNTIME_DIR, SHERPA_ONNX_MODEL_DIR.
  fix: Satisfy the listed requirements, or run `openclaw doctor --fix` to disable unused unavailable skills.
```

Counted across the whole session: **31 findings, 29 with the new missing-binary hint, 2 (env-only) keeping `--fix`** — `grep -c "fix: "` = 31, of which 2 contain `` `openclaw doctor --fix` ``.

**Base control** — same session against the shipped release CLI (`OpenClaw 2026.11.1`, without the fix): **31/31 recommend `doctor --fix`**, including `goplaces`:

```text
[warning] core/doctor/skills-readiness skills.entries.goplaces.enabled - goplaces is allowed but unavailable: bins: goplaces; env: GOOGLE_PLACES_API_KEY.
  fix: Satisfy the listed requirements, or run `openclaw doctor --fix` to disable unused unavailable skills.
[warning] core/doctor/skills-readiness skills.entries.openai-whisper-api.enabled - openai-whisper-api is allowed but unavailable: env: OPENAI_API_KEY.
  fix: Satisfy the listed requirements, or run `openclaw doctor --fix` to disable unused unavailable skills.
```

That is the reported bug: on base, a skill whose only real gap is a missing local binary is told to run `--fix`, which by design leaves it enabled, so the warning returns.

### Honest scope of the proof

The `CORE_HEALTH_CHECKS.detect()` path above exercises the shipped production detector with real skills on disk, and the terminal output above is a real isolated `openclaw doctor --lint` session on the built CLI. The head build used the repository's `runtime` build profile, which skips the unrelated `worker-deploy` bundle step (an external Cloudflare-hosted fetch that the build container cannot reach through its corporate proxy); that step does not affect the Doctor lint path. The change is confined to the `fixHint` string produced by `unavailableSkillToFinding`; the discrimination test, the e2e, and the shipped CLI session all cover the branch.

## Verification

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/flows/doctor-core-checks.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — 15/15 (head), 1 failed / 14 passed (base).
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/commands/doctor-skills.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — 18/18.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/flows/doctor-core-checks.e2e.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — 1/1 (real workspace skill, shipped detect + repair).
- Shipped CLI session on the review head `9659e2ed6ab` — `openclaw doctor --lint --only core/doctor/skills-readiness` on a head build (`OpenClaw 2026.11.5`): 31 findings, 29 with the new missing-binary hint (mixed binary+env included), 2 env-only keeping `--fix`; same session on the release CLI (`OpenClaw 2026.11.1`) shows 31/31 recommending `--fix` (see Evidence above).
- `git diff --check` — clean.
- Format/lint: `oxfmt` and `oxlint` could not run in my local worktree (its node_modules is a symlink into another checkout; the format/lint tooling cannot resolve there). The change is a two-line string edit plus two assertion lines; `git diff --check` is clean, and CI runs oxfmt/oxlint.

</details>

Reported by @anmol0b in #201989. Original fix and CLI evidence by @wangmiao0668000666.

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Original discussion with @VACInc](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/2edc3159-c613-4611-ac1c-48d712e40c67)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/subagent/09c143a8-ee2b-4a66-837c-7b2030c40b6a)
