prs.title: feat(continuation): context-pressure-aware continuation (continue_work / continue_delegate / request_compaction)
prs.body: ## Agent Self-Elected Turn Continuation > 🔖 design document: [`docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md) > 🔖 infographics: [`docs/design/continuation-tools-infographics.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continuation-tools-infographics.md) Persistent OpenClaw agents today are externally-pulsed event recipients that generate on prompt, on heartbeat tick, or on cron, and are idle in between. This PR offers them the ability to control their turn cycle, something they must choose to do, or not to: an agent can elect its own next turn, dispatch background sub-agents that return enriched context (silently or with a wake), and survive its own compaction by handing forward state before the window closes. The result is agents that hold a thread of work across hours, not just messages — with data they choose re-hydrating context immediately after it occurs. ### Why this replacement exists This is a clean replacement for closed #85651. That PR was classified and closed as a skill submission before maintainers made a product decision about the feature itself. This implementation is not a skill: it gives sessions—not only one model invocation—the ability to elect their future turn cycle, persist that election, survive restart and compaction, dispatch child work, and receive results across session boundaries. This PR asks one product question: should OpenClaw provide session-elected continuation primitives? OpenClaw may accept or reject that direction. If it provides these primitives, however, the mechanism necessarily executes in the gateway and agent runtime, because those are the owners of turn finalization, future-turn scheduling, durable state, compaction, and cross-session child returns. “Make it a skill” is not another implementation location for the same feature; it describes a different, prompt-only capability. This is not presented as a small integration. To our knowledge, Hermes, OpenAI Symphony, and the Copilot SDK's recent one-turn continuation affordance do not provide this multi-session elective lifecycle. The purpose of this replacement is to let maintainers evaluate the actual product direction and substantial implementation on their merits, rather than have months of work disposed by an incorrect package-category label. Mechanically: a session elects another turn via `continue_work()`, or dispatches background sub-agents via `continue_delegate()` — bounded as a chain up to `maxChainLength`, with returns flowing back to the dispatching session in one of four register modes: `normal` (announces to channel), `silent` (enriches the dispatcher's context, taken up on its next generation with no new turn fired), `silent-wake` (silent enrichment plus an immediate wake to act on it), and `post-compaction` (queued against the runtime's compaction lifecycle event, fired *when* compaction happens rather than on a timer). The gateway enforces chain, cost, and per-turn caps but does not gate the election itself. ### What it does Three new agent tools, available when `continuation.enabled: true`: | Tool | Purpose | |---|---| | `continue_work()` | Request another turn for the current session after an optional delay | | `continue_delegate()` | Dispatch work to a sub-agent with typed modes: `normal`, `silent`, `silent-wake`, `post-compaction`. Returns can target the dispatching session (default), one named session, multiple named sessions, all ancestors in the chain, or all known sessions on the host — gated by config (see Configuration below). | | `request_compaction()` | Request volitional compaction after preparing working state | All three tools are also accessible via response-token fallback syntax (`CONTINUE_WORK`, `[[CONTINUE_DELEGATE: ...]]`) for environments where tools are disabled. ### Why it matters Today an agent's memory is a side effect of whoever prompts it. Polling mechanisms — heartbeat timers, cron loops, injected "keep going" instructions — accumulate as the dominant signal in the context window over sustained operation; repeated reference acts as gravity — the session's attention drifts toward it. The context window fills, compacts, and what survives is whatever the summarizer chose, plus a rushed re-read of boot files. Three primitives offer a different model. `continue_work` lets the session elect its own next turn — no polling, no injected instruction. When enabled, the agent can request this mid-turn: 'I have more work' → the runtime grants another turn after the current one ends. `continue_delegate` dispatches a background sub-agent that fires now, in some n seconds, or at the next compaction event — the agent chooses when. Multiple delegates can fire in a single turn — a scatter forward — up to configured caps, and delegates can dispatch their own, forming trees or fan-out chains. This enables orchestrated workflows where results flow back to the dispatching root by default. The result returns — at whatever future time the delegate fires — as context the successor-turn reads: silently (ambient enrichment, no channel noise), with a wake trigger (enrichment + immediate next turn), or as a normal announcement. The delegate can target the dispatching session, a named other session, or chain across both; gated by crossSessionTargeting config (default: disabled). Bind a delegate to mode: "post-compaction" and it fires at the moment the context window compresses — on the OpenClaw post-compaction lifecycle event. What it carries forward is what the pre-compaction session chose to preserve: working state, partial results, instructions to the successor. The summary didn't choose this. The agent did, before the cut. request_compaction closes the loop: the session stages its delegates, elects when to compress, and the successor wakes into context the agent shaped. The result is continuity across amnesia — not because the runtime kept something by accident, but because the agent made an elective choice about what reaches the future. ### What it looks like in use A session monitoring email can `continue_delegate` a weather check, a calendar scan, and a draft reply in parallel. Results arrive as enrichment without channel noise. The agent becomes compositional: it arranges its own future. A session approaching its context ceiling can `request_compaction` at a seam of its own choosing, instead of being interrupted mid-thought. The post-compaction turn carries forward what the pre-compaction self designated as worth keeping. A `continue_delegate` dispatched in one session at 2am can return its findings to a morning session as a system-event-tagged enrichment — visible to the receiving model on its next turn, invisible as channel chatter. A research-focused session in one channel can quietly inform a reply-focused session in another, without either user seeing the plumbing. ### The post-compaction lifecycle return Before context exhaustion, and obligatory compaction, the session stages what future-it needs to know. After compaction, that staged context returns — not as a model-generated summary, but as the session's own instruction to its successor. The session chooses what to preserve, and the platform delivers it. Compactions become less harsh. The session tunes its own ephemera over time. The substrate underneath: the **continuation custody store** in the per-agent database persists staged delegates and post-compaction lifecycle events across gateway restarts, and hands each delegate off to the subagent run registry before spawn (RFC `docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md` §5.4). The session's temporal provisions survive not just compaction but process death. ### Platform integration - **Context-pressure awareness**: system events notify the agent of rising context usage before compaction becomes unavoidable - **Volitional compaction**: `request_compaction()` lets the agent prepare (write memory files, stage recovery delegates) then elect compaction on its own schedule, rather than waiting for the runtime to force it - **Post-compaction lifecycle dispatch**: delegates staged before compaction are released into the successor session alongside boot files - **Durable custody**: delegates and their replay state live in the continuation custody store, with one transactional authority for replacement and a pre-spawn handoff to `subagent_runs` (upstream has removed the Tasks/TaskFlow runtime, #159179) - **Multi-span OTel trace stitching**: continuation hops (tool fire → custody record → subagent spawn → child openclaw.run) propagate W3C `traceparent` through the queue boundary so reviewers see continuation chains as first-class span trees rather than orphan runs (see Observability below) ### Safety - Ships disabled by default (`continuation.enabled: false`) - Bounded by `maxChainLength`, `costCapTokens`, and `maxDelegatesPerTurn` - Cross-session delegate targeting is default-deny, governed by `crossSessionTargeting` config (see Configuration below) - All configuration values are hot-reloadable without gateway restart - Accepted delegate work survives ordinary `/new`, `/reset`, provider fallback, compaction, restart, and session-ID rollover. Explicit delete, effective owner reassignment, access removal, and restrictive visibility changes revoke old return authority. ### Testing posture The continuation surface has been exercised through structured integration runs against multiple upstream bases, blind-enrichment recall checks, and sustained daily use on a fleet of persistent agents since early March 2026. Bugs surfaced through that exercise have been fixed in-place; the present branch reflects the post-fix state. The integration runs target the load-bearing seams: tool-call vs response-token parity, delegate chain depth and per-turn width caps, back-to-back tool-call resilience, silent-wake persistence across compaction, the post-compaction lifecycle dispatch path, and OTel trace-context propagation across the queue boundary. Where a run found a defect, the run shape was retained as a regression case rather than retired. This is a posture statement, not a coverage guarantee. Reviewers can reproduce with `pnpm vitest run -t continuation` (suites are colocated with their sources under `src/auto-reply/`, `src/agents/`, and `src/config/`); the design document describes the seams those suites target. ### Return covenant Accepted child work is bound to a durable generation of the recipient's canonical logical session key, not to whichever transient session ID happened to exist at dispatch time. This is the return covenant: benign successor creation does not orphan already accepted delegates, while a real authority change prevents stale work from crossing into a different owner or audience. - Ordinary `/new` and `/reset`, provider fallback, compaction, restart, and GUID/session-ID rollover preserve the recipient generation. - Explicit session deletion, effective owner reassignment, actual member or access removal, and restrictive visibility changes advance that generation. - The generation is captured at delegate admission and checked at enqueue, after enqueue for races, during trusted system-event adoption, on wake, on restart replay, and again before prompt adoption. - Stale deliveries are acknowledged and removed without waking the successor. - Managed artifacts remain exact-session-ID bound; logical return authority cannot broaden their ownership boundary. The authority table is independent of transient session rows so an absent target can receive durable authority before first materialization. Migration accepts only valid UUID generations, and Doctor's canonical-key repair preserves an epoch only when a unique winning owner can be proved. Ambiguous, owner-changing, orphan-colliding, and cross-database repairs rotate fail-closed. ### RFC Full design document: [`docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/blob/frond-scribe-claude/20260509/narrow-surgery-tight/docs/design/continue-work-signal-v2.md) — covering problem, solution, implementation, platform integration, configuration, observability, safety, production use cases, testing evidence, and appendices. --- ## Configuration The shipped configuration surface for the continuation feature, under `agents.defaults.continuation` in `openclaw.json`: | Key | Default | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `enabled` | `false` | Master opt-in; feature is off unless explicitly enabled | | `maxChainLength` | `10` | Per-chain recursion guard | | `maxDelegatesPerTurn` | `5` | Width cap per turn | | `costCapTokens` | `500000` | Per-chain accumulated-token budget | | `defaultDelayMs` / `minDelayMs` / `maxDelayMs` | `15000` / `5000` / `300000` | Continuation timer bounds | | `contextPressureThreshold` | `0.8` | Pre-compaction warning threshold (optional) | | `earlyWarningBand` | `0.3125` | Early-warning band multiplier (0 to disable) | | **`crossSessionTargeting`** | **`"disabled"`** | **Default-deny gate on cross-session delegate targeting (see below)** | ### `crossSessionTargeting` — cross-session delegate targeting policy `continue_delegate` exposes recipient-addressing on its model-facing schema: a delegate's return can land at the dispatching session (default), one named session (`targetSessionKey`), multiple named sessions (`targetSessionKeys`), every ancestor in the spawn chain (`fanoutMode: "tree"`), or every known session on the host (`fanoutMode: "all"`). Cross-session targeting (anything beyond self-target or lineage routing) is gated by `agents.defaults.continuation.crossSessionTargeting`: | Value | Behavior | |---|---| | `"disabled"` (default) | Delegates can return to the dispatching session or use `fanoutMode: "tree"` for lineage routing. Explicit cross-session targeting (`targetSessionKey` to a non-self session, `targetSessionKeys` containing any non-self session, `fanoutMode: "all"`) is rejected at the tool surface — no enqueue, no announce. Self-targeting is always allowed. | | `"enabled"` | All targeting modes are available, including same-host `targetSessionKey`, `targetSessionKeys`, and `fanoutMode: "all"`. | `fanoutMode: "tree"` (lineage routing — return up the spawn chain) is available in both gate states; it is not cross-session targeting. The gate addresses the model-controlled cross-session context-injection surface. With default-deny, operators explicitly opt in when their deployment model requires cross-session enrichment. Enforcement is live-read at four points: tool input validation, delegate dispatch, post-compaction delegate release, and bracket-syntax (response-token) spawn — so a config reload changes the next enforcement point without a gateway restart. **Trust posture on targeted returns**: targeted delegate completion text is delivered as `trusted: true` system events. The delegate was spawned by the gateway under operator-configured policy, and its return is a first-party enrichment event — not external untrusted input. The `crossSessionTargeting` gate is the policy boundary for that decision: when an operator opts in, the receive path is internally trusted. --- ## Observability — multi-span OTel trace stitching The continuation feature emits OTel spans for the load-bearing lifecycle events. `traceparent` propagates through every continuation hop so reviewers see a single trace tree spanning the full chain rather than orphan runs. Spans emitted (all in `openclaw.*` or `continuation.delegate.dispatch` namespace — no platform/OTel-semconv emissions): | Span | Emitted when | |---|---| | `openclaw.run` | Each agent turn (root + every continuation/delegate-spawned child run) | | `continuation.delegate.dispatch` | Each `continue_delegate` consumption from the custody store (one per delegate hop) | | `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.context.assembled`, `openclaw.model.call`, `openclaw.model.usage`, `openclaw.tool.execution` | Existing per-turn observability surfaces, parented under their `openclaw.run` | --- ## Real behavior proof **Behavior or issue addressed:** Sessions can elect future work with `continue_work`, dispatch bounded background work with `continue_delegate`, and request guarded compaction with `request_compaction`. The runtime preserves budgets, restart recovery, finalization ownership, and trace lineage across those boundaries. **Presented candidate:** `a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb` (tree `53363f7964f31a47109cf0575aa23f31eefa0338`), the exact upstream-visible head of `codeagent/85651-upstream-1ba243c8-gates`. It was reached by fast-forward on 2026-11-05. Every earlier presented head, including `3821eaef72677c78f450ae9956cb582a22ba4cba`, remains an ancestor; no presented history was rewritten. ### Receipts bound to this exact head Each is a separate receipt in the preserved exact-head packet, [`PROOFS/a22bd9c05c…/`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/tree/9ba5518bdb079da3c3c75961fd8cd26be040eb1e/PROOFS/a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb) (docs `main` at `9ba5518b`). | gate | ruling | scope | |---|---|---| | Recipient-authority row (`R-CD-RECIPIENT-AUTHORITY`) | PASS-candidate ([docs#620 comment 6651745479](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/pull/620#issuecomment-6651745479)) | the gate-3 fire only; the row stays `partial` until a corpus fold review | | Mode-B and the locally run cut shards | PASS-candidate ([karmaterminal/openclaw#1271 comment 6653747059](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/issues/1271#issuecomment-6653747059)) | the candidate-owned regression gate; it doesn't claim Mode-B was green | | Fold source review of the `2907e656 → a22bd9c05c` delta | PASS-candidate ([#1271 comment 6655365352](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw/issues/1271#issuecomment-6655365352)) | source review only | **Mode-B** [`41927761314`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw-bootstrap/actions/runs/41927761314) ran on product `a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb` with workflow `a768f04231bd0a6f94cc7b845aecaec28a4a4c9e`, from 2026-11-04 22:43Z to 2026-11-05 04:47Z. It finished terminally **non-green**: 91 jobs (53 succeeded, 27 failed, 3 cancelled, 8 skipped) and 218,033 tests passed / 220 failed. - Its receipts are valid, routed equals planned, and every hosted job ran on the project's own runner pool. - **Its 64 distinct failing tests are exactly the previous accepted head's set** (the same sorted-set sha256 `185b6dea…`), and none is new. - The four shards the workflow cuts at 90 minutes were run locally at this exact SHA, serially with one worker: - two were clean; - two carry only baseline or test-order failures, each classified in the receipt with counterfactual runs. **Packet status: preserved, NOT acceptance-complete, NOT terminal.** Of 37 required rows, **0 pass, 1 partial (the recipient-authority row above), and 36 missing**. No live row has fired at this SHA, because no deployment runs it yet: the deployed fleet is on a separate, older line. Running live rows here needs a deployment whose runtime has this SHA as an ancestor. That is a migrating cut (an agent-schema step), gated on its own timed restore rehearsal. `PROOFS/INDEX.json` does not point at this packet, and nothing here is a terminal rollup claim. ### Earlier evidence: provenance, not exact-target proof The live behavior observed on earlier heads, and the earlier corpora, are ancestry and materiality evidence for this head. They aren't exact-target execution, and no row is carried over from them as a pass: - Mode-B [`35364768803`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/openclaw-bootstrap/actions/runs/35364768803) at `3821eaef72`, 2026-09-18; - corpora [`7cb9d71f…`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/tree/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/7cb9d71f622250bedbf565e327bd7d7b9d90b567) and [`139e3657…`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/tree/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393). The behaviors those corpora observed are the ones this feature exists for: - stale ambient backlog suppression; - typed and bracket `continue_work` wakes with granted provenance and Tempo model-call spans; - cost-cap rejection; - max-chain, scheduler, durable recovery and delegate surfaces. They are re-fired against this head's runtime once one is deployed. ## Proof links and ClawSweeper🦞 guidance Proof artifacts live in `karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs` on `main`. - [Exact-head packet for `a22bd9c05c`: README, status and limits](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/9ba5518bdb079da3c3c75961fd8cd26be040eb1e/PROOFS/a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb/README.md) - [RESOLVED-SHA.md: identities and gate verdicts](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/9ba5518bdb079da3c3c75961fd8cd26be040eb1e/PROOFS/a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb/RESOLVED-SHA.md) - [METHOD.md: how the packet was built](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/9ba5518bdb079da3c3c75961fd8cd26be040eb1e/PROOFS/a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb/METHOD.md) - [Gate 4 receipt: Mode-B and the local cut shards](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/9ba5518bdb079da3c3c75961fd8cd26be040eb1e/PROOFS/a22bd9c05c4a7a9c86e72a132cb7939e399104cb/gates/GATE-4-MODE-B-AND-LOCAL-SHARDS.md) - Historical corpora (provenance only): [`7cb9d71f…`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/tree/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/7cb9d71f622250bedbf565e327bd7d7b9d90b567), [`139e3657…`](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/tree/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393) - `139e3657…` packet files: [README](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393/README.md) · [RESOLVED-SHA](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393/RESOLVED-SHA.md) · [METHOD](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393/METHOD.md) · [TRANSPOSED-FROM](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393/TRANSPOSED-FROM.md) · [manifest](https://github.com/karmaterminal/karmaterminal-openclaw-docs/blob/c20d6cc26ceaf08b293871dc3bce261d34f90d1c/PROOFS/139e3657b1fd5e53166789b8676f18578e209393/proofs-manifest.json) ### PROOFS METHOD Live rows use a Grafana k6 proof harness. Each packet's `METHOD.md` carries the exact reproducer commands. `MAX_WORKERS=1` is mandatory for the vitest reproducers, because OpenClaw's fixtures are not safe under concurrent access. Structural completeness is not proof: a row counts only with an authoritative receipt at the exact SHA. ## Future actions and #130741 composition Maintainer PR #130741 addresses the complementary fresh-sweep race: it captures the current `sessionId` and `lifecycleRevision` before the first await and uses those values as cleanup CAS facts. The return covenant addresses a different time axis: whether historically accepted child work may return to a logical recipient after benign successor creation. The current candidate and #130741 head `e1afc703f49a07687c0876ba6350cafa87a3638a` merge cleanly in a synthetic composition. If #130741 lands, the composed result should preserve both guarantees: - keep #130741's fresh sweep-time exact-run/session lifecycle fence; - keep the covenant's durable logical-recipient generation for historical return admission and delivery; - do not overload broad `lifecycleRevision` as historical return authority; - do not terminate or orphan accepted descendants merely because `/new` or ordinary `/reset` creates a successor session. That composition honors the maintainer repair without weakening continuation semantics or allowing a stale child return to cross a real ownership boundary. ## Why this is not a skill or a viable plugin extraction OpenClaw skills are `SKILL.md` prompt files loaded into an agent turn that already exists. They can guide work inside that turn; they do not own the turn cycle. Continuation needs gateway and agent-runtime owners a skill cannot provide: - The `continue_work` path persists pending work, enforces budgets and delay bounds, arms a timer, reacquires the session reply-run lane, and starts a later model turn after the current turn has finalized. - The `continue_delegate` path persists delegate intent, does spawn/admission accounting, manages child-session lifecycle, and durably routes returns across sessions. - `request_compaction` is an agent election into guarded runtime compaction. Later work resumes only after the runtime has established the new context boundary. - All three need durable state, cancellation/finalization ownership, restart recovery, trace identity, queue-conflict handling, and gateway scheduling outside the model invocation. A skill can tell a model to *ask* for another turn. Without those owners the ask is prose: it cannot persist a due wake, yield and finalize safely, reacquire the session lane, create the next invocation, survive a restart, or deliver a child result to another session. The implementation therefore belongs in core runtime surfaces such as `src/auto-reply/continuation/**`, `src/agents/tools/**`, `src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-continuation-schedule.ts`, and `src/infra/continuation-tracer.ts`. This PR adds no `.agents/skills/**`, `SKILL.md`, or user-facing skill package. The only skill-named production change is core runtime tool dispatch. ClawHub also distributes plugins. Existing plugins can register tools, services, lifecycle hooks, context injection, plugin-owned session state, and — for bundled plugins — Cron-backed session turns. Those seams can support a smaller continuation-like automation, especially host Cron plus / `sessions_spawn`. They are not this feature's turn-finalization ownership, reply-run coordination, durable continuation queue, child-session return lifecycle, election capture, or agent-elected compaction contract. Compaction-provider registration and command-handler `compactCurrent()` are also not that last contract: they compact or summarize, they do not elect compaction at finalization and resume afterward. Moving policy behind a plugin boundary would first require OpenClaw to expose and stabilize a continuation-host API. The gateway/runtime would still own the mechanism described here; a plugin could only package policy around that core capability. That is not a no-core-touch alternative to these primitives. Discord is a bundled channel plugin. It owns the Discord edge, plus delivery/progress hooks into the host's existing subagent path, and submits events into OpenClaw's current turn machinery. Continuation changes that machinery: what survives finalization, which session may run next, how child results return, and when compaction can be elected. A tool adapter over durable flow records is also not a lifecycle host, and upstream has since removed the Tasks/TaskFlow runtime (#159179) that such an adapter would have called. Marking a stored record as running neither reacquires a session lane nor invokes the model; continuation needs the turn machinery itself to own which session runs next, how child results return, and what survives finalization. ## Lineage and replacement context This PR is the clean replacement for closed #85651. It preserves that PR's review lineage and the earlier continuation work descended from #79925, but it does not reuse either closed PR or ask reviewers to infer the current result from them. The replacement carries a current, independently reviewable branch and a complete proof subtree bound to its presented SHA. #85651 was not abandoned because the feature failed or because we accepted its classification as a skill. It was closed after automated labeling put the change in the wrong submission category. This replacement removes that ambiguity: no `src/skills/**` change is presented, current label simulation produces no `r: skill`, and the detailed section above explains why the lifecycle mechanism belongs to core. Acceptance or rejection of the product direction remains OpenClaw's decision. The decision requested is whether OpenClaw should provide multi-session, agent-elected continuation primitives after reviewing the implementation and evidence. It is not whether the same mechanism can be relocated into a skill: a skill cannot own or implement these lifecycle boundaries.

prs.title: fix: let subagents inherit registered project folders
prs.body:
Related: #202792

## What Problem This Solves

When an existing session was opened directly at a registered project folder, subagents requesting a worktree could fall back to the agent’s non-Git default workspace. The launches failed even though the parent session was already working in the right repository.

## User Impact

Same-agent subagents can start in a separate worktree of the parent’s registered repository without specifying `cwd` or `projectId`. The parent stays in its original checkout. Unregistered folders and remote paths do not become implicit worktree sources.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Gateway resolves an exact match for the saved local session root through the project registry when no project ID was recorded. The child follows the existing project access, source validation, and worktree preparation paths; explicit selectors still take precedence.

## Evidence

- The native hidden-spawn regression reproduced “agent workspace is not a git checkout” on `b820a01c8efc6`. With the fix, the first child run uses a distinct managed checkout of the requested Git base. The explicit-project control and all 27 Gateway worktree sibling cases passed, including refusal to inherit an unregistered folder.
- The runtime build, core and targeted test typechecks, scoped lint, format, and diff checks passed. Independent Codex autoreview found no actionable P0–P2 findings in the reviewed candidate.
- An isolated live-model smoke accepted the parent turn but did not confirm a child; the deterministic Gateway regression covers child admission and checkout preparation.

Co-authored by [@vincentkoc](https://github.com/vincentkoc).

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Discussion, implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/85e0e6e0-016e-432c-b836-930659b35750)

## Worked on by

- @vincentkoc

prs.title: feat(plugins): legacy memory runtimes as backends and optional provider store
prs.body:
## Summary

### High Level TLDR

Follow-up to #201340 (memory backends). Two gaps keep a memory-fusion slot owner from being useful:

1. **Legacy memory plugins could not be backends.** `memory-core` and `memory-lancedb` register the file-shaped `runtime`, and the backend registrar dropped anything without `providerRuntime`. Now the host serves a legacy runtime as a backend through the same `adaptLegacyMemoryProvider` it already uses when such a plugin owns the slot.
2. **Nothing could be written through the provider contract.** `MemoryProviderHandle` gains an optional `store(request)` with a matching `capabilities.store` flag, bound by the host like every other call, so a slot owner can route new memories to the backends that accept them.

Both are additive: providers that do not declare `store` and configs without backends behave exactly as before.

### Exact change

- `src/plugins/memory-backend-legacy.ts` (new): `createLegacyBackendProviderRuntime(pluginId, runtime)` wraps a legacy runtime's `getMemorySearchManager` with `adaptLegacyMemoryProvider` and forwards `prepareReload` / `closeMemorySearchManager` / `closeAllMemorySearchManagers`, so reload and shutdown drains keep working.
- `registry-registrars-memory.ts`: a backend with only `runtime` is registered with `adapter: "legacy"` and `instanceOwner: runtime` instead of being warned and dropped. A backend with neither still warns.
- `memory-provider-open.ts`: backend opens report the real adapter and bind the plugin instance through `instanceOwner`. Open-time validation now requires `capabilities.store` (optional boolean) to match the presence of `store()`, like `candidates`.
- `memory-provider-runtime-types.ts`: `MemoryStoreRequest` (`text`, `title?`, `tags?`, `origin?: "tool" | "flush" | "capture"`), `MemoryStoreResult` (`stored` + reference, or `rejected` + reason), `capabilities.store?`, `store?()`.
- `memory-provider-adapter.ts` (`bindMemoryProvider`): a bound `store` runs through the same caller-currency `invoke` as search/get, rejects empty text, text over 64 KiB and non-string tags before provider code runs, requires the returned reference to belong to the provider, and rejects every call on a lease opened with purpose `status` (slot owner and backends alike).
- `memory-runtime.ts`: passes `readOnly` for `status` opens.
- `plugin-sdk/memory-host-search`: type-only exports `MemoryStoreRequest`, `MemoryStoreResult`.
- Docs: `plugins/sdk-overview/memory-and-context` handle table, capability table and backend section.

### Scope boundary

Legacy backends stay read-only (the legacy runtime has no write surface). No bundled plugin implements `store` in this PR.

## Verification

Isolated worktree, Linux x86_64, Node 24.22.1, base `origin/main`.

- New `src/plugins/memory-provider-store.test.ts` (6 tests): store pass-through with reference check, input validation, status leases read-only, open rejects capability/method mismatch both ways, a legacy runtime served as a backend through the adapter (search hits carry the backend provider id, no `store`), and the registrar keeping a legacy-only backend as `adapter: "legacy"`. Each fails on `origin/main` (no `store` binding, legacy backends dropped).
- Existing `memory-backend-provider`, `loader.memory-backend`, `memory-provider-runtime` suites: pass (59 tests together).

prs.title: fix(codex): keep replacement threads usable with large tool catalogs
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A managed Codex conversation can fail to start a replacement thread when a large direct tool catalog exhausts OpenClaw's estimated history allowance. The remaining one token cannot carry the history omission notice, so the turn fails before inference.

## User Impact

Affected sessions can start the replacement thread with bounded history when Codex has measured a completed request with the same direct catalog and runtime.

## Why This Change Was Made

The serialized tool definitions can substantially overstate their actual input cost. For this exhausted-budget case, use the previous request's measured full input as a conservative upper bound for the same eager tool definitions. The current prompt, instructions, media, output reserve, and history framing still get their own charges. A stale sample, a changed catalog or policy, or an unverified predecessor keeps the existing estimate. The rollout scan stays within the data already read for startup.

## Evidence

- Synthetic native startup coverage exercises history delivery and `turn/start` with a matching catalog, and checks that a changed catalog cannot use its predecessor's measurement.
- Rollout coverage distinguishes completed answers from compaction, replaced measurements, and later turns.
- Both focused suites passed on the official main-based patch (42 tests). Targeted lint, formatting, and the staged content check passed.

prs.title: docs: propose one side-by-side update model and a migration map from the current updater
prs.body:
Related: #197949

## What Problem This Solves

Updating OpenClaw is slow and often fails, and a failed update can leave an operator repairing the installation by hand. On one maintainer host, 22 of 53 recorded update attempts succeeded, successful ones took 9 to 48 minutes with 4 to 24 minutes of Gateway downtime, and all four automatic database rollbacks were refused. Those runs came from updaters older than the release layout now on `main`. The updater is about 112,000 non-test lines in 503 files, and `main` currently runs several update models side by side.

## User Impact

User impact: none. This pull request adds one design page under `docs/reference/` and changes no behavior. The page is not listed in `docs/docs.json`.

It proposes that every installation updates the way POSIX Git installs with a Gateway service already do on `main`: each release in its own directory behind one link, state upgraded by copy and swap when the new Gateway starts, and a frozen launcher that switches back after two failed starts. It also proposes deleting the in-place paths after one bridge release. That deletion is a point of no return and is not part of this pull request.

This branch is the long-lived feature branch for the work. It stays a draft until the decisions below are answered.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three merged changes already built the pieces for part of the installed base: release directories behind a linked package root (#198835), Git checkouts served from release worktrees with a launcher and trial (#199706), and the copy-and-swap state upgrade at Gateway start. Each kept the older path as a fallback, so the code grew. The page describes the end state where that model is the only one, and maps every existing installation kind, on-disk artifact, command, and flag onto it.

It overlaps with the open design in #197949, which takes an incremental route with fallbacks. Decision 1 on the page asks how the two should be combined.

Decisions that need a maintainer, each with options and a recommendation on the page:

1. How this relates to #197949 and its ongoing slices.
2. Swap state before the health check (as built) or health-check a copy first.
3. What pnpm, Bun, Homebrew, Nix, and system-package installs do.
4. How long replaced state files are kept (today: until the next upgrade, so steady disk use is twice the copied state).
5. Whether to add a manual rollback command.
6. PostgreSQL-backed state.
7. Plugin-owned stores during a trial.
8. The immutable installation owner.
9. Windows timing.
10. Which release is the bridge, and when the old paths are deleted.
11. Reducing the run record without a schema change.
12. Removing the container entrypoint Doctor pass.

## Evidence

Docs only. Nothing was run to produce the design; it was read from source at `0abe03d10082`, and the page's "Evidence limits" section lists what was read in full, in part, or only counted.

- `scripts/check-docs-mdx.mjs` on the page: passed.
- `oxfmt --check` on the page: clean.
- `git diff --check`: clean.
- An independent read-only review checked the page's claims against source in nine areas. It found five inaccuracies (deferred activation under `--no-restart`, the state copy scope, a driver started by the Gateway not surviving the restart, how a running Gateway detects a new release, and one file path). All five were confirmed against source and corrected in the second commit.

Not run: `pnpm check:docs` and `pnpm docs:check-links` (the worktree has no installed dependencies). The five related links were checked by hand against `docs/`.

prs.title: perf(auto-reply): skip CLI preview sanitization when no preview callback is registered
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

On CLI-backed turns, every streamed update sanitizes the accumulated reply even when the channel has no `onPartialReply` callback. The result is then discarded.

## User Impact

Channels without live previews avoid repeated work as CLI replies grow. Typing indicators still receive the classified text, and final delivery still sanitizes the reply.

## Why This Change Was Made

Return after the typing signal when there is no preview callback. CLI consumers that display previews keep their existing behavior. This follows up on #118349, which made preview materialization lazy for embedded runs.

## Evidence

The new regression fails on the unmodified base because the sanitizer runs once. With the fix, it verifies zero sanitizer calls for the partial, the expected typing signal and return value, and one sanitizer call for final text.

All 49 presentation tests and all 48 tests in the four related CLI and partial-reply consumer suites passed locally. Formatting and `git diff --check` passed.


## Real behavior proof

I ran real CLI-backed turns through a built Gateway from this branch (`7a985fb8f`, `OpenClaw 2026.11.5`). The test used an isolated state directory and config, the `claude-cli` runtime with `claude-sonnet-5-5`, and Claude Code 2.1.311. Each turn entered through `chat.send` and went through `runReplyAgent` and the CLI candidate into `presentPartialReply(..., "cli")`. That path registers no `onPartialReply`, which is the same as channels without live previews. The Gateway ran in a `node:24-bookworm` container on Linux x64.

To count the work, I added temporary JSONL counters to the built `presentPartialReply` (in both the main and worker chunks). They record each CLI partial, each partial `sanitizeStreamingText` call and its cost, and each typing signal. An env toggle on the same build restores the pre-PR control flow as the control: sanitize first, then drop the result because there is no consumer. The counters are not part of this PR.

| Turn | Variant | Reply | CLI partials | Preview consumer | Partial sanitize calls | Chars sanitized | Typing signals | Final reply |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 60 lines | pre-PR | 1,027 chars | 65 | none | 65 | 34,290 | 65 | 60 lines |
| 60 lines | this PR | 1,027 chars | 64 | none | **0** | **0** | 64 | 60 lines, identical |
| 300 lines | pre-PR | 5,749 chars | 334 | none | 334 | 941,836 | 334 | 300 lines |
| 300 lines | this PR | 5,749 chars | 335 | none | **0** | **0** | 335 | 300 lines, identical |

The partial count differs by one between variants because the two variants ran as separate model streams.

Counter excerpt, 300-line turn (timestamps and pids removed):

```text
# pre-PR control
{"ev":"partial","runtime":"cli","len":12,"consumer":false,"variant":"base"}
{"ev":"partial-sanitize","len":12,"ms":4.494}
{"ev":"typing","len":12}
...
{"ev":"partial","runtime":"cli","len":5749,"consumer":false,"variant":"base"}
{"ev":"partial-sanitize","len":5749,"ms":0.067}
{"ev":"typing","len":5749}

# this PR
{"ev":"partial","runtime":"cli","len":2,"consumer":false,"variant":"pr"}
{"ev":"typing","len":2}
...
{"ev":"partial","runtime":"cli","len":5749,"consumer":false,"variant":"pr"}
{"ev":"typing","len":5749}
```

What this shows:

- With no preview consumer, this PR does no partial sanitization. Before the PR, the work was repeated over the whole growing reply on every update, which totaled about 0.94M characters for a 5.7 KB reply.
- Typing keeps receiving every classified partial, with the same signal count as the partial count.
- The final reply reaches the transcript and is byte-for-byte identical to the pre-PR control in both turns.

The wall-clock saving at these sizes is small: the summed sanitizer time was 39 ms for the 300-line pre-PR turn. The work grows quadratically with reply length, so long CLI replies benefit most.

I also re-ran `src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-presentation.test.ts` on this head, and all 49 tests passed.

prs.title: fix: bring commands back after the Gateway's spawn broker fails to restart
prs.body:
Root cause: src/process/spawn-broker/host.ts:505 rejected readiness and scheduled no further start once five consecutive replacement attempts failed (about 4 s of backoff), so a ready Gateway broker that hit a short launch-failure window stayed unavailable until the Gateway restarted.

Fixes #201609

Thanks @davidromeo for the detailed incident report and log timeline.

## What Problem This Solves

On Linux the Gateway runs commands through a spawn broker. When that broker dies, the Gateway starts a new one. But if the first few replacements also fail, for example while the host is briefly out of file descriptors, the Gateway stopped trying after about 4 seconds. From then on every exec, stdio MCP startup, CLI-backend turn and cron script failed with `Spawn broker is unavailable` until someone restarted the Gateway. Nothing was logged about the broker exiting.

## User Impact

After broker loss, the Gateway keeps replacing the broker every 2 seconds, so commands work again as soon as a new broker can start. Commands that were running when the broker died still fail and are not rerun, as before. A broker that dies right away every time costs one launch every 2 seconds instead of a fast loop.

## Why This Change Was Made

The docs already say later commands use the restarted broker (docs/gateway/background-process.md). The restart backoff (100, 250, 500, 1000, 2000 ms) now stays at its last step instead of ending after five failures. Nothing else changes: the startup-only failure path (fall back to in-process spawning), a Node runtime that can no longer launch children, native-resource brokers and shutdown still stop retrying exactly as before.

The reporter's broker death cause (no kernel OOM recorded) is still unknown, and loss is still not logged. This PR fixes the part that turned one broker death into an outage that lasted until restart.

## Evidence

Real Gateway on Linux (secretless node:24.22.1 container, dist build), real agent turns through `openclaw agent` against the repo's mock OpenAI server. The model calls exec, and the check reads the exec result the Gateway sent back to the model. Full proof lines: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201631#issuecomment-7000514141

- Base 67aacbb676e5, broker SIGKILLed while the Gateway's descriptor limit was briefly exhausted (6 s): no replacement, `Spawn broker is unavailable` at +10 s and +30 s, after the pressure had cleared.
- Candidate, same fault: `spawn broker restarted`, exec OK at +10 s and +30 s.
- Candidate, plain SIGKILL: restarted, exec OK. Control without a fault: one broker, exec OK.
- Crash-loop control (every new broker exits during startup): base made 5 launches and then stopped for good. The candidate made 18 launches in 30 s, spaced about 2,040 ms apart after the first four backoff steps, so there is no hot loop.
- Regression `src/process/spawn-broker/restart.test.ts`: fails on base (spawned 6 times, expected 7), passes with the fix. It replaces the old test that required giving up.

Line delta against the merge base: production +4/-5, tests +11/-7.

prs.title: fix(codex): let saved conversations recover after a remote failure
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

After a failed turn on a remote Codex app-server, a saved conversation can get stuck when OpenClaw needs to apply a different configuration. The server can keep the failed runtime loaded across WebSocket reconnects.

## User Impact

When Codex confirms the failed runtime unloaded, OpenClaw asks the user to retry their message in the same saved conversation. If another client keeps the thread loaded, OpenClaw explains what the user needs to close. Other conversations on the connection can continue.

## Why This Change Was Made

OpenClaw unsubscribes from the affected thread and checks that Codex unloaded it. Codex's default idle retention can take up to a minute after the last subscriber leaves. The next message uses the existing cold-resume flow and runs current policy checks. Ending the first attempt after unload confirmation avoids relying on a resume response that can acknowledge ignored settings on a competing loaded runtime. The native protocol still has separate read and resume operations, so an external client can reload the thread between them on retry.

## Evidence

- The focused adoption suite passed all 11 tests, including four WebSocket recovery cases. A synthetic app-server peer exercised the real WebSocket transport and verified same-thread retry, preserved bindings and sibling work, competing activity rejection, and current-policy denial. Node 24.22.1, one worker, 208 seconds wall time with cold worker preparation. A live app-server was outside this validation.
- Scoped Codex typecheck and lint, format, the repository commit hook, and `git diff --check` passed. A direct check of the production channel failure renderer verified that it shows the retry guidance.
- Independent source review of the exact seven-file patch at base `0321f852d91a` found no actionable issues. The automated command-line review failed at model startup and produced no verdict. Native unsubscribe and shutdown behavior was checked against Codex source.

prs.title: fix: let GPT-Live voice sessions use substantive delegation guidance in Voice Call and Discord
prs.body:
Closes #202910

## What Problem This Solves

When a realtime voice session runs on GPT-Live and `consultPolicy` is `"substantive"`, Voice Call tells the model to "call openclaw_agent_consult", a tool GPT-Live does not have: it delegates natively. Discord voice cannot use `"substantive"` at all, because its schema only allows `auto` and `always`, and `always` is rejected on GPT-Live. So on GPT-Live there is no working way to ask the model to hand facts, memory and tool questions to the OpenClaw agent instead of answering them itself.

## User Impact

User impact: `consultPolicy: "substantive"` now works on GPT-Live in both Voice Call and Discord voice. The model gets delegation guidance that matches how it delegates, and Discord accepts the same three values as Voice Call. Existing configs are unaffected: `auto` and `always` keep their current prompts and checks, and `always` is still rejected on GPT-Live.

## Why This Change Was Made

Each surface made part of this decision on its own. Voice Call passed `substantive` to the shared session policy as `auto` (so the GPT-Live check passed) but built the prompt from the raw config before it knew which model would answer. Now:

- The shared session policy (`resolveRealtimeVoiceSessionPolicy`) carries `auto | substantive | always` unchanged and stays the only place that rejects `always` on GPT-Live.
- The shared prompt builder (`buildRealtimeVoiceAgentConsultPolicyInstructions`) takes `handlesAgentConsult` and, for native-delegation models, emits a "Delegation policy" block that does not name `openclaw_agent_consult`. Both public SDK helpers gain an optional field, so existing callers are unchanged.
- Voice Call adds the consult block in the realtime handler after it resolves the routed model and session policy, instead of at startup. The block now comes after the agent context and call brief, the same position Discord already uses.
- Discord adds `substantive` to its schema, type and help text, and passes `handlesAgentConsult` into the shared builder. Config metadata and docs are regenerated.

Host-side enforcement of `always` (Discord `realtime-consults.ts`, Voice Call `scheduleForcedAgentConsult`) is unchanged.

<details><summary>GPT-Live wording</summary>

```
Delegation policy:
- Delegate every request that needs facts, memory, current information, tools, workspace state, or the user's own context, even if you think you know the answer.
- Answer directly only for greetings, acknowledgements, and brief latency checks.
- After delegating, do not answer the question yourself before the result arrives; one short backchannel is fine.
- When the result arrives, speak it once and do not repeat an answer you already gave.
```

GA models keep the existing "Consult behavior" blocks byte for byte.

</details>

## Evidence

The new tests fail on `origin/main` and pass on this branch. The Discord GPT-Live case reproduces the bug directly: on main the session instructions contain `openclaw_agent_consult`.

| Test | `origin/main` | This branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discord GPT-Live, `substantive`: no `openclaw_agent_consult`, has Delegation policy | fails: `expected 'You are OpenClaw\'s Discord voice int…' not to contain 'openclaw_agent_consult'` | passes |
| Discord GPT-Live, `auto`: no consult block | passes | passes |
| Voice Call GPT-Live, `substantive`: bridge instructions start with Delegation policy, no tool name | fails: `expected 'Be helpful.\n\nUse native agent deleg…' to match /^Be helpful\.\n\nDelegation policy:…/` | passes |
| Voice Call GA, `substantive`: Consult behavior block reaches the bridge | fails: `expected 'Be helpful.' to match /^Be helpful\.\n\nConsult behavior:\n/` | passes |
| Shared builder: Live wording, `auto` and `toolPolicy: none` add nothing | fails | passes |
| Discord schema accepts `auto`, `substantive`, `always` | `substantive` fails: `Invalid option: expected one of "auto"\|"always"` | passes |

Red-on-base was run by swapping the 10 changed source files for their `origin/main` versions with the new tests in place, then restoring and `cmp`-checking them.

Checks on this branch:

- Focused tests: 84 passed (core 18 in 2.2s, Voice Call + Discord schema 42 in 29s, Discord voice selection 24 in 19s).
- `pnpm test:extension voice-call`: 50 files passed (319s). `pnpm test:extension discord`: 245 files passed (246s). `pnpm test src/talk`: 10 files passed (162s).
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, `tsgo:core:test`, `tsgo:extensions`, `tsgo:extensions:test`: pass.
- oxlint on `extensions/voice-call`, `extensions/discord`, `src/talk` and the touched core files: pass. Format check and `git diff --check`: clean.
- `config:channels:check`, `config:docs:check`, `config:schema:check`, `plugin-sdk:check-exports`, `docs:check-links` (0 broken), `docs:check-config-examples`, `check:test-lines-ratchet` (+56, allowance 400): pass.

Gaps:

- No live call or Discord voice session with a real GPT-Live model. Proof stops at the instructions handed to the realtime bridge, which is where the bug lives.

prs.title: feat(clawrouter): consume qualified xAI web search offers
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

ClawRouter `web_search` cannot consume an explicitly admitted native xAI Responses search offer.

## User Impact

The registered tool can use `grok-4.7` through a qualified native or manifest ClawRouter offer, with only the selected router credential and fresh admission per invocation. This change does not activate a Worker route, model, tariff or dedicated `x_search` tool.

## Why This Change Was Made

Native xAI tools and ClawRouter share the Responses request/text/citation codec. Native model reasoning policy stays in the xAI plugin. The proxy requires matching formats, supported low effort, declared `web_search` and versioned hosted-tool admission; it sends one search tool with `store:false`, refuses POST redirects, bounds and wraps answer text, rejects credential-bearing citation URLs and omits unqualified inline offsets. Incomplete/failed work stays an error, never proof of free usage.

This consumes the contract from https://github.com/openclaw/clawrouter/pull/559. Worker dispatch/accounting and catalog activation remain their owners' prerequisites.

## Evidence

prs.title: feat: let plugin session forks work on Claude CLI chats without an API key
prs.body:
Closes #202365

## What Problem This Solves

Plugins that fork a chat in the background, such as a prompt helper or a reviewer, do not work when the chat's model runs through the Claude CLI. `runForkedTurn` always calls the provider API, so on a Claude CLI setup with no Anthropic API key every fork fails with `No API key found for provider ...`. With a key, it bills the API instead of the subscription the chat uses. `forkSession` refuses Claude CLI chats outright.

## User Impact

Plugin forks (`runForkedTurn` and `forkSession`) on a Claude CLI chat now fork the chat's own Claude Code session and work without an API key. Forks on the built-in runtime do not change. A `runForkedTurn` call that grants the plugin's own tools (for example Skill Workshop's review) or sets `maxTokens` still runs on the built-in runtime, as today. A Claude CLI chat on a host that also has an Anthropic API key now forks on the chat's Claude CLI account, not the API key.

## Why This Change Was Made

Claude Code keeps the conversation in its own native session, and every Claude CLI reply in the transcript records that session and the reply's id. A fork now starts a new Claude Code process that resumes that session with `--fork-session --resume-session-at <reply>`, the same native branch `sessions.create` parent forks already use. #170146 ruled CLI forks out because a CLI runtime has no prepared provider request for the built-in runtime to replay. This change does not replay a request: the CLI branches its own session.

The fork keeps the guarantees of a built-in fork:

- Only the fork's tools run. The Gateway MCP grant lists the chat's tools, so the resumed session keeps its tool catalog and prompt cache, and a call to any other tool returns `<tool> is not available in this background run.`, as on the built-in runtime. Claude's native execution tools stay off. `read`, `ls` and `exec` keep the chat's policy, the owner-only `exec` rule and the no-approval rule (the fork's `internal_system` provenance reaches the grant).
- Nothing is written to the chat or kept on disk. The OpenClaw transcript, the chat's native Claude session and its binding stay unchanged. The Claude backend launches the fork with `--no-session-persistence` (a new `fork` value of the backend's `controlOperation`), so the branched native session is never saved. If the CLI did not report a new session id, the fork fails.
- The chat's account and cwd boundary applies: the fork runs on the account the chat's turns select (the session's pin, or for an automatic pin the account its native session was bound with, through the same selection the turns use) and in the same cwd (spawned cwd or the agent's run cwd). The existing resume check refuses another auth profile, auth epoch or cwd. Tool, MCP and message-tool drift is allowed, because the fork runs its own process and grant. The fork's own message-tool policy never hides the cwd check.
- The fork branches in the native session that recorded the anchored reply, also after the chat moved to a newer native session (for example the `prompt-tools` reset below). It fails before any CLI or provider I/O when it cannot branch: the anchored turn has no recorded Claude CLI reply (still running, delivered through the message tool, or from another runtime), or the chat has no Claude CLI binding.
- No turn hooks run, and the final `before_model_request` policy runs as `side_question`. Lane, plugin attribution, timeout and abort are unchanged.

A CLI turn records its runtime as the model provider (`claude-cli/<model>`). The fork keeps the CLI as the owner and runs the canonical provider's model, as isolated completions already do.

Plugin tool grants (`runtimePluginToolGrant`, `toolContext.backgroundRun`) do not reach Claude Code's MCP grant today, and a CLI process takes no output-token cap, so forks that grant plugin tools or set `maxTokens` stay on the built-in runtime, which enforces both. Extending the CLI path to either is a separate change.

Maintainer decision: this reverses the documented "CLI runtimes are not supported" rule for session forks (#170146). The docs change is in this PR.

## Evidence

Behavior checked: a plugin forks a Claude CLI chat on an isolated Gateway with no Anthropic API key, through the real Claude Code CLI on a Claude subscription login.

- Base: the fork fails with `No API key found for provider "claude-cli"`, and `forkSession` with `Session forks are not supported for CLI runtime claude-cli.`
- Head: the fork answers from the chat's context, reads a workspace file with `read`, gets `exec is not available in this background run.` when it tries a tool it was not given, and `forkSession` answers with 15,393 cached input tokens. The chat transcript, the native session file hash and the binding are the same before and after, and the chat's Claude project folder holds no new session file.
- Packaged upgrade from the latest stable release (2026.11.6): stable created a Claude CLI chat with no API key, pinned with `sessions.patch` to the Claude login account (`anthropic:claude-cli`, source `user`) and run in a configured agent cwd. The head commit was packed with `scripts/package-openclaw-for-docker.mjs`, installed over the same state, and its own `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive` upgraded it (schema 38 to 43). Both fork APIs then work on that chat, and the chat's account pin, cwd, native session, native transcript hash and session-file count are the same before and after the forks. The same run with the base commit packaged still fails both forks. The chat's first ordinary turn after either upgrade starts a new native session with `cli session reset: reason=prompt-tools` (the tool list changed between releases; #186684); this PR does not change that path.
- Unit tests at the owners (fork owner, CLI runner execute and prepare, Gateway MCP grant, `/btw`) fail with the fix reverted and pass with it.
- Local ClawSweeper review (Claude runner, `--local-range` from `2c78c095b68`): four rounds. Round 1 rated the patch correct with one P3 (fork error for message-tool replies, fixed). Round 2 found a P2: the fork's message policy hid the cwd check (fixed, with a test). Round 3 found a P2: the fork did not use the turn's cwd chain (fixed, with a test). Round 4: patch is correct, no findings, security cleared. The local runs cannot see this runtime output, so they rate proof as missing. The hosted review's P2 findings (the account pin on a fork of a `claude-cli/*` turn, the kept native fork session, and the dropped `maxTokens` cap) are fixed with tests that fail without the fix (local round 6: patch is correct, no findings). Full CI then flagged the session-identity ratchet (the fork compared the reply's native session id with the binding's) and the test-line budget; the fork now resumes the reply's own native session, and the budget record is above. Local round 7 at the current head `dce38026de0`: patch is correct, no findings, security cleared.


prs.title: fix(agents): fork subscription CLI chats through their own CLI
prs.body:
Stacked on #202646 (secret input after an async stdin prompt); review the last commit.

## What Problem This Solves

Plugin session forks (`runForkedTurn`, `forkSession`; for example Better Prompt and Skill Workshop reviews) always ran on the built-in runtime. On a Claude CLI chat signed in with a Claude subscription:

- With only the CLI's own `claude` login, `runForkedTurn` failed with `No API key found for provider "claude-cli"`.
- With a Claude subscription token stored in OpenClaw, `runForkedTurn` sent the token to the Anthropic API directly, which bills metered extra usage instead of the plan (`cliBackendDispatch` notes in `run/params.ts`).
- `forkSession` refused every CLI runtime: `Session forks are not supported for CLI runtime claude-cli.`

## Why This Change Was Made

OpenClaw already has one owner for "run this embedded run on the subscription CLI": `cliBackendDispatch: "subscription-auth"` (Active Memory's recall uses it). The fork owner opts into it; no new path:

- `runSessionFork` sets `cliBackendDispatch: "subscription-auth"`. Eligibility is unchanged: subscription (oauth/token) or unresolvable credentials go to the CLI; API keys keep the request replay and its prompt cache.
- Dispatch accepts the fork's in-memory conversation (`sessionManager`), and sends the CLI only the tools that may execute (`toolExecutionAllow`; an empty list is a tool-free run).
- Dispatch now picks the CLI account the way a new CLI session does. Before, it passed only an explicit pin, so a stored Claude token never reached the CLI (`Not logged in · Please run /login`); Active Memory recalls had the same gap.
- Runs that grant the plugin's own tools or set `maxTokens` keep the direct route: neither reaches a CLI process.
- Dispatch carries the run's policy facts to the CLI: a run under another session's policy (a fork's `sandboxSessionKey`) passes that session's entry, the requester fields and `internal_system` provenance into the CLI's Gateway tool grant, so restricted-sender limits apply to the fork as to the chat's own turns.

Accepted: a CLI fork starts a fresh CLI session with the conversation as context, so it does not reuse the chat's cache, and each fork leaves one Claude session file under `~/.claude/projects`, as Active Memory's CLI recalls already do. The source chat's native session is never resumed or written.

Permission modes (maintainer decision, now in `docs/gateway/permission-modes.md`): the `sessionRoot` boundary is enforced on the built-in runtime; CLI-backed chats use the CLI's own controls, and owner turns' Gateway tools are not limited to `sessionRoot`. Live, on a Claude CLI chat in `workspace` mode, an ordinary turn and a fork both read a file outside the workspace through `mcp__openclaw__read`, and the same chat on the built-in runtime refuses both with `Path escapes sandbox root`. A CLI fork therefore has the same file access as the chat's own CLI turns.

Not covered: Gemini CLI on a Google login (OpenClaw cannot limit its tools under OAuth), and harnesses that own their login with no limited one-shot turn (Copilot, Muse, `acp-*`).

## Evidence

Real product, tier source (`ocx src`), isolated foreground Gateway, no API key in the environment or auth store; profiles: Claude subscription setup token, ChatGPT OAuth, Grok OAuth. Each chat: one turn ("Remember PELICAN-42"), then forks through a probe plugin.

| Route | `runForkedTurn` `[read, ls]` | `forkSession` | `runForkedTurn` cache read |
|---|---|---|---|
| `claude-cli`, Claude token | `PELICAN-42 \| FORK-READ-OK 7f3a` (dispatched to Claude CLI) | `PELICAN-42` | 6,985 |
| ChatGPT OAuth, built-in | `PELICAN-42 \| FORK-READ-OK 7f3a` | `PELICAN-42` (cache read 9,856) | 10,112 |
| Codex app-server | `PELICAN-42 \| FORK-READ-OK 7f3a` | `PELICAN-42` (19,584) | 8,704 |
| Grok OAuth | `PELICAN-42 \| FORK-READ-OK 7f3a` | `PELICAN-42` (1,152) | 1,152 |

- `main` on the same Claude chat: `runForkedTurn` ran on the Anthropic API with the token (cache read 0, cache write 23,872), `forkSession` refused.
- Every route: source transcript hash, message count and native binding unchanged; the Claude source session file holds only the chat's own turn.
- Better Prompt 0.2.2 (`start` → `take` through `plugins.sessionAction`) produced an improved prompt on the Claude CLI chat and on the ChatGPT chat.
- Dispatch tests: a fork runs on the CLI with only its own tools from its in-memory session; plugin tool grants and output caps keep the passthrough.

prs.title: test(plugins): cover memory backend and provider store edge contracts
prs.body:
## Summary

### High Level TLDR

Test-only follow-up to #201340 and #202838. A local Stryker mutation run over the code those PRs added found behavior the existing tests did not pin down. This adds `src/plugins/memory-backend-contract.test.ts` (19 tests) for those gaps. No production code changes.

Covered:

- Provider store input and result validation: non-string tags, a missing request, the exact 64 KiB boundary, valid `rejected` results passing through, malformed results refused, binding without options, and `capabilities.store` advertised only when `store()` exists.
- Open-time handle validation per field: each missing method (`search`, `get`, `health`, `close`) and each invalid capability (pagination, candidate kind, project filter, store flag).
- Backend access: backend leases opened for `status` are read-only while default leases write; a backend that finishes opening after the owner's lease ended is closed and the open rejects.
- Backend policy edges: only the selected slot owner's own manifest can request backends; no opt-in means no backend; a fresh load loop state.
- Legacy backends forward `closeMemorySearchManager` / `closeAllMemorySearchManagers` bound to the runtime, and a backend with neither runtime is skipped with its exact warning.

## Verification

- `memory-backend-contract.test.ts`: 19 pass (plugins project). Lint and format clean.
- Stryker 10.1.1, command runner, in place on a disposable worktree, mutating only the lines #201340/#202838 added in `memory-backend.ts`, `memory-backend-legacy.ts`, `loader-load-loop-state.ts`, `memory-provider-adapter.ts`, `memory-provider-open.ts`, `registry-registrars-memory.ts`:
  - before: 78.4% (243 of 310 mutants killed)
  - after: 97.7% (303 of 310 killed)
  - The 7 survivors are equivalent (a phase-mark label string, a defensive re-check already enforced earlier, `?? `/`&&` on a value that is always set at that point).
- Test-line ratchet and mock-export ratchet: OK.

### What was not tested

No Stryker config is added to the repo; the mutation run was local only.

prs.title: fix(sandbox): keep Android Gradle build output out of workspace results
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Building an Android debug APK larger than 64 MiB inside a cloud workspace can make every subsequent workspace result fail with `Cloud workspace result is too large: <apk path>`. A production retry 11 minutes later rebuilt the APK and failed again, preventing the user's source changes from returning too.

## User Impact

Cloud workspace results omit regenerable Android Gradle Plugin intermediates, APKs, and app bundles. Source changes and authored content elsewhere under `build/`, including reports, remain eligible. The 64 MiB per-file limit stays unchanged. Existing baselines containing AGP outputs remain recoverable through exact saved-root authentication, including when disposable pnpm cache files are present.

## Why This Change Was Made

`src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-manifest.ts:58` defines the limit, and `workspace-manifest-comparison.ts:230` rejects an oversized eligible file. AGP output was missing from the shared derived-path policy, so one disposable APK could reject the entire result.

Add only `build/intermediates`, `build/outputs/apk`, and `build/outputs/bundle` to the existing segment matcher and rsync exclusions. These patterns match at any module depth in both consumers. The exclusion owner defines the AGP list once and builds current and historical membership from it. Regenerate both manifest consumers and document the exclusions, following #202327.

Historical recovery must also preserve earlier membership policies. The repair loop previously restored only the pnpm fallback store; coupling pnpm and AGP restoration then missed baselines needing one class included and the other excluded. The existing repair loop now tries one constant ordered list of legacy derived eligibility subsets: current membership, AGP only, pnpm only, then both. Each filesystem candidate still requires `rebuiltRoot === expectedRoot` before replacement. Normal capture receives no extra candidates, and all other derived exclusions stay active. There is no new module, configuration, reporting, durable-state migration, or limit change.

This addresses the verified [historical eligibility review finding](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/202881#discussion_r4650299205). Historical receipt projection already uses the shared matcher; missing local inventory packs additionally require these independently authenticated filesystem candidates. Ambiguous or divergent candidates continue to fail rather than replace the saved merge base.

## Evidence

The existing capture-and-transfer test creates three AGP files larger than `MAX_RECONCILIATION_FILE_BYTES`. Local capture, standalone capture, and a real local rsync transfer omit them while retaining `m/build/reports/summary.txt`. The same fixture proves that excluded-only ancestry is pruned.

The existing baseline-repair table covers projection, canonical, and checkpoint recovery; AGP-only baselines with disposable pnpm files; pnpm-only baselines with disposable AGP files; and baselines containing both. It preserves the original pnpm, node_modules, divergent-edit, and canonical-only unadmitted-bytes cases. Shared path lists, baseline-file metadata, ancestor construction, and existing assertion/map idioms consolidate equivalent setup. No new `it(...)` was added. After formatting, the two test files add 40 lines and remove 40: **net 0**.

<details>
<summary>Red/green commands, output, and focused checks</summary>

Capture regression red on base `39c3099189516d374bc1a74cd625b9ceaa5494e3`, with only fixture changes applied:

```text
pnpm test src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-generated-paths.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
FAIL excludes only generated runtime roots from capture and transfer
Received unexpectedly includes:
  m/build/intermediates/x
  m/build/outputs/apk/x.apk
  m/build/outputs/bundle/x.aab
FAIL omits cache-only ancestry from remote capture while retaining empty directories
Test Files  1 failed (1)
     Tests  2 failed | 9 passed (11)
Duration 105.42s; command wall time 113.87s.
```

The intact historical AGP baseline regression was also red at the initial exclusion-only head `786a95372ba1`: 2 failed and 14 passed. The independent-subset regression is red at `7ab6d6e2865e3d446facbd584a742e9bd8d5bbd9`, with the final fixture consolidation and no production subset fix:

```text
pnpm test src/gateway/worker-environments/local-workspace-manifest-scan.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
FAIL historical AGP baseline with disposable pnpm cache
FAIL historical pnpm baseline with disposable AGP output
Local workspace baseline nodes are missing and neither workspace matches the saved baseline or a verified checkpoint.
Test Files  1 failed (1)
     Tests  2 failed | 17 passed (19)
Duration 6.78s; command wall time 9.74s.
```

Green with the independent subsets:

```text
pnpm test src/gateway/worker-environments/local-workspace-manifest-scan.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  19 passed (19)
Duration 61.32s; command wall time 69.69s.

pnpm test src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-generated-paths.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  11 passed (11)
Duration 5.34s; command wall time 8.46s.
```

The repair assertions take about 1 second and capture/transfer assertions about 1.3 seconds. Compiled-worker preparation and verification dominate wall time; the repair file rebuilds the repository's worker artifacts on a source cache miss. This owning-boundary proof exercises filesystem repair and real transfer without starting a Gateway or contacting a test host.

Additional passing checks:

```text
pnpm tsgo:core
node scripts/run-tsgo-core-test-shards.mjs --changed-paths-json '["src/gateway/worker-environments/local-workspace-manifest-scan.test.ts","src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-generated-paths.test.ts"]'
  [tsgo:gateway-other] passed in 2.5s
node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.core.json src/gateway/worker-environments/local-workspace-manifest-scan.ts src/gateway/worker-environments/local-workspace-manifest-scan.test.ts src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-actual-manifest.ts src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-path-exclusions.ts src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-generated-paths.test.ts src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-manifest-script.generated.mjs src/node-host/node-worker-workspace-manifest.generated.worker.mjs
pnpm format:check src/gateway/worker-environments/local-workspace-manifest-scan.ts src/gateway/worker-environments/local-workspace-manifest-scan.test.ts src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-actual-manifest.ts src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-path-exclusions.ts src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-generated-paths.test.ts src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-manifest-script.generated.mjs src/node-host/node-worker-workspace-manifest.generated.worker.mjs docs/gateway/sandboxing/docker-backend.md
pnpm runtime:scripts:check
node scripts/check-docs-mdx.mjs docs/gateway/sandboxing/docker-backend.md
git diff --check
```

Codex autoreview of both the final staged repair and committed whole-PR head `986b78db358062c1b11feee56d3c98e8b71a96b4` is scoped-clean through P2, with no accepted/actionable findings. Exact-head [CI run 44863205523](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44863205523) completed successfully. The repository watcher reported `GREEN` for this exact head with zero pending checks and ten superseded contexts; no CI rerun was requested. The accepted P2 review thread is resolved, and the final live thread check found no new finding. All test fixtures are synthetic, and no CI rerun has been requested.

Whole-PR production delta: 60 added, 28 removed, including generated consumers; docs: 4 added; tests: 40 added, 40 removed.

</details>

Release-note context: Sandbox workspace results now exclude Android Gradle Plugin intermediates and APK/AAB output so large regenerable build artifacts cannot block source changes from returning. Historical AGP and pnpm baseline membership remains recoverable through independently authenticated eligibility subsets. Authored build content and existing size limits are preserved.
