prs.title: fix(config): repeated $include entries make config loading take minutes
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: config loading takes minutes when config files include the same child file several times across a few levels of `$include`.

## User Impact

User impact: a config tree with repeated includes now fails fast with an error that names the limit and the recovery step, so the CLI, the Gateway and config reloads stop spending minutes on it. Real configs stay far below 1024 include file loads.

```
Maximum include file loads (1024) exceeded at: ./l10.json. Each repeated $include entry loads its file again, and arrays from every load are concatenated. Combine the included files into fewer files that give the same merged config, keeping array entries from every load in order, then rerun openclaw config validate.
```

Recovery for an existing installation that hits the limit is the step the error names. Include merging concatenates arrays, so a file included twice adds its array entries twice. For example a file that sets `mcp.servers.docs.args: ["mcp-server-fetch"]` and is included twice gives two arguments. Removing a repeated reference therefore keeps the merged config only when the file sets no arrays, or when the user moves the array entries that the repeat added into the remaining files. A repeat that comes after a different file (A, B, A) also applies A over B again. The upgrade run below shows the recovery on a config tree whose included files set no arrays.

## Why This Change Was Made

`$include` already has a depth limit of 10 and a cycle check, and each file is capped at 2 MB. Both checks look at one include chain. A file may still list the same child file several times (`"$include": ["./b.json", "./b.json", ...]`), and each repeat reads, parses and merges the whole subtree below it again. The work grows as fan-out to the power of depth. Nine levels that each include the next level four times load 349,524 files, built from eleven files of about 100 bytes.

The include resolver now counts file loads in one resolution and throws a `ConfigIncludeError` once it reaches 1024 loads. The check sits next to the depth check in `loadFileSync`, and the error flows through the same config validation path as the depth and cycle errors. The docs list the new limit next to the depth limit, together with the same recovery step.

## Evidence

The proof script generates nine levels where level i includes level i+1 F times, then runs `openclaw config validate` from source (`node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs src/entry.ts config validate`) with `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` pointing at that tree. Wall time includes about 30 s of dev-mode CLI startup on this machine.

| Fan-out | Include file loads | main `00b62dd` | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 10 | 28.0 s, Config valid | 31.0 s, Config valid |
| 2 | 1,023 | 30.0 s, Config valid | 30.8 s, Config valid |
| 3 | 29,524 | 67.3 s, Config valid | 29.7 s, include error |
| 4 | 349,525 | 389.9 s, Config valid | 30.9 s, include error |

Branch output for fan-out 4:

```
Config needs correction: .../fan4/openclaw.json
  - <root>: Maximum include file loads (1024) exceeded at: ./l10.json
```

Calling `resolveConfigIncludes` directly on main for the same trees took 0.56 s, 7.3 s and 80.3 s for fan-out 2, 3 and 4. On this branch fan-out 2 resolves in 0.39 s and fan-out 3 and 4 throw the include error.

### Upgrade from the latest stable release

This run installs `openclaw@2026.11.3` (npm `latest`, commit `847611d`) into a local npm prefix, then runs the same configs with this branch built from source (`pnpm build:runtime` at `4e62b0f`, run as `node openclaw.mjs`). Both CLIs share one state dir and one HOME inside the proof dir, and the stable release runs first. Node 24.22.1 on Linux.

Configs:

- `normal`: a modular config with eleven files. It uses include arrays (`logging`, `agents.defaults`), sibling overrides (`gateway.port`, `messages.responsePrefix`, `agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds`), and nested includes three levels deep (`openclaw.json` to `agents/index.json5` to `agents/defaults.json5` to `shared/timezone.json5`, and the same shape under `messages`).
- `fanout4`: nine levels where each level includes the next level four times (349,525 include loads).
- `recovered`: `fanout4` after following the error's advice, so each level lists the next level once (10 include loads).

| Config | Command | 2026.11.3 | this branch `4e62b0f` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| normal | `config validate` | 2.8 s, Config valid | 4.0 s, Config valid |
| recovered | `config validate` | 2.8 s, Config valid | 4.0 s, Config valid |
| fanout4 | `config validate` | 158.4 s, Config valid | 6.0 s, include load error |
| normal | `gateway run` until `/readyz` 200 | 32.1 s, ready | see below |
| fanout4 | `gateway run` until `/readyz` 200 | 945.0 s, ready | 18.5 s, exits 78 with the include load error |

`config get --json` for `gateway`, `logging`, `messages` and `ui` on the normal config, and `ui` on the recovered config, print byte identical output on both CLIs. The gateway token prints as `__OPENCLAW_REDACTED__` on both. Merged values on both:

```
logging   {"level":"info","consoleLevel":"warn"}
messages  {"responsePrefix":"[proof]","ackReaction":"eyes","ackReactionScope":"all", ...}
gateway   {"port":18891,"mode":"local","bind":"loopback","auth":{"mode":"token","token":"__OPENCLAW_REDACTED__"}}
```

The sha256 of every authored config file is the same before the stable run and after the branch run. The stable Gateway added `openclaw.json.last-good`, a byte copy of `openclaw.json`.

Branch `config validate` output for `fanout4` at `4e62b0f`. Commit `e65d63e` changed only the wording after the first sentence, to the message quoted at the top.

```
Config needs correction: <proof>/configs/fanout4/openclaw.json
  - <root>: Maximum include file loads (1024) exceeded at: ./l10.json. Each repeated $include entry loads its file again. Remove repeated $include references to the same file or merge those files, then rerun openclaw config validate.

Run `openclaw doctor --fix` to repair, or fix the keys above manually.
Run openclaw config schema to inspect supported settings and values, then rerun openclaw config validate.
```

Branch `gateway run` on `fanout4` prints the same problem under `OpenClaw config is invalid` and exits with code 78.

Limits of this run, all from the host and unrelated to this change. The branch Gateway on the normal config stops before readiness because the stable release left the agent database at schema 27 and the branch expects 41, so it asks for `openclaw doctor --fix`. Doctor and `config get agents.defaults` on the branch need an OpenClaw temp root whose ancestors are private, and on this host every directory under `/scratch` sits below a root owned `0777` directory, so both stop with `No safe OpenClaw temp root is available`. `config get agents.defaults` on 2026.11.3 prints the merged include values (`userTimezone` from the third include level, `thinkingDefault: "medium"` from the later array entry, `timeoutSeconds: 1200` from the sibling override).

### Tests

Commands run on this branch:

- `pnpm exec vitest run src/config/includes.test.ts src/config/includes.top-level-key.test.ts src/config/include-write-boundary.test.ts src/config/mutate.agent-delete-include.test.ts`: 42 passed on `e65d63e`, including a new test that pins the array concatenation for a file included twice. Both limit tests match the full error text, recovery step included. With the previous message they fail. On main the two new tests fail. The budget test resolves 1025 loads without an error, and the fan-out test runs for 101 s and resolves without an error. On this branch they take 660 ms and 352 ms.
- `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` on the touched files, `git diff --check`: clean.
- `pnpm tsgo:core`: passed.
- `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/check-test-lines-ratchet.mts`: OK at `4e62b0f`, net +34 test lines. `e65d63e` adds 7 test lines (+41), within the 400-line allowance. On `e65d63e`, `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` are clean on the touched files.

prs.title: fix(doctor): diagnose immutable state without pending writes
prs.body:
Related: #178178

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: on macOS, `openclaw doctor` reports "Doctor complete." and exits 0 when the state database is immutable (`chflags uchg`) and no migration is pending. Nothing can write to that database, and Doctor doesn't say so.

## User Impact

User impact: Doctor again reports an immutable or otherwise unwritable state database, with its path and the macOS `chflags nouchg` remedy, and exits unsuccessfully, even when no migration is pending.

Doctor runs during `openclaw update`, so an installation whose state database is immutable or on a read-only mount now gets this diagnosis and a non-zero Doctor exit there too. That's the behavior #178178 intended, and the Gateway can't write state on those installations anyway. Installations with writable state behave exactly as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

The storage diagnosis only fired when some write during the Doctor run happened to fail. Doctor's state admission now checks write access itself: after the existing permission hardening, it opens the existing database read-write without truncating it, then closes it. An immutable file, a read-only mount or an unwritable file now reaches the existing command-boundary diagnosis and recovery guidance. Database contents are untouched. Owned 0444 files are still hardened first, and foreign-owned writable files and unsupported `chmod` still pass. `docs/gateway/doctor/running.md` describes the check.

<details>
<summary>Root cause</summary>

The macOS-only regression `src/commands/doctor-state-storage.test.ts` › "diagnoses an immutable database at the command boundary" (`it.skipIf(process.platform !== "darwin")`, so Linux CI skips it) has failed since 6ce326091a9b (#184245). Until then, the test's plugin fixture caused an incidental state write that hit the immutable file. When the fixture was removed, a current database with no pending migrations finished without ever attempting a write. The test's assertions are unchanged here.
</details>

## Evidence

- End-to-end on macOS, real CLI, isolated state, migration-current database: with the fix, Doctor names the path, gives the `chflags nouchg` remedy and exits 1 with the database bytes unchanged. After `chflags nouchg` it completes with exit 0. With only the new line reverted, it prints "Doctor complete." and exits 0. Transcripts: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/199509#issuecomment-6891457646
- Published driver × candidate: `published-upgrade-survivor` with published `openclaw@2026.11.3` updating to `f4fbc7ca4925` passed (849 s): updater success, candidate Doctor, post-Doctor config validation, seeded state survival, Gateway start and readiness. Fresh install `docker-package-install` passed (84 s) with npm, pnpm, Bun and npm on musl. This was the manual-restart variant; automatic restart and idempotence were not covered.
- Bisect, single case under Node, from 11ad47f0ea86 (#178178, passes) to main: first bad is 6ce326091a9b (#184245). 15 historical runs, none skipped.
- The macOS case, `--maxWorkers=1`:

  | | Node | pinned Bun |
  |---|---|---|
  | before the fix | fail | fail |
  | with the fix | pass | pass |
  | fix reverted | fail | fail |

- Full `doctor-state-storage.test.ts`: 6/6 pass on both runtimes (60.5 s Node, 33.5 s Bun).
- 24 direct-consumer test files: 296/296 pass on both runtimes.
- Targeted lint, both core type-check lanes, formatting, ratchets, MDX validation and commit hooks pass. Independent review is clean.
- Test cost: no new tests. The existing macOS case is unchanged (about 18 s Bun, 53 s Node in single-worker local runs).

### Rebased-head validation

- Rebased without conflicts onto main `786cd278fb1d51e5256b374a654483969242e871`; candidate `045047bac19d912d62b660e3c203b9f238287e58`. `git range-diff` confirms the product patch is unchanged.
- Focused `doctor-state-storage.test.ts` and `doctor-config-preflight*.test.ts` selection: 122 tests across 16 collected files passed under Node and the default pinned Bun runtime. All six storage-diagnosis cases passed on macOS under both runtimes, including the immutable-database regression. Runtime preparation and `git diff --check` passed.
- Codex autoreview of `786cd278fb1d51e5256b374a654483969242e871..045047bac19d912d62b660e3c203b9f238287e58`: scoped-clean through P2, no actionable findings.
- The standard test configuration excludes the opt-in `doctor-config-preflight.legacy-driver.live.test.ts`. An explicit optional invocation stopped in shared live setup before executing tests because the local auth source uses schema 19; no local installation was modified. That optional proof remains a gap. The published-driver evidence above remains prior-head evidence, including its manual-restart limitation.
- Fresh PR CI for this exact candidate: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44852229076

prs.title: fix(agents): long provider error messages stall the Gateway
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: one failed model request whose error message carries a long run of id-like text (letters or digits joined by `-`, `.`, `:` or `/`) freezes the whole Gateway for about 20 seconds and makes that failed turn take 11 to 29 seconds longer.

## User Impact

User impact: a provider, proxy or local model server that answers with a large error body no longer blocks other sessions, channels, the Control UI or `/healthz` while OpenClaw classifies and logs that error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three checks on the provider failure path start with an id-like pattern and then look for a fixed part after it. On a long id-like run without that fixed part, the engine walks to the end of the run from every position in it, so the cost grows with the square of the run length:

- the Ollama retirement check in `isModelNotFoundErrorMessage` (`<id> was retired at <date> ... (ref:`), used by failover classification, error observation and the auth-key rate-limit check
- the same retirement wording in the run failover policy
- the `x-api-key: ...` style header pattern in the diagnostic credential redaction that projects every provider error

The streaming transport reads up to 64 KB of an error body, and one failure classifies and projects the message several times. In the run below the redaction runs on the Gateway main thread, and the retirement checks add their time to the failed turn.

Each check now finds its fixed part first (` was retired at ...`, or the credential header name and its colon) and then looks back over the id or header prefix with the same pattern. They accept exactly the same inputs as before, the redacted text is byte-identical, and each character is scanned a bounded number of times. In the failover policy the retirement wording moves out of the shared alternation into its own check with the same word boundaries.

## Evidence

Gateway from source (`node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs src/entry.ts gateway run`), loopback, `/v1/chat/completions` enabled, with a mock OpenAI-compatible provider on loopback that answers HTTP 400 with the named error message. A separate process requests `/healthz` every 100 ms during the turn.

| Checkout | Provider error message | Turn | Longest `/healthz` wait | Gateway stall report |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| main `cb8c849` | prose control, 64,000 chars | 2.7 s | 77 ms | none |
| main `cb8c849` | `-a` repeated, 64,000 chars | 31.2 s | 20,369 ms | `main-thread stall: elapsedMs=17715 task="gateway:http"`, profile in `redactCredentialText` |
| main `cb8c849` | `a:` repeated, 64,000 chars | 13.8 s | 511 ms | none |
| this branch | prose control | 1.7 s | 109 ms | none |
| this branch | `-a` repeated | 1.8 s | 315 ms | one 324 ms report |
| this branch | `a:` repeated | 1.6 s | 67 ms | none |

The `a:` run leaves the credential header pattern fast (`:` ends its run), so its 11 extra seconds on main come from the retirement checks alone. Each turn made exactly one provider request on both checkouts. The branch rows come from two Gateway runs of the same commit `4175774`.

Rebased on main `fe3df80d15` (2026-11-17) after #200073 and #199234 added tests at the same place in `live-model-errors.test.ts` and `credential-redaction.test.ts`. Both sets of tests are kept, and the source changes are unchanged. The three test files pass (40 tests) on the rebased head.

With only the two retirement checks fixed, the same `-a` turn still blocked `/healthz` for 18.7 s, and the Gateway stall profile pointed at `redactCredentialText` under `projectProviderError`. That is why the credential header pattern is part of this change.

Single calls on a 64,000-character `-a` run:

| Helper | main | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `isModelNotFoundErrorMessage` | 3,915 ms | 2.8 ms |
| `classifyFailoverReason` | 4,151 ms | 43 ms |
| `isApiKeyRateLimitError` | 3,885 ms | 13 ms |
| `buildApiErrorObservationFields` | 7,485 ms | 91 ms |
| `redactDiagnosticText` | 3,737 ms | 45 ms |
| `projectProviderError` | 14,009 ms | 210 ms |

Differential fuzzers compared old and new results on 600,000 random strings per check. The strings mix id characters, spaces, newlines, quotes, partial and complete retirement suffixes, the other model-not-found phrases, and credential header names with and without `x-` style prefixes. They found 0 differences in `.test()` results for both retirement checks and 0 differences in `replace()` output for the header pattern (about 15,000 of those strings were redacted).

Commands run on this branch:

- `pnpm test src/agents/live-model-errors.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/failover-policy.test.ts packages/ai/src/utils/credential-redaction.test.ts packages/ai/src/utils/provider-error.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: all passed. The three new tests fail on main (2,228 ms, 2,375 ms and 17,917 ms against their 500 ms bound) and take a few ms here.
- `pnpm test src/agents/failover-error.test.ts src/agents/failover/failover-classification.corpus.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/assistant-failure.test.ts packages/ai/src/transports/transport-stream-shared.test.ts src/agents/payload-redaction.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 297 passed. These include the existing Ollama retirement fixtures and the provider error redaction consumers.
- `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` on the touched files, `git diff --check`: clean.
- `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:core:test`: passed.
- `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/check-test-lines-ratchet.mts`: OK with the 33-line allocation in `config/test-lines-allocations/provider-error-retired-model-scan.txt`.

prs.title: fix: report invalid PostgreSQL vector dimensions in Doctor
prs.body:
Closes #202761

## What Problem This Solves

PostgreSQL vector search builds its tables and triggers by writing the index's `dimensions` value straight into SQL. Only store admission checks that the value is an integer from 1 to 16000. The same DDL builder also runs on search extension definitions read back from stored schema metadata during schema verification, without that check, so a malformed stored value would become part of the executed DDL.

## User Impact

No change for valid stores: supported dimensions render the same DDL as before. A malformed dimensions value now fails with the existing admission error (dimensions must be from 1 to 16000) instead of producing broken SQL. This is defense in depth; no current path from an untrusted caller is known.

## Why This Change Was Made

A small file-local `postgresVectorDimensions` check now runs in `postgresSearchSql`, the builder that both admission and schema verification use. Admission calls the same check, so the rule and the error message live in one place. `rebuildPostgresSearch` and the vector refresh in `postgres-vector.ts` run only on admitted schemas and keep using the admitted value. Identifiers in these statements were already quoted; dimensions were the only unchecked value.

## Evidence

**Shipped CLI against live PostgreSQL 17.11 with pgvector 0.8.7.** A fresh OpenClaw with `database.engine: "postgres"` creates its stores, then the state store's stored `openclaw_schema_meta.search_extensions` is set to one vector index with `dimensions: 3.5`. `openclaw doctor --non-interactive` then opens that store:

- Base (main b4a41aa642c, fix reverted and rebuilt): the value is rendered into the generated DDL and sent to PostgreSQL. The server rejects it with `invalid input syntax for type integer: "3.5"`, and doctor reports only `current transaction is aborted`.
- Head (eaac48b): doctor reports the admission error, `dimensions must be 1–16000`, before any vector DDL is built.
- Both runs leave no `proof_vectors` table and no scratch verification schema behind.

Other checks:

- Unit test `src/infra/database-engine/postgres-search-schema.test.ts`: 7 pass. 1536 still renders `vector(1536)` and `bit(1536)`; a DDL-fragment string, a numeric string, a fraction, 0, 16001 and NaN are refused. With only the fix reverted (`git apply -R`), 6 of 7 fail.
- PostgreSQL suites `postgres-vector-search-schema`, `postgres-search-admission` and `postgres-search.conformance` pass on the same server version (20 tests), covering 3, 2001 and 16000 dimensions and the binary prefilter DDL.
- Local review: ClawSweeper `review --local-range` at head eaac48b, complete, checkout access verified, no findings, security cleared.
- `pnpm check:changed`: typecheck, lint, format and the other guards pass. The dead export scan reports exports in files this change does not touch (`extensions/knowledge/src/scribes-state.ts`, `test/helpers/fake-model-transports.ts`, `test/prompt-cache-prefix-randomized.test-support.ts`).
- **Current-head CI:** [Run 44850502036](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44850502036) passed on `c47f9e9`, including all five PostgreSQL jobs, both Control UI shards, baseline ratchets, and the required `openclaw/ci-gate`.
- The [original run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44829887273) failed three route asset assertions and lost the baseline runner. Updating the branch brought in the upstream UI fixes (#202694, #202795); the two-file PostgreSQL patch is byte-for-byte unchanged.

<details>
<summary>Runtime output (openclaw doctor, base and head)</summary>

Setup, identical for both builds: throwaway PostgreSQL 17.11 cluster with `vector`, `unaccent` and `pg_trgm`; isolated config and state; config `{"database":{"engine":"postgres","postgres":{"connection":{"source":"env","provider":"default","id":"OPENCLAW_DATABASE_DSN"},"schemaPrefix":"openclaw"}}}`. A first `node openclaw.mjs doctor --non-interactive` on a clean database exits 0 and creates the stores. Then, as the database owner:


prs.title: fix: release completed lease callers and keep input tests portable
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A completed lease heartbeat Worker could retain a previous caller's context through callbacks left on the Worker object. Two closed-stdin admission tests also failed when their IPC synchronization invoked Execa's Node-internal reference-counting methods, despite the child exiting successfully.

## User Impact

Completed heartbeat workers release their caller state explicitly. Lease ownership, expiry, renewal, and shutdown settlement remain unchanged. The input-admission tests keep their existing behavior and cleanup assertions across Node and both Bun runtimes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The heartbeat carrier now removes only the callbacks it owns when a member closes, registration fails, or the worker exits. It adds no waits or timers. The lifetime fixture no longer injects an error after the documented final Worker exit event; its first-loss and exactly-once assertions remain intact.

The closed-stdin fixture uses an extra stdio pipe for its exact `finish` signal, preserving the admission ordering without requiring Execa's private IPC hooks. Production input handling is unchanged. Related runtime support: upstream https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/pull/36405 .

## Evidence

The original failures return when only their corresponding repair is reverted. No assertions were relaxed, and no runtime branches, dependency patches, or retries were added.

| File | IDs | Stock before | Fork | Stock after | Node | Control | Wall seconds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `src/process/exec-input-admission.test.ts` | preserves empty text / empty bytes completion when an admitted child has closed stdin | 2 fail, 12 pass | 14 pass before and after | 14 pass | 14 pass before and after | Original fixture: same 2 failures | Node 27.504 → 26.866; stock after 23.699; fork after 31.000; control 33.093 |
| `src/state/openclaw-state-lease.retention.test.ts` | releases caller state after lease timers are completed-worker | 1 fail, 1 pass | 2 pass before and after | 2 pass | 2 pass before and after | Original carrier: same retained-caller failure | Node 71.736 → 35.049; stock after 109.390; fork after 43.501; control 119.771 |

These are complete wrapper times, including worker compilation and verification, rather than runtime performance comparisons. The one-time listener retirement work measured below 0.7 µs per registration/detachment cycle for all four callbacks, including registration, on each runtime.

The lifetime suite passes 24/24 and startup passes 3/3 on all three runtimes. The native heartbeat suite passes 17 tests on Node and fork (two PostgreSQL connection-gated cases skipped). Stock passes the 16 carrier/lease cases, with the same two skips, but the unchanged SQLite activation fixture fails at its initial `node:module.registerHooks` call before importing the heartbeat worker; stock does not implement that API. Lifetime wrapper wall time was 39.562s before and 24.403s after on Node, 15.105s after on stock, and 18.458s after on fork.

Unchanged stock-runtime investigation failures are recorded rather than hidden: `test/jsdom-compat.test.ts` needs Worker execArgv preloads (upstream https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/pull/42620), and `src/state/openclaw-state-db.wal.test.ts` needs a shared process clock origin. Standalone probes reproduce both differences on stock and pass on Node/fork. Neither file, runtime pin, nor assertion is changed here.

Targeted services/state typechecks, lint, formatting, diff checks, and independent review through P2 pass. Node documents extra stdio pipes at https://nodejs.org/api/child_process.html#optionsstdio and Worker exit as the final event at https://nodejs.org/api/worker_threads.html#event-exit .

prs.title: improve: shorten WAL pins during cold transcript archival
prs.body:
Related: #200076

## What Problem This Solves

Preparing a large cold transcript keeps its read snapshot open while decoding, publishing, syncing, and rereading each archive chunk. This does not block the writer, but it pins the WAL and delays reset, increasing subsequent checkpoint work.

## User Impact

Cold archival releases its read snapshot earlier while producing identical archives. On the existing 50,000-event fixture, median snapshot hold time drops 29.3%, from 4.851 s to 3.429 s. No schema, config, environment, dependency, writer, or hot-to-cold flip changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The snapshot still reads, JSON-encodes, compresses, and hashes every chunk. It retains the compressed buffers alongside the existing metadata. After the snapshot closes, each chunk follows the original decode-verify → publish → file-verify order. Encoding limits, recursive splitting, and pass-budget errors stay inside the snapshot. The writer still performs its existing session revalidation before committing.

A later publication/verification failure rejects preparation and commits nothing. Cleanup ownership is unchanged: `publishEncodedSessionTranscriptArchive` and `trackSqliteArchiveWorkerCleanup` handle staging files. Already-published cold files can remain unreferenced, as explicitly documented in the cold-storage retention contract; ordinary disk-budget pruning does not delete them. There is no existing orphan-chunk sweep to claim or extend here. A retry can reuse identical content-addressed files. No new cleanup or consistency check was added.

Production grows by **6 net lines**: the compressed buffer array, retention, and the post-snapshot loop/comment. The additional benchmark code provides opt-in stage profiling without production instrumentation; the focused regression adds 44 lines.

## Evidence

Acceptance rule, set before measurement: use the existing synthetic 50,000-event / 220,291,661-byte fixture; stop if decode verification, publication, and file verification account for less than 20% of the baseline snapshot. Otherwise compare five alternating baseline/candidate fresh-process runs, requiring shorter snapshot holds and identical chunk SHA-256 values and archive metadata, with memory reported. The OS page cache is warm from the benchmark's existing pre-measurement digest; “cold” describes transcript storage, not a cold filesystem cache.

### Initial breakdown

Baseline `eac1324110867ef3c37f61d00e1c99d967a575fa`; times are milliseconds. The initial measurement used temporary timers around the unchanged statements; the repeat uses the included `--snapshot-profile` loader. Profiling overhead is excluded from the alternating comparison below.

| Inside snapshot | Initial | Reproducible profiler repeat |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Native row reads (including SQLite payload decompression) | 2697.644 | 3353.066 |
| JSON encoding and envelope assembly | 495.803 | 521.578 |
| zstd compression | 63.750 | 65.303 |
| Chunk SHA-256 | 0.769 | 0.796 |
| Decode verification | 558.838 | 585.828 |
| Publication (write/fsync/link/directory sync/internal readback) | 539.497 | 434.554 |
| Separate file verification | 1.512 | 1.674 |
| Other control/schema/query-building/timer overhead | 129.534 | 132.038 |
| **Snapshot total** | **4487.347** | **5094.838** |
| **Movable stages** | **1099.847 (24.51%)** | **1022.056 (20.06%)** |

Both measured runs clear the requested 20% threshold.

### Five alternating pairs, without stage instrumentation

Fresh copies of the same closed fixture; one baseline then one candidate per pair; run serially. Apple M3 Ultra, 512 GiB RAM, Node v26.12.1. Recorded one-minute host load ranged from 19.98 to 33.86, so the observed spread is included.

| Metric | Before median | Before max | After median | After max |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Snapshot hold, ms | 4851.053 | 4904.111 | 3429.372 | 3772.077 |
| Complete preparation, ms | 4899.007 | 4951.498 | 4234.544 | 4616.213 |
| RSS increase from preparation entry to return, MiB | 238.829 | 265.688 | 163.842 | 190.330 |
| Process peak RSS through preparation, MiB | 1109.859 | 1113.438 | 884.000 | 913.297 |

Snapshot samples (before → after, ms): 4851.053 → 3772.077; 4518.085 → 3405.281; 4275.216 → 3241.668; 4904.111 → 3429.372; 4860.802 → 3456.215. With five samples, nearest-rank p95 is the reported maximum.

Peak retained compressed buffers: **1,011,884 bytes (0.965 MiB), 14 chunks**, compared with one chunk at a time before (largest 84,405 bytes). Compression remains inside the snapshot. RSS is measured with `process.memoryUsage().rss` before/after preparation; process peak uses `process.resourceUsage().maxRSS` and includes earlier import/digest work. It is not a heap-allocation measurement.

All ten runs produced exactly equal prepared archive metadata, chunk metadata, and chunk SHA-256 values. Snapshot-only mode fixes `Date.now()` so `archived_at` is also identical. The ordered manifest SHA-256 is `19b27f7b16387c43f64a750d9916ee210489d3c9cd6e0b6fd9d3f868b9a00ed5`; the production publication/verification path validates the actual files.

### Reproduction

```sh
node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/session-cold-writer.mjs --prepare --state-dir <new-seed>
# Use a fresh copy of the seed for each invocation.
node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/session-cold-writer.mjs --snapshot-only --snapshot-profile --source-root <baseline-checkout> --state-dir <fresh-profile-copy>
node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/session-cold-writer.mjs --snapshot-only --source-root <baseline-checkout> --state-dir <fresh-baseline-copy>
node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/session-cold-writer.mjs --snapshot-only --state-dir <fresh-candidate-copy>
```

Validation:

- New regression fails on the baseline because the real snapshot connection still reports an active transaction during the second chunk's verification. It passes with the change, observes the closed snapshot, rejects preparation, preserves the complete transcript snapshot, and leaves both cold archive tables empty.
- Changed chunk suite: 13/13 tests passed (53.68 s Vitest / 60.05 s wrapper including worker build; the new regression itself took 52 ms in the full run).
- All cold-storage test files plus SQLite cold-read coverage: 168 tests passed across 18 files (408.95 s wrapper). The opt-in PostgreSQL selection case then passed separately against a task-owned local PostgreSQL 17 container (1/1, 130.19 s wrapper including worker build). **169 tests passed across all 19 files**, with no remaining skipped case.
- PostgreSQL's first local attempt failed at setup because the fresh database had not enabled `unaccent`. Enabled the documented `unaccent`, `pg_trgm`, and `vector` extensions in that disposable database, then reran successfully. This was a local fixture setup correction, not a product change or CI rerun.
- Core and agents/sessions test typechecks, targeted core/script lint, formatting, and `git diff --check` passed. Initial benchmark lint style errors were fixed before publication.
- **Exact-head CI passed** on `e757d5c6912617c45fdcfb8a05bad1781aa5fe48`: [CI run 44850860418](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44850860418), with `openclaw/ci-gate` also passing. No CI failures or reruns. The changed Node boundary and compact-large lanes took 1m50s and 2m18s respectively (whole-lane costs, not isolated test-file timings). All four PostgreSQL shards and the PostgreSQL 16 smoke lane passed; the slowest shard took 25m45s.

```sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/sessions/session-cold-storage*.test.ts src/config/sessions/session-accessor.sqlite-cold-read.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
node scripts/test-database-conformance.mjs --engine postgres --connection <isolated-local-test-dsn> -- src/config/sessions/session-cold-storage-selection.postgres.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental
node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.agents-sessions.json --incremental
```

Remaining gaps: no production systems accessed, and no Linux/Btrfs benchmark. This synthetic fixture is highly compressible; retained memory scales with the complete compressed transcript size. Already-published orphan files retain the existing documented behavior. No autoreview was run, per task instruction. This handoff leaves the PR ready and unmerged.

prs.title: fix(plugins): tell hooks which turn started the command a completion run reports
prs.body:
Related: #200664, #152204

## What Problem This Solves

When an `exec` call goes to the background (`yieldMs`), its completion later runs as its own agent turn, with `trigger: "event"` and `inputProvenance: { kind: "internal_system", sourceTool: "exec" }`. Plugin hooks on that run have no field naming the turn that started the command. `senderId`, `chatId` and `requesterDeviceId` (#200664) are set only for `trigger: "user"`, so they're absent here.

The trace can't be used to recover the starter either. When the session is busy, the completion runs after the turn that was running when the command finished, and its trace is that turn's trace. A plugin that follows the trace gets the wrong turn.

## User Impact

A plugin that applies a rule per requester, such as gating a tool call on who asked for it, has two bad options on a completion run today. It can treat every completion as unknown, which blocks legitimate follow-up work, or it can guess, which can attribute the work to whoever happened to be talking at the time.

With this change, hooks on that run get `ctx.execRequestOwners`, which names the turn that started the command. Nothing changes for plugins that don't read the field.

## Why This Change Was Made

The host already keeps this ownership. The completion run inherits the starting request's exec owners in `src/infra/exec-request-context.ts`. This change exposes a read-only copy of those records on the hook context and adds no new bookkeeping:

- `readInheritedExecRequestOwners(runId)` returns one frozen `{ runId, sessionKey?, sessionId?, ownerDeviceId? }` entry per inherited owner. `runId` is the run that called the tool, not a later continuation. Owners the run created for its own request are left out. The function returns `undefined`, never an empty array, when the run continues no other request or the run id isn't the current run.
- `buildAgentHookContextIdentityFields` takes `runId` and always adds the field, whatever the trigger. So every agent hook context built through it gets the field without per-builder edits. The CLI runner's prepared hook context passes it along.
- The Codex harness needs no change of its own: its prompt, lifecycle and compaction hooks go through the shared `buildAgentHookContext`, which calls the same identity builder, and its dynamic tools go through the shared `before_tool_call` wrapper. No plugin SDK export is added.
- `before_tool_call` gets the same field through `PluginHookToolContext`.
- The field comes only from the host's exec records, and the array and its entries are frozen. It is ancestry metadata only: the type doc says it grants the run none of the starter's authority or approvals.

## Evidence

Head: 30f02842760. The first commit adds the field. The second follows the first review: it removes the Codex projection and the SDK export, and routes the tests through the shared builder.

**Real model, real exec, busy session.** I built this head's package with `node scripts/package-openclaw-for-docker.mjs` (`OpenClaw 2026.11.5 (30f0284)`) and ran a loopback gateway with `openai/gpt-5.4-mini`. A small plugin logs each hook's `ctx`, and a paired-device operator client sends `chat.send`. Device ids are masked to their last 4 characters.

1. Run A: "Use the exec tool to run exactly: sleep 30; echo a-done -- set yieldMs to 1000 so it keeps running in the background…". The model called `exec`, the command yielded, and run A ended.
2. Run B, sent once A had ended: "Use the exec tool to run exactly: sleep 40; echo b-done -- in the foreground…". This kept the session busy while A's command finished.
3. When B ended, the completion ran as its own turn (`trigger: "event"`, `sourceTool: "exec"`):

```
23:50:03 before_agent_run      real-b-…  user   owners=ABSENT
23:50:47 agent_end             real-b-…  user   owners=ABSENT
23:50:48 before_prompt_build   528f2655… event  exec  owners=[{"runId":"real-a-…","sessionKey":"agent:main:real-busy2","sessionId":"70c717a4","ownerDeviceId":"..73f0"}]
23:50:48 before_agent_run      528f2655… event  exec  owners=[same]
23:50:52 before_agent_finalize 528f2655… event        owners=[same]
23:50:52 agent_end             528f2655… event        owners=[same]

trace ids: run A …595ca, run B …bbb48, completion …bbb48
```

The completion's trace is run B's, and `execRequestOwners` names run A, the run that started the command. The field is absent on A's and B's own hooks.

**Mock model, more cases** (first head 318096fb79e; the agent hook path is the same at this head). With an OpenAI-shaped mock that calls `exec` with `yieldMs: 1000`:

- idle: the completion names its starter on before_prompt_build, before_agent_run, before_tool_call, before_agent_finalize and agent_end;
- busy: same result as the real-model run;
- two overlapping execs: two completion runs, each naming its own starter.

**Unit tests** (`src/plugins/hook-agent-context.test.ts`, 5 new). They cover idle, two overlapping execs, the busy-session case, before_tool_call matching the agent hooks, and absence outside a run.

- On base a4be1ae09e3 with the source changes reverted, 5 fail. The idle, overlap and busy tests fail on the missing field through the existing `buildAgentHookContextIdentityFields` (for example `expected {} to deeply equal { execRequestOwners: [ … ] }`). The other two fail because the tool-context helper is missing.
- On this head, 11 pass.

**Checks on this head:**

- `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:extensions` pass.
- `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` are clean on the changed files.
- `check:test-lines-ratchet`, `check:max-lines-ratchet`, `check:assertion-safety`, `lint:tmp:export-name-collisions` and `lint:tmp:tsgo-core-boundary` pass.
- `pnpm plugin-sdk:api:diff --base a4be1ae09e3 --head HEAD` exits 0 (digest `efb88881`). The change is one optional context field, with no new function export.
- On the first head, every other `lint:tmp:*` script passed, along with `lint:kysely`, `check:database-worker-ratchet`, `check:test-timeout-race-ratchet`, `check:temp-path-guardrails`, `check:database-first-legacy-stores` and `git diff --check`. The second commit touches only the four files above.

## Accepted edge cases

- `after_tool_call` and hooks outside agent runs (`reply_payload_sending`, `message_sending`, `before_dispatch`) don't carry the field. The real run shows this.
- `ownerDeviceId` is left out when the starting connection had no verified paired device, for example a shared-token client with no device identity.
- One completion run that drains two owners returns two entries. The unit test covers this, but in the real run the two overlapping execs completed as two separate runs.
- The subagent-session heartbeat wake (trigger `heartbeat`, `sourceTool: "exec"`), the CLI runner and the Codex harness reach the same shared builders and are covered by types and unit tests. I didn't run them end to end.

prs.title: fix: hide revoked conversations from session recall
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Session recall can return a transcript match after a conversation becomes private or the reader's membership is removed while the search is running. The other session-search routes already check current disclosure facts when publishing their responses.

## User Impact

Recall no longer publishes hits or page metadata from an invalidated sharing snapshot. This does not change the authority lifetime of already-admitted agent or automation work.

## Why This Change Was Made

Publish the complete recall response inside the existing prepared-row callback. Reuse the same visibility decision for worker filtering and final publication, and use the projection's existing sharing revision to discard stale pages and their counts together before one retry. Both Gateway and embedded callers now use that publication boundary.

No new permission policy, manager, cache, schema, or configuration is introduced. A scope that changes again during the retry asks the caller to retry instead of returning stale or partial metadata.

Main was integrated at `949e51dff17c0e1c4cc37f82af8ac5942c0f67e1` to resolve the conflict with merged #201490. Its candidate-batch preparation is preserved inside the shared authorization owner: one preparation per worker batch and one fresh final disclosure snapshot, not per matching key.

## Evidence

The real authenticated WSS Gateway regression fails on the original production code by returning the private transcript snippet after membership removal. It passes with this change and also verifies that the next request remains denied. Authentication, RPC dispatch, transcript search, and sharing writes are real; only the completed worker-read timing is controlled. No model/provider call is needed for this read-only endpoint.

- After conflict resolution, all 75 focused search-scope, inventory-privacy, and embedded-caller/history tests pass, including upstream batch/singleton equivalence across physical owners and both sharing-revocation metadata regressions. The four-file run took 127.21 seconds including compilation.
- The actual WSS membership-revocation test passes again in the documented network-isolated Linux runner (54.04 seconds including transformation). Its complete isolated runtime build also passed (154.1 seconds). The host's automatic runtime-preparation separation check was refused; the supported isolated route was used without bypassing that guard.
- Core, Gateway-method test, agent-tool test, and root E2E TypeScript checks pass; scoped type-aware production lint, test lint, formatting, and diff checks pass.
- Independent Codex autoreview through P2 is `scoped-clean` on the complete integrated candidate against main `949e51dff17c0e1c4cc37f82af8ac5942c0f67e1`, committed unchanged as `3b67c579f6f38f88dfd760b8b5cdb651bc6d410a`. No findings. The reviewer assessed supplied source/evidence; test execution was performed separately. Updated exact-head CI and landing gates remain pending.

- Benchmark caller follow-up for [CI run 44427434900, job 135237801255](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44427434900/job/135237801255): reproduced TS2741 and the actual benchmark's missing-callback runtime failure. The script now supplies the required publication callback and preserves its existing historical `--owner-ref` comparison mode; no production safeguard was made optional. The full scripts typecheck, 15 focused owner tests, type-aware lint and formatting pass. Both current and historical owner ABIs complete five-sample, ten-iteration allocation measurements with independent result assertions; this verifies the measurement path, not a performance-improvement claim. Independent Codex P0–P2 review of this follow-up is `scoped-clean`, committed unchanged as `44db084d25dfc2a12f83fb9ab6db4da224114360`. Updated exact-head CI remains required.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction, prior proof, and scope</summary>

Both native sharing-revocation regressions are red before the repair and green afterward, including stale count/truncation metadata. Initial validation also passed all 60 focused search and embedded-caller/history tests. No production authority behavior changed in this follow-up. Its 28 focused cases and static checks passed, with independent Codex P2 review `scoped-clean` for the delta from `7b1190514ffad1fae3d8d7f790ad25fbfcea42d4`, committed as `d9c6e7fafa396cba683eaecf63299f12dcfccd73`; that repair remains in ancestry unchanged.

`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-methods/sessions-search-scope.test.ts src/agents/tools/embedded-gateway-stub.test.ts src/agents/tools/embedded-gateway-stub.history.test.ts src/agents/tools/sessions-list-privacy.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`

Closes #201438

## What Problem This Solves

<!--

what goes wrong or is missing, and why it matters. For a fix, include the trigger
when known. For other changes, describe the need without inventing a bug.

until you notice and re-enable it."
Bad: "Fixes incorrect operator-authority invalidation on session identity mutation."

Describe the experienced problem, not just the code change. Save function names,
missing checks, and the root-cause walkthrough for the explanation below.
-->

Developers investigating native chat startup delays can measure client receipts, but those timestamps alone cannot locate Gateway and provider work. Background model calls also make one-request-per-chat accounting unreliable, so incomplete or unattributed captures need to fail rather than produce plausible timings.

## User Impact

<!--
"User impact: <what users, operators, or developers can now do or expect>."
Lead with the concrete outcome in plain language, usually one sentence.
For internal-only changes, say there is no user-visible change; do not invent a benefit.
Keep important risks, breaking changes, migrations, and required user actions visible here.
-->

User impact: **there is no user-visible change**. This is opt-in developer tooling for an explicitly owned, isolated synthetic Gateway. It does not launch or reconfigure an installed Gateway, change authentication, or expand operator timing eligibility.

The preload adds unmeasured instrumentation overhead. Its output is diagnostic evidence, not uninstrumented performance or a speedup claim. Self-owned foreground evidence does not establish externally supervised packaged-service behavior.

## Why This Change Was Made

<!--
Briefly explain how the change addresses the problem without repeating the impact.
Keep the body short. Leave file lists, internal acronyms, and root-cause walkthroughs
in the diff or optional <details>; include technical detail only when it explains
behavior or a material tradeoff. Do not hide risks or required actions in <details>.

Combine an authenticated attach-only synthetic driver, a self-contained process-local preload with build/owner qualification, and an offline reducer with the existing mock provider. Captures contain allowlisted synthetic identities, purposes, timing and counts, not prompts, bodies, credentials or generated content.

The reducer requires complete measured chains and reconciles every Responses request with a measured or purpose-tagged background call. Unexplained requests, retries, loss, HTTP errors and incomplete measured shutdown fail explicitly. Embeddings remain separately counted without invented ownership or latency; background completion after 2xx headers remains unverified.

The author simplification pass retained this as one coherent developer-tooling stage: capture and producer accounting cannot safely land without their strict reducer and rejection controls. No production timing seam, new runtime registration or default instrumentation was added. The full diff adds 2,200 lines and removes two. The explicit 362-line allocation covers 762 net test lines beyond the 400-line default; those cases protect distinct capture, emitted-binding, request-accounting, lifecycle and rejection boundaries.

## Evidence

<!--

terminal output, focused tests, CI results, live observations, redacted logs,
and artifact links are all useful. For visual web/macOS/iOS/Android changes, follow

https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/.agents/skills/openclaw-pr-maintainer/references/media.md#pr-visual-proof

or optional <details>. Keep the useful evidence summary and meaningful gaps visible.

Focused proof passes all 38 tests across three files, including actual opt-in mock HTTP accounting and a real Node preload subprocess. Negative controls reject unknown extra traffic, retry identities, mismatched windows/instances, lost events, incomplete measured chains, HTTP errors, wrong shutdown targets and missing main completion. Emitted-owner regressions exercise renamed bindings, shadowed callback parameters, unchanged results, unsupported declarations and duplicate anchors.

**Current-head behavior proof also passes:** a disposable source-built Gateway processed one authenticated `gateway-client/ui` turn through the mock provider. The unchanged reducer accepted **two Responses requests: one measured and one explicitly attributed session-activity summary**, plus one separately counted embedding. The actual loaded owner hashes match the qualified build.

The exact-target shutdown was scheduled, the main capture exited 0 with all eight anchors and zero dropped events, unclassified identities or write failures, and all six captured Node PIDs were observed stopped before final producer accounting. The orchestrator also observed its CLI wrapper exit 0 but did not retain that wrapper's PID. The main-process claim rests on its authenticated stop target, capture-end, captured chain `40652 -> 15944 -> 56560`, and observed-gone PIDs, not a fully linked launcher tree.

The run retained a boolean `listenerClosed` observation. A separate later socket recheck, recorded at `2026-11-18T22:01:23.062Z`, returned `ECONNREFUSED`; that error code was not recorded by the original run. Helper `native-chat-33760.jsonl` never wrote `capture-end`; it was observed gone and excluded only from the exhaustively accounted main-process Responses scope. This does not certify its clean exit, whole-process-tree completeness or embedding ownership.

Validated head: `6fdf5abb9fef568d12029f90c8ef2ac70ef8b2fa`, based on `b400e8deed133ac0fa084072424fe1285f162952`, on Windows ARM64 / Node 26.13.0 / pinned pnpm 12.15.0. Two independent Copilot subagent code reviews covered the original base-to-candidate change and separately reviewed the emitted-owner correction against actual compiled owners at P0-P2, reporting no significant issues. They also reviewed the real capture evidence; two provenance-accuracy items were corrected as disclosed above. Codex CLI was unavailable; these were narrative reviews, not the shared helper's isolated/frozen-input machine result.

<details>
<summary>Exact local commands and results</summary>

<details>
<summary>Executed real Gateway capture, accounting and cleanup</summary>

The ordinary source CLI owner was `node scripts/run-node.mjs gateway run --bind <loopback> --port <task-port>` (the implementation of the package's `openclaw` script). prs.title: fix(android): finish setup after node access is approved
prs.body:
Closes #201481

## What Problem This Solves

Android setup can remain on “Approve node access” after the phone has already been approved. With Camera enabled, Gateway policy can admit the capability and permission while withholding capture commands; setup incorrectly waits for those commands. Background refreshes also make the exact approval command flicker and fall back to a literal `REQUEST_ID`.

## User Impact

Users should be able to finish setup once their enabled capabilities and permissions are approved, without requiring commands the Gateway deliberately disallows. The recovery screen keeps a known request ID stable during reads and only shows an exact approve command when an ID exists.

**Draft: not yet built, installed, or verified on a phone.** The affected user’s recovery is not confirmed. No Gateway policy, pairing, authentication, or command permission is changed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Separate onboarding capability readiness from policy-owned command admission. Explicit in-app approval still verifies the entire actual pending surface, approved/connected state, authority, and request identity. Preserve the previous approval snapshot during refresh, retire exact IDs on failed reads or connection invalidation, and preserve ID-less pending states so polling can recover after repeated failures. A manual check can continue from verified readiness even if Compose never observes a very short refreshing state.

## Evidence

- Live observation with Android 2026.11.40 / Gateway 2026.11.4: phone connected and approved, no pending request, Camera capability and permission present, but `camera.snap`/`camera.clip` absent from admitted commands. The same filtering occurs before the pairing request is stored. No private device identifiers or setup credentials are included here.
- Added regression coverage for policy-filtered Camera commands, retention of request IDs during reads, consecutive failed reads followed by recovery, and nullable recovery commands/manual-check readiness. Extended the existing WebSocket/Compose onboarding test rather than recreating the screen.
- Independent read-only review found a repeated-failure polling defect in the initial patch; addressed with a runtime-boundary regression. Follow-up found no remaining P0–P2 issues in the reviewed diff. Canonical shared autoreview tooling was unavailable; this was direct independent review, not an autoreview run.
- `git diff --check`: passed.
- Android compilation and focused tests: **blocked before execution** by missing Android SDK (`SDK location not found`). Gradle/JDK and pinned source dependencies were prepared, but no SDK/emulator or attached adb device is available in this environment. No remote Android build capacity is provisioned.
- `./gradlew :app:ktlintCheck --no-daemon --max-workers=2`: passed after fixing the reported style violations (21 actionable tasks). This is formatting/lint proof, not Android compilation or behavioral test proof.
- Required clean and annotated before/after native UI captures: **missing** for the same device/emulator gap. Red/green runtime proof is also outstanding. Keep draft until the exact head passes the required build/tests and visual-proof gates. Automatic PR CI may skip drafts; a maintainer or qualified Android runner must supply exact-head proof before ready/merge.

Intended focused validation from `apps/android`:

```sh
./gradlew :app:testPlayDebugUnitTest \
  --tests ai.openclaw.app.GatewayNodeApprovalTest \
  --tests ai.openclaw.app.GatewayDevicePairingRuntimeTest.nodeRefreshKeepsIdsDuringReadsAndRecoversAfterRepeatedFailures \
  --tests ai.openclaw.app.ui.OnboardingFlowLogicTest \
  --tests ai.openclaw.app.ui.InitialOnboardingLayoutTest.nativeNodeApprovalWaitsForCameraButNotPolicyBlockedCaptureCommands \
  :app:ktlintCheck --no-daemon --max-workers=2
```

prs.title: fix: keep unused Code Mode lookups from tainting memory
prs.body:
Closes #196857

## What Problem This Solves

Unused Code Mode tool lookups could mark an entire turn as external content and quarantine session-memory snapshots. At the same time, the host memory-write observer missed Code Mode’s per-result provenance and could leave genuinely consumed external metadata trusted.

## User Impact

Unused discovery no longer makes later owner-requested memory writes untrusted. Consumed or emitted external metadata, MCP declarations, and network tool results retain their existing provenance protections. Previously quarantined files are not reclassified; there is no migration or configuration change.

## Why This Change Was Made

Code Mode returns lazy callable handles, so its guest already records when external metadata is read or serialized. Stop eagerly marking unused search hits, and forward the existing per-result provenance to the host’s memory-taint observer instead of looking only at static tool metadata. Ordinary Tool Search, execution, stored-value provenance, and memory classification policy are otherwise unchanged.

## Evidence

- Reproduced unused-search turn taint on base c5ef395ba7204c83240074b584e97f550a3aab7d. Isolated real-model Gateway testing also exposed the host observer’s missing dynamic provenance; the production-wrapper memory regression fails on consumed descriptions, emitted handles, and declarations until that observer is fixed.
- The same memory regression passes with the fix; reading a description (even when discarded), returning a handle, and reading a declaration still produce untrusted memory.
- Focused suites: 78 tests passed across Agent-loop, Code Mode output, Tool Search metadata, and network-error provenance suites. Changed test file: 26 tests, 16.51 seconds wall time (CI timing pending).
- Core and affected test typechecks, targeted lint, formatting, changed-page MDX, and `git diff --check` passed. Full `pnpm build` passed (2m 58s), followed by a final `pnpm build:runtime` (1m 8s); it reported non-fatal Control UI asset-budget warnings in unchanged UI code.
- An isolated Gateway with a real agent, provider model, and loopback MCP server verified both paths with zero MCP tool executions: unused discovery produced `agent` memory; consuming the external description produced fenced output and `untrusted` memory. The Gateway, sockets, and temporary state were cleaned up. Live test: 36.65 seconds wall time.
- Local autoreview (P0–P2) of the final pre-commit snapshot against c5ef395ba7204c83240074b584e97f550a3aab7d: scoped-clean, no actionable findings. The committed patch at 5be12feb75a3ad2fc65c415e187fc8104eaa6606 is byte-identical to that reviewed snapshot. The reviewer inspected the supplied source context but did not rerun tests.

Simplification: remove the duplicate eager observation and reuse the existing internal result-source fact. No new state, owner, public option, trust exception, or provenance mechanism. Production delta: +8/-3 lines; tests: +91/-2; docs: +7. The small production growth forwards the existing source fact into the memory observer.

## Contributor credit

Reported by @Ricardodpalmeida. Fix requested and directed by @vincentkoc.

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Original discussion with @vincentkoc](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/subagent/f302039d-42df-481f-8864-d448f956f8bd)

## Worked on by

- @vincentkoc

prs.title: fix: explain how to call deferred tools after a direct call
prs.body:
Closes #186716

## What Problem This Solves

A model that calls a deferred tool directly in structured Tool Search mode gets only “Tool <name> not found,” even though the tool is available through discovery. That gives it no actionable way to recover in the same turn.

## User Impact

The embedded harness now tells the model to call `dispatch_action` with the tool name in `id` and its parameters in `args`. The rejected direct call does not execute or expose the tool. Unknown, filtered, ambiguous, and exact-ID-only names keep their existing behavior. No configuration, defaults, permissions, executor, or native-harness behavior changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing deferred-tool resolver was installed only for Code Mode and directory mode. It now also handles recovery when the structured dispatcher is actually registered, using the same current catalog lookup and returning guidance before tool adaptation.

The resolver moves intact into one named execution-boundary module so the capped preparation source and test suite do not grow past their limits. Code Mode guidance and directory hydration retain their existing owner and hooks; there is no second execution path or new state. Simplification pass: production +39 net lines (mostly the extracted boundary’s typed input), regression +85 lines, documentation +3 lines.

## Evidence

- Before the fix, the production-wired agent-loop regression received `Tool probe_write not found` instead of dispatcher guidance. The final focused regression verifies the guidance, no direct execution or provider exposure, unchanged filtered/unknown rejection, and exactly one real file write through `dispatch_action`.
- Final resolver and preparation suites: 27 tests passed. The new suite took 11.60 seconds including imports/transforms; the two-shard command took 51.79 seconds including cold worker preparation.
- Tool Search selection and prompt-prefix stability suites: 37 tests passed.
- Full `pnpm build` passed again at published head `db16310f5ddf9086622cca30a0a63e5e56357c30` (1m 47.9s; clean build inputs). Core production and agents-other test typecheck leaves passed.
- Targeted lint, formatting, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Independent autoreview of the complete local candidate against `c5ef395ba7204c83240074b584e97f550a3aab7d`, with the catalog, agent loop, and client-tool assembly supplied as context: GPT-6.1 Sol, P0–P2, scoped-clean; no actionable findings. The reviewer did not run tests. Hosted ClawSweeper also reported no actionable patch findings at the published head.
- The [exact-head CI gate passed](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44411080008/job/135186193541).

### Real isolated Gateway recovery proof

Passed at the published head through the repository's compiled Gateway test lane, using `createOpenClawTestInstance`, its standard authenticated synthetic test client, and a local scripted model provider. This exercises the actual Gateway and embedded agent; it is not a live third-party-model test.

The provider first emitted a direct `sessions_list` call. It received the recovery error, followed that guidance with `dispatch_action`, and received the real session-list result. The target remained absent from all three provider tool declarations, and the turn completed without rerouting:

```text
head: db16310f5ddf9086622cca30a0a63e5e56357c30
provider requests: 3
sessions_list declared directly: [false, false, false]
dispatch_action declared: [true, true, true]
direct result: Tool sessions_list is deferred and not directly callable. Call dispatch_action with id "sessions_list" and its parameters in args.
dispatch result: count=1
terminal status: ok
terminal reply: PROOF_DONE
rerouted: false
```

The Gateway proof took 7.064 seconds; its test lane completed in 14.56 seconds including preparation. Earlier source-only startup and operator-CLI attempts hit worker-ownership and attribution guards. The standard compiled synthetic test fixture supplied the successful proof without disabling either safeguard. The previous end-to-end verification gap is resolved; no source push or CI rerun was needed.

Thanks to @xyrolle for the report and proposed recovery approach in #186718, and @vincentkoc for requesting the repair.

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

prs.title: fix: keep invited collaborators from loosening your session's guardrails or approving your commands
prs.body:
Related: #201526 (part D)

## What Problem This Solves

When you invite someone into a session (a role with `sessions.others: "invited"` plus a session membership), they could change its permission mode to something looser than you set, for example from **Ask me** to **Auto-review**, and approve shell commands your own turns were waiting on. Inviting a collaborator could quietly remove the guardrails you chose.

## User Impact

User impact: **only invited collaborators are affected.** For someone whose access to a session comes from an invitation:

- **Permission mode is tighten-only.** They can tighten it but not loosen it or reset it to the default.
- **Approvals are their own.** They can only see and resolve approvals raised by their own turns.

**Everyone else keeps exactly the behavior on `main`:** the session creator, admins, teammates whose role grants `sessions.others` `view`/`suggest`/`write`, unprofiled paired devices, non-admin iOS approvers and their pushes, sessionless and node approvals, history from deleted sessions, and older sessions with no recorded creator. These rules only ever *add* a restriction for invitees; they never replace an existing device, reviewer or custody check.

## Why This Change Was Made

This is the scoped version chosen after an audit showed the earlier global version changed behavior for team roles, iOS approvers, unprofiled devices and sessionless approvals. Invited access is decided from the resolved Gateway profile role policy plus actual session membership (the profile role is the single authority since #201610), so it applies the same way whether the invitee arrives through OpenClaw ID, Cloudflare Access or a trusted proxy.

Permission-mode changes are checked once, by the shared session patch owner, so the single and bulk RPC, tool, create-adoption and reset paths follow the same rule. Approvals record which profile's turn raised them; a schema 41 migration (SQLite and PostgreSQL) adds the nullable `requested_by_profile_id` column with no backfill. Only invitees consult it.

## Evidence

**Compatibility matrix (written first, red on the previous head, now green):** a real-Gateway matrix of 137 cells. Rows: creator, admin, team `view`/`suggest`/`write`, invited collaborator (with `operator.write`, and with `operator.approvals`), unprofiled non-admin device, non-admin iOS approver, sessionless/node approval, deleted-session history, legacy owner session with no creator. Columns: loosen mode, reset to default, tighten mode, list/get/resolve another person's approval, list/resolve own approval, push eligibility. 41 cells failed against the previous global head; all 137 pass now. Every non-invitee cell matches `main`.

**Call sites:** 30 production paths were classified (session permission authorization, patch/create/reset, approval lookup/list/get/wait/resolve, generic approval records, history, events, web and iOS push). Each either applies the invite-only deny filter or keeps main's check unchanged.

Local verification on this head:
- Migration and conformance: 42 tests, including real PostgreSQL 17.12 and SQLite v40→v41.
- Core approval 31, review regressions 25, repaired fixtures 20, workspace policy 18, live Gateway 3.
- Production typecheck and all four Gateway test-type scopes; lifetime, test-lines and line-cap ratchets; database-worker ratchet 166→166.
- Two independent reviews; the runtime findings from the first were fixed, the second found no P0–P2 issues.

Not certified locally (bounded runs timed out during compilation/teardown on this host), so CI is the authority for: the wider approval consumer sweep, the plugin-approval routing E2E, and the final typed-lint subset.

**Test-line allocation:** recorded in `config/test-lines-allocations/201526-session-member-authority.txt` for the real-Gateway matrix and approval boundary coverage; these are new security behaviors with no existing tests to extend.

<details><summary>Commands</summary>

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  src/gateway/server.invite-scope-matrix.test.ts \
  src/gateway/server.session-member-authority.test.ts \
  src/gateway/server.sessions.create.workspace-policy.test.ts \
  --maxWorkers=1
```

Plus the approval, push, persistence, migration (SQLite and PostgreSQL) and generated-schema suites.

</details>

**CI on the final head (`d2ed75fa`, run 44819517110):** landed with these failures, none caused by this PR:
- `checks-node-changed-compact-large-19`: `src/agents/mcp-config-mutation.test.ts` (keep/replace custody) fails identically on `main` `f6298a19`.
- `checks-node-compact-small-5` and `-12`: runner apt setup failed (ondrej/php PPA label change) before any test.
- `android-access-native (4096, google_apis)`: emulator could not load the SDK `devices.xml` before any test.
- `checks-ui-e2e (2/4)`: skills and skill-settings asset-request bounds. `ui/` is unchanged by this PR and the shard passed on the previous head.
- `ios-screenshots`: `testReleaseChatScreenshot`. `apps/ios/` is unchanged by this PR and the job passed on the previous head with the same Swift change.
- `Intersect shared OpenClawKit dead code` (not required): flags two UI declarations this PR doesn't reference.

Proof limits: the packaged upgrade proof ran on `c115c774`, not the final head, and there is no live shipped-Gateway/real-model run.

prs.title: feat: prepare restricted connections for Session Share steering
prs.body:
Supersedes #201173 and #202627. Builds on #202397.

## What Problem This Solves

A remote publication integration needs a narrowly scoped transport for steering, without granting its device a human identity or general chat/admin access. A genuine person also needs to discover the exact active backend before submitting an active-only correction.

## User Impact

User impact: operators can opt into a restricted, signed-device writer transport. It only admits `session-share.steer.target` and `session-share.steer.send` when the Session Share plugin registers those handlers with the matching scope. This PR does not implement those source handlers or enable any live configuration.

`gateway.sessionControl.publicationWriteEnabled` defaults off. Each new request, including retries, passes admission; disabling denies new requests but does not revoke admitted work. Work admitted immediately before disable may still deliver. `gateway.sessionControl.steeringEnabled` separately gates genuine-person host target discovery and active steering. Publication reader access remains independent and its current epoch behavior is deliberately unchanged for a separate correction (#202636).

A correctly paired device that connects while its purpose is off now gets `publication transport is disabled; enable gateway.sessionControl.publicationReadEnabled` (or `publicationWriteEnabled`) and the handshake failure reason `publication-transport-purpose-disabled`. Before, both the reader and the writer reported a token requirement the device already met. A caller whose token, scopes or pairing do not validate still gets the credential error and learns nothing about the switch.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared transport owner preserves signed singleton device tokens, exact plugin/method ownership, minimal hello/tick disclosure, current device grants, and no human fallback. `sessions.steerTarget` uses the same personal session-write authority and physical controller as `sessions.steerActive`. Discovery does not inject input; replacement, idle and unsupported backends cannot become implicit new runs. Accepted/indeterminate steering retains the original message ID; retries reconcile, never replay under a new key.

Writer and steering revocation-generation machinery and obsolete writer off/on test variants are absent. Reader-only revocation tests remain with the unchanged reader contract. The admission function throws one typed error with a closed reason (`purpose-disabled` or `invalid-admission`); the disabled reason is raised only after the device identity validates.

## Evidence

- Head `3d45ff7e083898e1fd3ed0b1a2a4ee371cc250b7` merges main `b4a41aa642ce` into the reviewed work. The PR's own patch is the patch reviewed on #202627 at `427a4db1339a` plus one commit, `c2838a35a9d` (typed disabled-purpose error, table-driven handshake assertion, contract comment). The only merge conflict was `docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256`, regenerated with `pnpm config:docs:gen` on a Blacksmith Testbox (`tbx_01m7x9k05js7c5ak90855rb5kk`) against the merged tree.
- Same Testbox run: `pnpm test src/gateway/server.auth.publication-reader.test.ts` passed, 49 tests and 2 intentional reader-only skips, 257.71s. This suite drives real signed WebSocket handshakes for both scopes, including the disabled-purpose message for each.
- Implementer proof before the merge, on the pre-merge tree: 107 focused Gateway, steering, retry, rotation and schema tests; the `gateway-methods` and `gateway-server` typecheck lanes; typed lint; formatting; import-cycle checks. Not rerun by hand on the merged head; hosted CI on this head is the proof for it.
- Against main `b4a41aa642ce`: production +358/-148 (net +210), tests +755/-434, docs +48, generated +2036/-2026 (protocol predicates and config baseline). Production growth is the restricted writer transport, exact-backend discovery and the typed handshake outcome; the existing publication owner file was extended, not duplicated.
- Config surface: one new default-off key, `gateway.sessionControl.publicationWriteEnabled`, and one new operator scope, `operator.session-share.steer`. No existing key, default or scope changes. Named enablement path: `docs/gateway/protocol/rpc-session-control.md`.

Sibling Codex inspected at `4b0d9669cc46ba97bf85fa6312431b630d80498d` by the implementer and at `a6fdb11eda9` during review: `codex-rs/core/src/session/turn_input.rs:624-706` checks once under the active-turn lock and queues; `codex-rs/app-server/src/turn_admission.rs:35-64` refuses new turn starts on drain and lets admitted ones finish. This PR follows the same request-start rule.

Limits: the signed-WSS suite uses real handshakes against an in-process Gateway with fixture devices; there is no live native-model delivery proof. The Session Share plugin handlers for the two writer methods are not in this PR, so the writer transport is exercised only with test-registered handlers. No Swift changes and no live configuration, enablement, deployment or restart.
